William Crimsworth, after a month fruitlessly searching Brussels for his dismissed pupil Frances Henri, discovers her mourning at her aunt's fresh grave in the Protestant Cemetery, escorts her home through a storm, shares tea in her spartan lodgings, and privately resolves to win her as his wife.

William Crimsworth, disgusted by Pelet's drunken jealousy and the impending marriage of Pelet and Zoraide Reuter, resigns his position on moral grounds, choosing destitution over the temptation of remaining under the same roof as a woman still infatuated with him.

William receives two letters—Frances Henri's joyful news of a new teaching post and Hunsden's mocking announcement of his Brussels visit—and, agonized that his own dismissal and poverty bar him from proposing to Frances, resolves to seek a job recommendation from M. Vandenhuten (whose son he once rescued from drowning), only to find the family absent from town.

Having quit Pelet's pensionnat after Zoraide's marriage, William suppresses his longing for Frances, endures Hunsden's mocking visit and learns of Edward's financial ruin and sale of Crimsworth Hall, then discovers Hunsden secretly sent him his mother's portrait rescued from the auction, and finally secures a Brussels college professorship through Vandenhuten's recommendation.

William visits Frances, reads her revealing love poetry, impulsively proposes marriage which she accepts on condition she keeps her teaching post, then returns home and suffers nine days of hypochondria.

William Crimsworth brings Yorke Hunsden to meet Frances Henri; Hunsden—shocked William would marry a mere lace-mender—spars with her in a heated debate on English and Swiss national character before departing grudgingly impressed by her spirit and intelligence.

William and Frances marry, build a thriving school in Brussels over ten years, then retire to an English country home near Hunsden's estate, where their domestic happiness, Frances's dual role as wife and school directress, and the upbringing of their intense son Victor are described in the novel's closing retrospect.

Testi/Bronte/Atomized/The_Tenant_of_Wild.plot: Gilbert Markham, narrator and gentleman farmer, introduces his family and local society, then recounts neighborhood excitement over the mysterious Mrs. Graham who has taken up solitary residence at ruined Wildfell Hall, culminating in Gilbert's first charged glimpse of her at church.

Gilbert Markham, hunting on the moors, catches Mrs. Graham's young son who falls from Wildfell Hall's garden wall; she reacts with alarmed suspicion before recognising him, then coldly dismisses him, and he retreats to Eliza Millward's company to soothe his wounded pride.

Mrs. Graham (Helen Huntingdon) pays her first call at Linden-Car, where she clashes sharply with Gilbert Markham and his mother over child-rearing: she defends shielding young Arthur from vice while Gilbert argues virtue requires exposure to temptation, and Helen exposes the hypocrisy of applying different moral standards to boys and girls.

At the Markham family's November 5th party — from which Mrs. Graham (Helen) is conspicuously absent — neighbors gossip about her unconventional method of teaching her son to despise alcohol; Mr. Lawrence defends her approach in a debate with the vicar; and Gilbert's mother reprimands him for flirting with Eliza Millward.

Gilbert and Rose visit Helen's studio at Wildfell Hall, where Helen paints under a false name to hide her whereabouts, a mysterious man briefly appears at the window, and Gilbert discovers a face-down hidden portrait that Helen sharply reclaims before they part on uneasy but cordial terms.

Over several months Gilbert repeatedly seeks out Mrs. Graham on the moors, befriends her son Arthur, and finds himself increasingly drawn to her; after a charged encounter by the brook and a sparring exchange with Lawrence about his interest, he returns home to a domestic debate with his mother and Rose on marriage and gender duty.

Gilbert Markham joins neighbors visiting Wildfell Hall, then accompanies Mrs. Graham (Helen) and a mixed party on a coastal picnic excursion to the cliffs, during which his attraction to her deepens as he seeks her company and sketches beside her, while neglecting Eliza Millward.

Gilbert Markham visits Wildfell Hall with a copy of "Marmion" as a gift for Mrs. Graham, who refuses it to avoid obligation, sparking a tense exchange that ends with her accepting the book on her own terms and their friendship cautiously reaffirmed.

At a neighbourhood party, Gilbert witnesses guests spreading slander about Mrs. Graham's character and suspected connection to Mr. Lawrence; he defends her silently, steals a private garden conversation with her and her son Arthur, then ends the evening in furious hostility toward Lawrence, whom he now suspects of concealed designs on her.

Gilbert visits Wildfell Hall, shares a near-romantic garden encounter with Helen who firmly confines him to friendship and hints at a secret vow, then confronts Lawrence on the lane, accusing him of duplicity toward her.

Gilbert defends his friendship with Helen (Mrs. Graham) against his sister Rose's warnings about village gossip, then the vicar arrives to report he has formally rebuked Helen for scandalous conduct, enraging Gilbert who storms out and heads to Wildfell Hall.

Gilbert visits Helen at Wildfell Hall, confesses love and urges her to clear her name by uniting with him, but she defers her secret confession to the next day; when Gilbert lingers and spies through the garden wall he sees Helen walking intimately with Mr. Lawrence, plunging him into a paroxysm of jealous despair.

Gilbert, brooding and ill-tempered after his disillusionment about Mrs. Graham, forces himself to tend to farm business at Ryecote Farm, endures spiteful mockery from Eliza and Miss Wilson, then deliberately turns away to avoid a chance hillside encounter with Mrs. Graham and her son, leaving him doubly miserable.

Gilbert, consumed by jealous rage, strikes Lawrence with a whip-handle during a chance road encounter, leaves him injured on the ground, then discovers Lawrence chooses not to report the assault — apparently to protect Mrs. Graham's reputation.
Gilbert confronts Helen in a tense standoff over what he overheard; she refuses to explain but finally thrusts her private diary into his hands to read as her defense.

Young Helen, back from her first London season, recounts her aunt's warnings about imprudent marriage, her charming first encounter with Huntingdon at a ball, and her firm rejection of the tedious suitor Boarham's proposal.

At a dinner party Helen watches Huntingdon flirt with Annabella, is rescued by him from an unwanted suitor, nearly hears his declaration before her aunt intervenes, then endures a long lecture warning her against a man of poor character — but she resolves to love and reform him regardless.

Huntingdon arrives for a shooting party at Helen's uncle's estate, discovers her secret portrait sketches of him, provokes her into burning the miniature in anger, then coldly redirects his flirtations to Annabella Wilmot while playing both her and Lord Lowborough, leaving Helen consumed by jealousy and regret.

Stung by Huntingdon's public slight in favour of Annabella's singing, Helen weeps alone in the library; Huntingdon follows, declares his love, and proposes; her aunt interrupts and defers approval to the next day.

Young Helen accepts Arthur Huntingdon's marriage proposal through her uncle while sparring with her aunt over Arthur's character and engaging in a scriptural debate on universal salvation versus eternal damnation.

Helen's engagement to Huntingdon is fixed for Christmas; Milicent and Annabella respond with doubt and veiled rivalry, while Huntingdon relays his bachelor friends' bitter complaints that the marriage will end their dissolute brotherhood.

During a riding party, Huntingdon recounts Lowborough's ruin through gambling and drink and casually reveals that Annabella (Miss Wilmot) privately confessed to despising Lowborough while courting him for his title; Annabella then announces her engagement to Helen, and Helen weeps over Huntingdon's moral callousness rather than the deceived lord.

Eight weeks into marriage, Helen confides in her diary that Arthur is selfish and superficial — he rushed their honeymoon and now demands she subordinate her religious devotion to him — while she argues back that true love of God deepens rather than diminishes earthly love.
Helen and Arthur quarrel after he boasts of past affairs; she maintains cold reserve for two days until his contrition breaks the standoff and they reconcile, agreeing to travel to London together.

Helen records months of anxious solitude at Grassdale after Arthur sends her home from London under pretense of business, learns Milicent Hargrave has been coerced into marrying Hattersley, and finally receives Arthur back debauched and exhausted—then nurses him to health while he plans a shooting party including Lord Lowborough, Annabella, and Walter Hargrave.

Helen suppresses jealousy as Annabella and Huntingdon openly flirt while Lord Lowborough suffers visibly; the party then visits the Grove where Helen silently condemns Mrs. Hargrave's social-climbing hypocrisy and its toll on her daughters.

Helen catches Arthur openly flirting with Annabella, confronts him that night and extracts a half-hearted promise to stop, then endures Annabella's cold taunting during a private exchange the next morning.

Helen's diary entries spanning two Christmases record her deepening disillusionment with Arthur's self-indulgent character, his refusal to take her to London, his months-long absence, and her bitter conclusion that she can never trust his word.

During Arthur's prolonged dissipated absence in London, Walter Hargrave returns to the neighbourhood and makes repeated sympathetic visits to Helen, who holds him at a guarded distance while learning from him that Arthur has been deliberately deceiving her about his planned return date.

Helen endures Arthur's debauched return home, restrains his drinking with Hargrave's covert help, watches him depart to Scotland and return briefly improved, yet dreads the approaching spring and his likely relapse.

Helen records a series of disgraceful autumn house-party evenings in which Arthur and his companions drink themselves into chaos, Hattersley physically brutalises Lord Lowborough and Milicent, Annabella shows cold contempt for her husband, and Helen endures it all in silent despair.

Helen and Milicent discuss Esther's future and their own unhappy marriages; Hattersley bluntly reveals his indifference to Milicent while praising Annabella; Helen confronts him about his cruelty; then Hargrave attempts to disclose an alarming secret about Huntingdon, which Helen refuses to hear.

Helen discovers Arthur's affair with Annabella by witnessing them together in the shrubbery, then confronts Arthur and declares their marriage a name-only arrangement after he refuses to let her leave with their child.

Helen confronts Annabella Lowborough privately about her affair with Huntingdon, refuses to expose her to Lord Lowborough or Milicent, and urges her to leave the house, while privately recording her hatred of her husband and wariness of Hargrave's calculated sympathy.

On the eve of the guests' departure, Helen endures Annabella's provocations and Arthur's open flirtation, repels Hargrave's advances in the library, and disciplines her fury through forced composure until the party leaves the next morning.

Helen records the cold, hostile coexistence with Arthur over three years of marriage: he drinks, mocks her, flaunts Annabella's love letter, and undermines her authority over their son, leaving Helen resolved to endure through faith alone.

Helen's diary recounts Walter Hargrave's persistent, escalating attempts to seduce her during Arthur's absences; she rejects him each time with moral firmness, ultimately giving him an ultimatum to stay silent or leave, and he departs for Paris.

Lord Lowborough discovers his wife Annabella's two-year affair with Huntingdon, confronts Helen for concealing it, refuses Hattersley's offer to arrange a duel, spends a near-suicidal night resisting self-destruction, then departs with Annabella at dawn while Huntingdon jeers.

Helen resolves to flee Grassdale with her son to escape Huntingdon's debauchery, secretly paints to raise funds; Hargrave makes a forced declaration which she rejects, then Huntingdon publicly accuses her of infidelity, and she compels Hargrave to clear her name before the men.

Arthur Huntingdon reads Helen's secret diary, discovers her escape plan, destroys her painting materials, confiscates her money and valuables, and reduces her to a small allowance, leaving her feeling utterly imprisoned and despairing of rescuing her son.

With her husband temporarily absent, Helen systematically conditions young Arthur against alcohol, negotiates a secret refuge plan with her brother Frederick, and counsels Esther Hargrave to resist a coerced marriage.

Helen shows Hattersley his wife Milicent's anguished letters to shame him into reforming his dissolute ways; he vows amendment and reconciles emotionally with Milicent, while Arthur Huntingdon remains absent and unreformed.

Helen, having discovered Huntingdon's governess Miss Myers is his mistress, secretly prepares flight with son Arthur and faithful servant Rachel, writes farewell letters to friends and family, and on the eve of departure records her final night at Grassdale before escaping under the alias Mrs. Graham.

Helen's diary records her predawn flight from Grassdale with son Arthur and Rachel to Wildfell Hall, where brother Frederick shelters her; Huntingdon hunts for her and bargains for the child's return; the chapter closes with Gilbert Markham as frame narrator noting the diary pages are torn where Helen was about to describe him.

Gilbert finishes reading Helen's diary, visits her at Wildfell Hall where they exchange forgiveness but she insists on permanent separation; he then goes to apologise to her brother Frederick Lawrence for a previous assault and they reconcile.

Gilbert waits out Helen's remaining months at Wildfell Hall while befriending her brother Lawrence, then warns Lawrence off a match with the malicious Jane Wilson, steering him away from the unsuitable alliance.

Gilbert Markham hears rumours Helen has reconciled with her husband, rides to Woodford, learns the truth from Lawrence, and reads Helen's letter describing her voluntary return to Grassdale to nurse the gravely ill Huntingdon while securing a written custody promise for their son.

Gilbert reads Helen's letter describing her exhausting nursing of the ailing Arthur Huntingdon and their cold exchange about forgiveness and the future, then uses the revelations to clear Helen's name in the neighbourhood, with digressions on the eventual fates of the Millward and Wilson families.

Gilbert reads Helen's letters describing Arthur Huntingdon's agonizing deathbed — relapse from drink, paralysing fear of damnation, desperate clinging to Helen — culminating in his death as she holds his hand.

After Huntingdon's death, Markham endures months of anxious waiting, unable to contact Helen due to pride and class concerns while Lawrence withholds news; the chapter then dispatches secondary characters — Lady Lowborough's ruin and death, Lord Lowborough's redemptive remarriage, and Hattersley's reform.

Alarmed by Eliza Millward's rumour that Helen is marrying Hargrave, Gilbert races through snow to Grassdale church, only to discover the bride is Esther Hargrave and the groom his friend Frederick Lawrence.

Gilbert travels to Grassdale then Staningley seeking Helen, but on learning she has inherited a vast fortune he halts at her gates and resolves to retreat, deeming the class gulf now unbridgeable and his pursuit an imposition on her.

Gilbert Markham unexpectedly encounters the newly wealthy Helen at Staningley, suppresses his feelings due to her inheritance, but Helen signals her love through a Christmas rose and they become engaged, closing the novel with their happy marriage.

Testi/Bronte/Atomized/Villette/Chapter_0.plot: Lucy Snowe, visiting her godmother Mrs Bretton, witnesses the arrival of small, grieving Polly Home, a child placed temporarily in Mrs Bretton's care after her mother's death and her father's illness-forced travels.

Polly Home, pining miserably for her absent father, is suddenly reunited with Mr. Home on an unexpected visit; later that evening Graham Bretton returns and engages Polly in a comically formal yet sparring exchange, with Lucy Snowe observing both reunions with cool detachment.

After her father's departure, Polly forms an intense, devotional bond with young Graham at the Bretton house—marked by playful skirmishes, tender Sunday readings, and a brief rupture—until a letter summons her to join her father abroad, leaving her sleepless and heartbroken the night before she departs.

Lucy Snowe, adrift after personal losses, becomes live-in companion to the crippled Miss Marchmont, who confides the tragic death of her fiancé Frank on Christmas Eve thirty years past, then dies peacefully that same night after a final lucid conversation.
After her employer Miss Marchmont dies, Lucy travels alone to London seeking new employment, arriving bewildered and penniless at night yet resolving to press forward rather than retreat.

Lucy spends an exhilarating day exploring London alone, then boards a night vessel to the continent, meets the frivolous and selfish Ginevra Fanshawe during a rough Channel crossing, and arrives penniless and friendless at a foreign port with no plan beyond survival.

Lucy Snowe, stranded alone in Villette at night without luggage or contacts, wanders the dark city guided briefly by a kind English stranger, and by apparent fate stumbles upon Madame Beck's pensionnat, where Paul Emanuel reads her character and Madame Beck hires her on the spot.

Lucy Snowe arrives at Madame Beck's pensionnat, is covertly inspected during the night, witnesses Madame summarily dismiss the drunken nursemaid Mrs. Sweeny, and is then pushed by Madame to take over an unruly class of sixty pupils, succeeding by locking the ringleader in a closet and thereby earning a promotion from nursery governess to English teacher.

Lucy settles into teaching at Madame Beck's school while Ginevra Fanshawe confesses she has been accepting costly gifts from a lovesick suitor she calls "Isidore," whom she openly scorns, preferring instead a dashing officer named Colonel de Hamal.

Testi/Bronte/Atomized/Villette/Chapter_1.plot: A young English doctor introduced as Dr. John sets Fifine's broken arm and becomes a regular visitor at the pensionnat through Désirée's feigned illness, while the overlooked Lucy recognizes him as the stranger who aided her on her arrival in Villette.

Lucy observes Dr. John emerge shaken from a secret encounter with flirtatious portress Rosine, while Madame Beck, who harbors romantic designs on the doctor, manages parental scandal over his school presence with shrewd diplomacy and then privately confronts her own bitter disappointment when she sees his indifference to her.

Lucy finds a love-note casket dropped into the forbidden garden alley, Dr. John (Graham Bretton) slips in at night to retrieve it and begs her silence, while Madame Beck covertly watches and later plays innocent to mask her suspicion.

Lucy catches Madame Beck secretly searching her belongings, then witnesses a second billet dropped from the neighboring house during Dr. John's visit to Georgette, after which Dr. John asks Lucy to act as guardian for a mysterious woman he admires—only for Madame Beck to interrupt the disclosure with an inadvertent sneeze while eavesdropping at the keyhole.

At Madame Beck's school fête, Paul Emanuel drafts Lucy Snowe into a last-minute male role in the vaudeville; she performs it with unexpected relish while Ginevra Fanshawe openly flirts with Graham Bretton (Dr. John) from the stage, and the night ends with Lucy confronting Ginevra about her callous treatment of Dr. John's devotion.

Left alone at the school during the long vacation while all others depart, Lucy Snowe descends into severe psychological and physical collapse, enduring weeks of desolation and feverish nightmares before wandering into a Catholic church to confess to a priest, then collapsing unconscious in the storm.

Lucy Snowe wakes from her breakdown in a room whose furnishings she gradually recognises as from her godmother's old home at Bretton, learns she has been taken in by Mrs Bretton, and reunites with Graham Bretton (Dr John), revealing that she had long known who he was while he had never recognised her.

Lucy Snowe, recuperating at La Terrasse under Mrs. Bretton's care, learns from Dr. Graham Bretton how he and a priest rescued her after she collapsed following a desperate visit to confession, and spends two tranquil evenings with the Brettons while silently observing Graham's unspoken longing for Ginevra Fanshawe.

Lucy loses patience and scolds Graham for his blind infatuation with the mercenary Ginevra Fanshawe; they quarrel, then reconcile that evening, after which Graham resumes confiding his lovesick obsession to a privately skeptical Lucy.

During her extended recovery at La Terrasse, Lucy visits galleries with Dr. John and encounters the Cleopatra painting, where Paul Emanuel forcibly redirects her to duller canvases on grounds of feminine propriety, then Dr. John rejoins her and dismisses Cleopatra by comparing her unfavourably to Ginevra.

Testi/Bronte/Atomized/Villette/Chapter_2.plot: Lucy accompanies Mrs. Bretton and Graham to a grand royal concert in Villette where, after Ginevra Fanshawe mockingly ridicules Graham and his mother, Graham's infatuation with Ginevra collapses and he declares his mother worth more than any beauty.

Lucy returns to the pensionnat after vacation, wages an internal battle between personified Reason and Hope over Graham's promised letter, receives that letter delivered by the intrusive M. Paul, and defuses his furious classroom outburst while secretly hoarding the unopened letter as a private treasure.

Lucy steals away to read Dr. John's letter in the school garret, encounters a ghostly nun-figure that terrifies her, flees to Madame Beck's salon where Graham Bretton happens to be present, recovers her stolen letter from him, and hears his diagnosis that the apparition was a spectral illusion born of nervous strain.

Graham takes Lucy to see the actress Vashti perform, whose demonic intensity overwhelms Lucy while Graham watches with cold curiosity; a fire panics the theatre crowd and Graham rescues an injured young girl, then escorts her to her hotel where he treats her injuries.

After seven weeks of agonizing silence, Lucy receives a letter from Mrs. Bretton inviting her to La Terrasse, where she discovers that the injured girl she met weeks ago is Paulina Mary Home de Bassompierre — little Polly, now grown — who remembers Lucy and their shared Bretton past with vivid precision.

Lucy and Paulina (Polly) spend a snowbound day at La Terrasse with Mrs. Bretton, the Count de Bassompierre, and Graham, during which Lucy's status as a working teacher is revealed, the Count proposes enrolling Polly at Madame Beck's school, and Graham and Paulina begin a tentative, charged reacquaintance that hints at mutual attraction.

Lucy observes Paulina (Polly) silently and tenderly revisiting Graham's childhood books at Mrs Bretton's house, then anxiously waiting for her father and Graham to return from town, revealing her deep but wordless attachments to both.

Lucy ritually buries Graham's letters in the garden pear-tree as symbolic interment of her dead hope, sees the veiled nun apparition again, declines Paulina's offer to live with her family, endures Paul Emanuel's jealous surveillance of her outings, and learns from Paulina that Ginevra's boastful tales of Graham as her devoted suitor have made Paulina awkward and cold towards him.

At a Labassecour civic ceremony Paul Emanuel delivers a fiery political oration, then at the Hôtel Crécy evening gathering Graham openly pursues Paulina while Lucy endures his condescension and Paul's stinging insult, before Paul and Lucy quietly reconcile in the vestibule.

Lucy braves Paul Emanuel's furious classroom to deliver an urgent summons, accidentally shatters his spectacles which paradoxically softens him; that evening he returns, seats himself beside Lucy (then exiles himself to the far end of the bench in a fit of pique), reads Shakespeare aloud, then privately lectures her on her supposedly worldly dress and ribbon while she stitches him a silk watchguard, and they part on unexpectedly warm terms.

Testi/Bronte/Atomized/Villette/Chapter_3.plot: On M. Paul's fête day Lucy crafts him a beaded guard but withholds it out of spite, clashes with him during his xenophobic tirade against England, then catches him secretly rifling through her desk.

Lucy catches Paul Emanuel secretly depositing books at her desk on his fête-day; after a tense confrontation over her deliberate refusal to bring him flowers, she presents him with a handmade silk chain, they reconcile, and the evening closes in warm, wordless companionship.

Lucy Snowe recounts M. Paul Emanuel's jealous, domineering pedagogy — his suspicions about her hidden classical learning, his contempt for "women of intellect," and their escalating battle over his demand that she perform an improvised public composition — ending with Lucy escaping while he fetches her water.

Lucy falls asleep in the classroom and wakes covered by shawls; Paul Emanuel reveals he secretly watches everyone through a rented window and a hidden garden key, and their twilight conversation about supernatural impressions ends when the ghostly nun sweeps violently past both of them in the garden.

Polly Home confides to Lucy Snowe that Graham Bretton secretly wrote her a love letter during her travels; she responds with careful restraint, and the two women discuss whether her father will ever sanction the match.

Paul Emanuel leads students on a country breakfast excursion, sharing moments of tender intimacy with Lucy and hinting at departure; that evening he urgently seeks her out, but Lucy panics and flees, Madame Beck intercepts and dismisses him, leaving Lucy in regret and suspense.

Lucy is sent by Madame Beck to deliver fruit to the monstrous Madame Walravens; sheltering from a storm, she is guided by Père Silas — her former confessor — who reveals that Paul Emanuel has devoted his income and celibacy to supporting Walravens's household out of undying love for the long-dead Justine Marie.

Lucy is dragged before two sneering college professors who doubt M. Paul's claim that her essay is her own; she vindicates him with a scathing impromptu piece on "Human Justice," then in a subsequent garden conversation M. Paul confesses his austere solitary life and proposes a deep brother-sister friendship, which Lucy accepts with quiet joy.

Lucy discovers Paul Emanuel's cold withdrawal was engineered by confessor Père Silas, who planted a Catholic conversion tract in her desk; Paul visits and they hold a frank interfaith dialogue that ends in unexpected spiritual accord, while Père Silas then visits Madame Beck to arrange his control of Lucy's religious direction.

Lucy acts as confidante and mediator as Graham Bretton seeks M. de Bassompierre's blessing to marry Paulina (Polly); the reluctant father relents, the couple weds and prospers, while Lucy remains a solitary, excluded observer.

Testi/Bronte/Atomized/Villette/Chapter_4.plot: Madame Beck announces Paul Emanuel's departure for Guadeloupe and maneuvers to block Lucy from a farewell; after being given an opiate that backfires into feverish excitement, Lucy slips out at midnight into an illuminated festival park where she covertly observes the Bretton–Bassompierre party and uncovers Madame Beck's conspiratorial circle, receiving only a note from Paul promising one last private meeting before he sails.

Lucy covertly watches Paul Emanuel at the night festival, learns he delayed his voyage and seems devoted to his ward Justine Marie, then returns to the dormitory to find the phantom nun exposed as a stuffed dummy with a mocking farewell note.

Ginevra Fanshawe elopes overnight with Alfred de Hamal — revealed via her letter to Lucy as the man behind the "nun" disguise — and Lucy recounts Ginevra's breezy, self-satisfied married life in the years that follow.

Paul Emanuel secretly prepares a house and schoolroom in Faubourg Clotilde for Lucy, defies Madame Beck's interference, declares his love and proposes she run her own school during his three-year absence in Guadaloupe, then sails away the next day.

During Paul Emanuel's three-year absence Lucy runs a thriving school sustained by his faithful letters, but as his return approaches a catastrophic storm strikes — implying he is lost at sea — while the narrator withholds the ending and closes the novel.

Testi/Bronte/Atomized/Wuthering_Heights/.plot: Lockwood visits his reclusive landlord Heathcliff at Wuthering Heights, is met with cold reserve and aggressive dogs, yet is fascinated enough to resolve on a return visit.

Lockwood visits Wuthering Heights a second time, is met with cold hostility from the young Mrs. Heathcliff (Cathy Linton) and the rough Hareton Earnshaw, is attacked by dogs when trying to leave, and is compelled to spend the night after Zillah intervenes.

themes: the past intruding on the present
Testi/Bronte/Atomized/Wuthering_Heights/.plot: Lockwood, sleeping in a forbidden chamber, discovers Catherine's childhood diary scrawled on the windowsill and suffers two nightmares—the second conjuring her ghost begging entry—before witnessing Heathcliff's desperate, tearful call for Catherine's spirit at the open casement at dawn.

Lockwood asks Nelly Dean about his neighbours' history; she begins her retrospective account of how old Mr Earnshaw brought the foundling Heathcliff home from Liverpool, sparking immediate resentment from Hindley while young Cathy accepted him, with Heathcliff already showing cold cunning in exploiting his hold over the master.
Old Mr. Earnshaw declines and dies in his fireside chair while Catherine and Heathcliff sit beside him; the two children comfort each other in grief as Nelly and Joseph react to the loss.

Hindley returns with a wife and degrades Heathcliff to a farm labourer; Heathcliff and Catherine sneak to Thrushcross Grange to spy on the pampered Linton children, Catherine is seized by the guard-dog and kept inside by the Lintons while Heathcliff is driven off, leaving her stranded among the gentry and widening the gulf between them.

Catherine returns from Thrushcross Grange transformed into a refined lady; her changed appearance humiliates the neglected Heathcliff, who is mocked and banished by Hindley during the Christmas visit of the Lintons, sparking Heathcliff's first vow of revenge.

Frances dies shortly after bearing Hareton, driving Hindley into reckless dissolution; Catherine maintains a double character between Heathcliff and Edgar Linton, and after a violent outburst during Edgar's visit the two confess their love.

Catherine confesses to Nelly that she accepted Edgar Linton's proposal for social reasons yet declares Heathcliff her true self ("I am Heathcliff"); Heathcliff overhears enough to flee into the storm, Catherine's anguish triggers a dangerous fever, and—after her recovery—she eventually marries Edgar while Heathcliff remains absent.

Heathcliff returns after three years transformed into a wealthy gentleman, is joyfully received by Catherine at Thrushcross Grange while Edgar remains coldly suspicious, and reveals he has lodged himself at Wuthering Heights with Hindley — all while Isabella develops an infatuation with him that Heathcliff privately notes with calculating interest.

Nelly finds Hareton feral and corrupted by Heathcliff at the Heights; back at Thrushcross Grange she catches Heathcliff embracing Isabella, triggering a violent three-way confrontation with Edgar Linton that ends with Heathcliff driven out and Catherine locking herself away in a hysterical fit, threatening to destroy herself if forced to choose between husband and friend.

Catherine collapses into feverish delirium after days of self-starvation, raving about Heathcliff and Wuthering Heights while Edgar stands helpless; Nelly fetches the doctor and discovers Isabella has eloped with Heathcliff.

Isabella writes Nelly from Wuthering Heights describing her grim arrival as Heathcliff's new wife—Hindley pacing with a knife-pistol and murderous intent toward Heathcliff, Joseph and young Hareton hostile, no proper room provided—while back at the Grange Catherine slowly recovers from brain fever under Edgar's devoted care.

Nelly visits Wuthering Heights to relay Edgar's cold refusal of contact with Isabella; Heathcliff then coerces Nelly into agreeing to smuggle him into Thrushcross Grange for a secret meeting with the ailing Catherine.

Heathcliff secretly visits the gravely ill Catherine at Thrushcross Grange; they share a desperate final embrace filled with anguished recriminations and declarations of love before Edgar returns from church and Nelly urges Heathcliff to leave.

Catherine Earnshaw dies hours after giving birth to infant Cathy; Nelly tells Heathcliff, who erupts in violent grief and begs Catherine's ghost to haunt him, secretly visits the corpse to exchange hair locks, then Catherine is buried on a plain slope at the edge of the moor.

Isabella flees Wuthering Heights and recounts Heathcliff's savage beating of Hindley the night before; Hindley soon dies drunk and in debt, leaving Heathcliff as mortgagee and de facto master of Wuthering Heights with Hareton wholly in his power.

During Edgar's absence, thirteen-year-old Cathy Linton secretly rides to Wuthering Heights, meets Hareton Earnshaw, and is shocked to discover he is her cousin and that Heathcliff has deliberately kept him illiterate and brutish.

Linton Heathcliff arrives at Thrushcross Grange after Isabella's death, briefly welcomed by Cathy and Edgar, but Heathcliff's servant Joseph immediately demands the boy back, forcing Edgar to concede Linton will be sent to Wuthering Heights the next morning.

Nelly delivers Linton Heathcliff to Wuthering Heights; Heathcliff receives his frail son with contempt and discloses his plan to use the boy to seize the Linton estates, keeping him alive only as an instrument of revenge.

Heathcliff engineers a meeting between Cathy Linton and Linton Heathcliff at Wuthering Heights, reveals his scheme to unite them in marriage to secure the Grange property, and weeks of secret love letters between the cousins follow until Nelly discovers and burns them.

themes: parental illness and fear of loss
Testi/Bronte/Atomized/Wuthering_Heights/.plot: Nelly accompanies a grieving Cathy on a walk where Heathcliff intercepts them and manipulates Cathy into believing Linton Heathcliff is dying for love of her, prompting Nelly to reluctantly escort Cathy to Wuthering Heights the next day.

Cathy and Nelly visit a sickly, peevish Linton Heathcliff at Wuthering Heights, where a quarrel over their parents' histories ends with Cathy accidentally triggering his coughing fit; Nelly falls ill afterward and, during her three-week convalescence, suspects Cathy is secretly returning to the Heights each evening.

Nelly discovers Cathy has been making secret nightly visits to Wuthering Heights to see the ailing Linton Heathcliff; Cathy recounts their bittersweet meetings and a violent confrontation with Hareton that left Linton coughing blood; Nelly then betrays the secret to Edgar, who forbids further visits.

Dying Edgar agonizes over Cathy's future and Linton Heathcliff's worthiness, eventually permitting supervised moor meetings, while Heathcliff secretly controls Linton's letters and both men decline toward death.

Cathy and Nelly meet a visibly failing Linton Heathcliff near Wuthering Heights, where his terrified deference to his absent father and his obvious deterioration alarm them, though they conceal the truth from Edgar on their return.

Heathcliff uses Linton Heathcliff's terror as bait to lure Cathy Linton and Nelly Dean into Wuthering Heights, locks them in, physically strikes Cathy when she tries to seize the key, and reveals his plan to force her to marry Linton before Edgar Linton dies, keeping them imprisoned overnight.

Nelly escapes Wuthering Heights, returns to dying Edgar at Thrushcross Grange and learns from Linton Heathcliff that Heathcliff struck Cathy; Linton secretly lets Cathy out, she reaches the Grange in time to be with Edgar as he dies peacefully, after which Heathcliff's bribed lawyer Green arrives to seize control of the estate.

Heathcliff arrives at Thrushcross Grange the evening after Edgar's funeral to claim Cathy Linton and take her to Wuthering Heights, then reveals to Nelly that he has opened Catherine Earnshaw's grave and been haunted by her ghost for eighteen years.

Nelly relays Zillah's account of Linton Heathcliff's death and Cathy's isolation at the Heights, Heathcliff's seizure of the inheritance through Linton's will, and Cathy's grudging descent into the household where her first cold encounters with Hareton hint at a future bond; Lockwood then announces he is recovering and plans to quit Thrushcross Grange.

Lockwood visits Wuthering Heights, delivers Nelly's note to Cathy, and witnesses a bitter clash between Cathy and Hareton over his secret hoard of books — ending with him striking her and burning the books — before Heathcliff arrives and mutters that he can barely look at Hareton because he sees Catherine Earnshaw's face in him; Lockwood then announces he is quitting Thrushcross Grange.
Lockwood returns to the neighbourhood after months away, witnesses Cathy and Hareton's tender literacy lessons and growing bond, and learns from Nelly that Heathcliff died three months earlier.

Cathy and Hareton's budding friendship provokes Heathcliff's fury, but when he glimpses Catherine Earnshaw's eyes in their faces he confesses to Nelly his loss of will to revenge himself and his all-consuming obsession with Catherine's ghost, sensing an approaching and undefined change.

Heathcliff, consumed by a mysterious ecstatic vision he cannot eat or sleep through, wastes away over several days and is found dead in the panelled room; Hareton grieves deeply, he is buried without ceremony, and rumors of his ghost walking the moors and Heights persist.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/American_Notes/Ch.plot: Dickens closes his American travel account with concluding remarks and a postscript, the unit consisting of a chapter heading and illustration list referencing emigrants, a solitary prisoner, racial contrast, and a domestic scene.

Dickens boards the Britannia steam-packet at Liverpool, humorously confronts the absurd gap between the agent's glamorous promotional lithograph and the cramped state-room, bids farewell to friends over a last dinner, and watches the ship finally cast off into the winter fog bound for America.

Dickens narrates the turbulent Atlantic crossing aboard the Britannia — enduring communal seasickness, a ferocious January gale, a night grounding on a mudbank near Halifax, and a brief stop at Halifax before finally reaching Boston.

Dickens tours Boston's public institutions—most extensively the Perkins Institution for the Blind where he recounts Laura Bridgman's and Oliver Caswell's education—then visits South Boston's asylum for the insane, houses of industry, correction, and juvenile reform, before observing American courts, Boston society, and a sailor-preacher's sermon.

Dickens travels by American railroad from Boston to Lowell, describes the chaotic rail journey and wilderness scenery, then tours the textile mills, praising the factory girls' cleanliness, savings, and self-improvement through the Lowell Offering magazine, contrasting the town's humane conditions favourably with English manufacturing misery.

Dickens travels by railroad and steamboat from Boston through Worcester, Hartford (visiting an insane asylum and state prison), and New Haven, arriving by packet boat to a vivid first sight of New York harbor.

Dickens tours New York — Broadway's bustle, the Five Points slum, The Tombs prison with its racial double standards and suicidal hooks, a badly-run lunatic asylum tainted by party politics, the almshouse, and a model juvenile refuge — before departing the city with unexpected grief at leaving new friends.

Dickens travels to Philadelphia, tours the Eastern Penitentiary's regime of absolute solitary confinement, profiles individual prisoners whose minds are being destroyed by isolation, delivers a sustained moral condemnation of the system as secret psychological torture worse than bodily punishment, and closes with the darkly comic anecdote of a voluntary prisoner who flees the moment an open gate catches his eye.

Dickens travels from Philadelphia to Washington, satirises the city's half-built grandeur and ubiquitous tobacco-spitting, condemns Congress for political corruption and brazen hypocrisy over slavery, and attends a presidential levee where Washington Irving is warmly feted by the crowd.

Dickens travels by night steamer and battered stagecoach through Virginia, observing slavery's moral and physical ruin at Richmond's tobacco manufactory and plantations, then continues to Baltimore and Harrisburg where he reflects on broken Native American treaties, before boarding a canal boat to head west.

Dickens recounts the canal boat journey to Pittsburgh — cramped sleeping, communal meals, curious fellow passengers including a boastful Mississippi "brown forester" — then the crossing of the Allegheny Mountains by inclined-plane railroad, arrival in Pittsburgh (compared to Birmingham), and waiting for the steamboat Messenger to depart for Cincinnati.

Dickens travels by steamboat down the Ohio from Pittsburgh to Cincinnati, observing the vessel's hazardous machinery and the silent, gloomy passengers, witnesses a poignant scene of emigrants left ashore with meager possessions, then explores Cincinnati's thriving streets, a large Temperance Convention, and its free schools.

Dickens travels by steamboat from Cincinnati through Louisville to St. Louis, meeting Pitchlynn (a Choctaw chief) who mourns his tribe's erasure by white civilization, encountering a giant showman, enduring the grim Mississippi, and witnessing a young mother's joyful reunion with her husband on arrival.

Dickens joins a group of fourteen on a jaunt to the Looking-Glass Prairie, travelling through mud and swamp, encountering rough frontier settlements and colourful characters like the itinerant phrenologist Dr. Crocus, before reaching the Prairie itself—which disappoints him with its flat, monotonous vastness—then dining on the plain and returning via Lebanon.

Dickens retraces his route from St. Louis back to Cincinnati, then endures a gruelling stagecoach journey across Ohio to Columbus and Sandusky—observing American customs and the forced relocation of the Wyandot Indians—before sailing Lake Erie to Buffalo and arriving at Niagara Falls, where the spectacle overwhelms him with transcendent peace.

Dickens narrates travels through Canadian cities (Niagara, Toronto, Kingston, Montreal, Quebec) and back into the United States, observing emigrant hardship aboard steamboats, visiting the austere Shaker Village at Lebanon, and ending at West Point Military Academy before departing for England.

Dickens recounts the return Atlantic crossing from New York to Liverpool: shipboard camaraderie and daily routines aboard, steerage emigrants fleeing failed American dreams in near-starvation, a sharp critique of the exploitative emigrant-shipping system, and the narrator's euphoric sighting of the Irish coast and arrival home in England.

Dickens dissects American slavery by classifying slave-owners into three types, demolishes "public opinion" as a defence of the institution by citing newspaper ads cataloguing the branded, maimed, and chained bodies of enslaved people, then piles up press reports of stabbings, shootings, and duels among free Americans to prove that a slave-culture brutalises the whole of society.

Dickens closes American Notes with sweeping critique of American society — universal distrust, "smart" dealing, licentious press — then appends an 1868 postscript acknowledging the nation's vast improvement since his first visit.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/A_Childs_History_.plot: Newly wealthy coal-dealer Nicholas Tulrumble is elected Mayor of Mudfog and stages a grand procession to rival London's Lord Mayor, but is publicly humiliated when his hired armored figure Ned Twigger gets drunk and staggers through the parade; chastened, Tulrumble abandons his pomposity, reconciles with old friends, and restores the Jolly Boatmen's music licence.

Satirical mock-proceedings of fictional scientific society sections where pompous doctors report absurd "cures" achieved by making healthy men ill, a medical student turns swallowed door-key into burglary tool, and statisticians deliver nonsensical calculations about children's fairy-tale reading habits, dog-meat barrows, and working-class leg-to-chair ratios.

At Mudfog Association meeting, mock-professors present absurd inventions — sewer-based city railway, rigged share-price machine, fire escape useless during actual fires — skewering Victorian railway mania and scientific pomposity.

A satirical correspondent travels by steamer to Oldcastle and reports on the absurd Second Meeting of the Mudfog Association, culminating in Section A debates on the disappearance of street bears and monkeys and a pseudo-scientific theory that bears-grease turns London youth into bears.

Dickens lampoons a mock scientific association presenting absurd inventions (pocket-picking machine, automaton police, spectacles for willful blindness), then extends the pantomime metaphor to all Victorian social life—fraud, parliamentary corruption, celebrity—arguing that real life and theatrical clowning are identical, and closing with a portrait of a feted literary "lion" performing for admirers at a dinner party.
Unit is a bare title header introducing "Mr. Robert Bolton, The Gentleman Connected with the Press" — no narrative content present beyond the character epithet.

In the parlour of the Green Dragon pub near Westminster Bridge, regulars trade banter about a dubious Pope autograph offered as loan security, until the self-important press-connected Mr. Robert Bolton arrives and rivets the company with a lurid—and likely fabricated—tale of a drunken baker who murders his son by boiling him alive.

Dickens (as Boz) addresses his magazine "Bentley's Miscellany" as "my Child," reflects on technological change symbolised by a forlorn mail-coach guard displaced by the railway, then announces he is resigning the editorship to his friend Mr. Ainsworth.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/A_Christmas_Carol.plot: On Christmas Eve, the miserly Scrooge rejects his nephew Fred's goodwill and refuses charity for the poor, then returns home where Marley's ghost — bound in chains forged by greed — warns him that three spirits will visit him as his only chance to escape the same damned fate.

The Ghost of Christmas Past escorts Scrooge through visions of his past — his solitary schooldays, sister Fan's joyful rescue, Fezziwig's generous Christmas party, and Belle's dissolution of their engagement because Scrooge chose gold over love — forcing him to confront the choices that made him who he is.

characters: Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
Testi/Dickens/Atomized/A_Christmas_Carol.plot: The Ghost of Christmas Present escorts Scrooge through London Christmas celebrations, including the joyful but impoverished Cratchit family dinner where ailing Tiny Tim's survival is cast in doubt, and nephew Fred's warm party, before revealing two allegorical children — Ignorance and Want — and vanishing as the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come arrives.

characters: Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
Testi/Dickens/Atomized/A_Christmas_Carol.plot: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come leads Scrooge through visions of a despised miser's death — his belongings looted by servants, his passing celebrated by debtors, the Cratchit family mourning Tiny Tim — and finally reveals the neglected grave bears Scrooge's own name, driving him to his knees to beg for the chance to alter his fate.

Scrooge wakes transformed on Christmas morning, sends a prize turkey to Bob Cratchit, donates to the charity collector, joins Fred's Christmas dinner, and next day raises Bob's salary — living as a second father to Tiny Tim and a changed man ever after.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/A_Tale_of_Two_Cit.plot: Narrator sets the paradoxical historical scene of 1775, cataloguing the violent disorder and injustice of both England and France while foreshadowing the coming Revolution.

Jarvis Lorry rides the Dover mail through foggy night on Shooter's Hill while Jerry Cruncher gallops up with a dispatch from Tellson's Bank; Lorry reads it and sends back the cryptic reply "Recalled to Life."

Jarvis Lorry dozes in the mail coach haunted by visions of a man buried alive for eighteen years whom he travels to recall to life, while Jerry Cruncher rides back to Tellson's Bank with a message, musing aloud about the cryptic summons.

Jarvis Lorry meets young Lucie Manette in Dover and reveals that her father—long believed dead—is alive after years of unjust secret imprisonment in France, news that causes Lucie to faint while Miss Pross rushes to her aid.

In the starving Saint Antoine slum, where spilled wine foreshadows future bloodshed, Defarge escorts Lorry and Lucie through a squalid tenement to a locked garret where the broken, isolated Doctor Manette is found silently making shoes.

Lorry and Defarge bring Lucie to her broken father Doctor Manette — a shoemaking prisoner who has lost his identity in the Bastille — and their emotional reunion flickers recognition in him before all three escape Paris toward England.
This unit is the bare title heading for Book the Second of A Tale of Two Cities, containing no narrative or character action.

Jerry Cruncher berates his wife for praying, takes his post outside Tellson's Bank, receives a messenger errand, while his son puzzles over his father's mysteriously rusty fingers — hinting at grave-robbing.

Charles Darnay stands trial at the Old Bailey for treason—accused of passing British military intelligence to France—while Jerry Cruncher delivers a note to Lorry in court, and Lucie Manette and Doctor Manette sit as witnesses against him, their visible distress drawing the crowd's attention.

Charles Darnay is tried for treason in an English court where Lucie Manette and Jarvis Lorry testify, false witnesses Barsad and Cly accuse him, but Sydney Carton's striking physical resemblance to Darnay destroys the eyewitness identification and Darnay is acquitted.

After Darnay's acquittal, his circle congratulates him outside the court; then Carton escorts Darnay to a tavern where, drunk and bitter, he confesses his self-loathing and hints at envy of the man who mirrors his own face.

Carton and Stryver drink through the night while Carton does the real legal brainwork as Stryver's "jackal," and after Stryver toasts Lucie Manette, Carton trudges home in dawn cold to weep over his ruined, purposeless life.

Jarvis Lorry visits the Manette household in Soho where Miss Pross reveals the Doctor silently relives his imprisonment in nightly pacing, Darnay's casual mention of a hidden prison inscription visibly disturbs Manette, and Carton and a violent thunderstorm together foreshadow a great crowd of catastrophe bearing down on them all.

The Marquis St. Evremonde (Monseigneur) attends a corrupt Parisian reception, then his speeding carriage kills a poor child; he contemptuously tosses a gold coin as payment, encounters Defarge consoling the bereaved father Gaspard, and Madame Defarge silently defies him by throwing the coin back into the carriage.

Marquis St. Evremonde travels through an impoverished French village, interrogates a road-mender about a mysterious figure clinging to his carriage, coldly dismisses a grieving widow's petition for a grave marker for her dead husband, and arrives at his chateau to learn Monsieur Charles (Darnay) has not yet arrived from England.

The Marquis St. Evremonde returns to his chateau, confronts nephew Charles Darnay who denounces their family's tyranny and renounces his inheritance, declares England his refuge; next morning the Marquis is found stabbed in his bed with a note from "Jacques."
Charles Darnay confesses his love for Lucie to Doctor Manette and extracts a promise of conditional blessing; the chapter closes with Manette relapsing into compulsive shoemaking after Darnay leaves.

Stryver announces to Carton his plan to marry Lucie Manette; Carton receives the news with studied indifference and heavy drinking, masking his own suppressed feelings while Stryver patronizingly advises him to find a landlady-type wife.

Stryver announces to Lorry his plan to propose to Lucie Manette; Lorry diplomatically discourages him, investigates in Soho, and confirms the advice — whereupon Stryver rewrites the episode in his own mind, pretending he was never seriously committed.
Sydney Carton visits Lucie Manette alone and confesses his hopeless love for her, declaring himself irredeemable but vowing he would sacrifice his life for her and those she loves.
Jerry Cruncher watches the riotous funeral of spy Roger Cly, then secretly goes grave-robbing at night as a resurrection man while Young Jerry follows and discovers his father's true illicit trade.

Defarge brings road-mender Jacques Five to a secret committee above the wine-shop, where the man recounts Gaspard's capture and hanging for killing the Marquis; the Jacques vote to register the chateau and its entire family for destruction, then escort the road-mender to Versailles to cheer the King and Queen—deliberately stoking royalist complacency to hasten the aristocracy's fall.

The Defarges return to Saint Antoine, learn of an English spy named Barsad whom Madame Defarge begins encoding in her knitting; Barsad visits their wine-shop probing for sedition and drops that Lucie Manette is to marry Charles Darnay, nephew of the dead Marquis, which Madame Defarge coldly records as yet another name destined for revolutionary reckoning.

Night before Lucie's wedding, she and Doctor Manette sit alone under the plane-tree; he recalls prison visions of an imagined daughter and affirms his happiness; Miss Pross joins for supper; Lucie slips to his bedside at 3 a.m. to pray over his sleeping face.

On Lucie and Darnay's wedding day, Doctor Manette suffers a traumatic relapse into his old prisoner persona—silently making shoes and unresponsive—while Mr. Lorry and Miss Pross secretly tend him for nine days, concealing the crisis from the departed Lucie.

Lorry obliquely consults Manette about his own nine-day relapse; Manette gives his prognosis and authorizes removal of the shoemaker's bench, which Lorry and Miss Pross then secretly hack apart, burn, and bury to protect Lucie from the truth.

Carton visits the newly-married Darnays and asks permission to come and go as a tolerated fixture; later Lucie privately pleads with Charles to be generous toward Carton, revealing she has seen the deep wounds in his hidden heart.

Chapter spans years of Lucie's peaceful Soho family life and Carton's rare visits, until the night of 14 July 1789 when Lorry brings news of Parisian panic; simultaneously the Bastille falls as Defarge leads the assault, discovers Doctor Manette's old cell (No. 105, North Tower), and Madame Defarge beheads the governor amid the revolutionary bloodshed.

The Saint Antoine mob, led by Madame Defarge and her husband, captures the aristocrat Foulon — who mockingly told starving people to eat grass — and lynches him along with his son-in-law, parading their heads on pikes through Paris.
Revolutionary agents burn the Marquis's chateau while the starved villagers watch in silent solidarity, and the tax collector Gabelle narrowly survives mob fury on his rooftop.

Darnay, at Tellson's Bank while Lorry prepares to leave for Paris, receives a desperate letter from imprisoned servant Gabelle and resolves in secret to go to Paris himself, departing without warning Lucie or Doctor Manette.
This unit is the title-page header for Book the Third of A Tale of Two Cities, containing no narrative content beyond the book's subtitle "The Track of a Storm."

Charles Darnay travels to Paris under armed patriot escort, is received at the city gate by Ernest Defarge who coldly refuses to help him despite their connection through Lucie, and is imprisoned "in secret" at La Force under the new laws targeting émigrés.

Lucie and Doctor Manette arrive at Tellson's Bank Paris to tell Jarvis Lorry that Charles Darnay has been arrested and sent to La Force; while a mob sharpens weapons at the courtyard grindstone during the September Massacres, Doctor Manette leverages his Bastille-prisoner status to rush into the crowd and seek Charles's release.

Lorry moves Lucie, her child, and Miss Pross to a safer lodging; Defarge arrives carrying Doctor Manette's note confirming Charles is safe plus a brief message from Charles himself, but Madame Defarge's cold, purposeful visit to "identify" the family casts a dark, unspoken threat over Lucie and her child.

Doctor Manette returns after four days, reveals he used his Bastille-prisoner status to keep Darnay alive at La Force's tribunal, and over the following year serves as inspecting physician of three prisons while the Revolution's terror intensifies around him.

Lucie keeps a daily two-hour vigil outside the prison for over a year hoping Charles can glimpse her from his window, witnesses the terrifying Carmagnole dance, then learns from Doctor Manette that Charles is summoned before the Tribunal tomorrow, and they rush to Jarvis Lorry at Tellson's Bank where a mysterious unseen visitor has just arrived.

Darnay is arraigned before the Revolutionary Tribunal as an émigré, but Doctor Manette's testimony and popularity sway the jury to acquit him, and the jubilant crowd carries him home in a chaotic procession of triumph.

Hours after Darnay's acquittal, Republican soldiers burst in and re-arrest him on a denunciation from the Defarges and an unnamed third accuser, leaving Doctor Manette powerless and the family in fresh despair.

Sydney Carton exposes spy Barsad (Miss Pross's brother Solomon) and, by threatening denunciation to the Revolution's committees, coerces him into granting access inside the Conciergerie prison — a card Carton plans to play now that Darnay has been rearrested.

Carton secures covert prison access through a spy, walks Paris at night purchasing chemicals while meditating on the resurrection scripture, then attends Darnay's second trial where Defarge produces Doctor Manette's old Bastille letter as a denunciation that condemns Darnay.

Doctor Manette's hidden written confession — describing how the Evrémonde brothers forced him to treat their dying peasant victims and then had him imprisoned to silence him — is read aloud at the Revolutionary tribunal, and its denunciation of the Evrémonde bloodline condemns Charles Darnay to death within twenty-four hours.

After Darnay's death sentence, Lucie and Charles share a final embrace in the tribunal; Carton carries the fainted Lucie home, then privately admits to Lorry there is no real hope, while urging Doctor Manette to petition the authorities anyway for Lucie's sake.

Carton spies at Defarge's wine shop and overhears Madame Defarge swear to destroy Lucie's entire family; he returns to warn Lorry and arranges the family's escape, while Doctor Manette arrives in full mental relapse, demanding his cobbler's bench.

Sydney Carton enters Darnay's prison cell, drugs him with a chemical, switches clothes, and takes his condemned place among the fifty-two headed for the guillotine, while the unconscious Darnay is smuggled out of Paris by Jarvis Lorry, Lucie, and the broken Doctor Manette.

Madame Defarge arrives to denounce and arrest Lucie's family but finds only Miss Pross, who physically grapples her to buy time; Madame Defarge's own pistol fires in the struggle, killing her, while Miss Pross escapes permanently deafened as the family coach flees Paris.

Sydney Carton rides to the guillotine in place of Darnay, comforts a young seamstress until her death, then faces execution himself, his final prophetic vision foreseeing peace for those he loves and immortality through a child who will bear his name.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Barnaby_Rudge/Cha.plot: At the Maypole Inn on a stormy March night, a mysterious stranger's questions about the Warren prompt parish clerk Solomon Daisy to recount how twenty-two years ago Reuben Haredale was found murdered, his steward Mr Rudge killed, and the gardener—chief suspect—vanished without trace.

Gabriel Varden the locksmith, riding home at night, nearly collides with a reckless mysterious stranger who reveals he nearly killed Gabriel before galloping off; shaken but lured by warmth, Gabriel abandons his resolve and turns back to the Maypole inn.

Gabriel Varden leaves the Maypole after Joe Willet's angry rebellion against his father, then on his night ride to London stumbles upon Barnaby Rudge holding a torch over a wounded and robbed stranger, whom together they load into the chaise.

Gabriel Varden returns to his Clerkenwell locksmith's shop and recounts to daughter Dolly how he found the wounded Edward Chester on the road and later slipped into a masquerade to quietly warn Miss Emma, while apprentice Simon Tappertit—consumed by jealous ambition over Dolly—works himself into a frenzy at the grindstone.

Gabriel Varden visits the widow's house to check on wounded Edward Chester; a mysterious stranger knocks and appears at the door, freezing Mrs. Rudge in terror and causing her to desperately prevent Gabriel from pursuing him.

Gabriel Varden questions the distressed widow Rudge about the mysterious nocturnal intruder, then goes upstairs to find the wounded Edward Chester, who recounts being robbed on the road; the raven Grip interrupts with comic interjections, and Varden departs having lied to protect the widow while privately suspecting her of dark complicity.

Gabriel Varden returns home late to face his wife's capricious ill-temper and Miggs's theatrical sympathy, then falls asleep by the fire while Simon Tappertit secretly uses a duplicate key to slip out of the locked house undetected.

Simon Tappertit steals away at night to a squalid underground cellar where, as "captain," he presides over the 'Prentice Knights, initiates a new member with grotesque mock-ritual, and proscribes Joe Willet as an enemy of the society.
Miggs catches Simon Tappertit sneaking out at night, sabotages his forged key by filling the lock with coal-dust, then leverages his helpless return to extract flattery and assert herself over him.

Sir John Chester arrives at the Maypole inn with studied elegance, sends Barnaby Rudge to deliver a sealed note to Geoffrey Haredale at the Warren, and awaits Haredale's reply — establishing a secret meeting between two known enemies.

Maypole regulars speculate that the waiting Mr Chester and the expected Haredale intend to fight a duel upstairs, swapping rumours about a bloodstain at the Warren that will never fade, until Haredale himself arrives, is announced by a rattled John Willet, and goes up alone to meet Chester.

Geoffrey Haredale and Sir John Chester meet privately at the Maypole and, despite deep mutual hostility, strike a cold alliance to separate their children Emma and Edward by any means including jealousy, intrigue, and lies.

Joe Willet, dispatched to London on a quarterly errand, detours past the Warren for a covert signal from within, then calls at the locksmith's to court Dolly Varden, but is thwarted by Mrs Varden's sanctimonious hostility and Dolly's cheerful departure for a party, leaving him miserable and fantasising about enlisting to get himself killed.

Edward Chester secretly visits Emma Haredale at the Warren but is caught and expelled by her guardian Geoffrey Haredale, who voids their pledge; returning to the Maypole, Edward discovers his father Sir John Chester has been there conferring with Haredale and abruptly flees back to London.
Sir John Chester coldly reveals the family fortune is exhausted, admits he bred Edward to marry wealth, and forbids pursuit of Emma Haredale, leaving Edward stunned and wretched.
A mysterious fugitive haunts London's dark streets nightly, evading all contact, then tracks the widow (Mrs. Rudge) home and forces his way into her house.

A desperate fugitive (the Chigwell road robber) forces his way into the widow's parlour, hides in a closet while Barnaby and Grip return home unaware, then examines the sleeping Barnaby before departing and warns the widow he now holds her son as leverage for revenge.

A tormented man wanders London all night in despair, stumbles upon Simon Tappertit emerging from a secret underground gathering, then bribes the blind man Stagg for shelter in his cellar and collapses asleep as Stagg covertly examines him.

Edward Chester visits the Varden household to ask Dolly to carry a secret letter to the Warren; after prolonged domestic squabbling and Mrs Varden's theatrical collapse, the family drives out to the Maypole inn, from where Dolly slips away across the fields to deliver the note.

Dolly Varden secretly delivers Edward Chester's letter to Emma Haredale at the Warren, is cornered and questioned by Geoffrey Haredale who lets her keep the reply, then is stalked by an unseen figure on the darkening path home.

Hugh of the Maypole ambushes Dolly Varden alone on a dark path, physically menaces and harasses her, steals her letter and bracelet, and intimidates her into silence before Joe Willet's timely shouts drive Hugh off and he escorts the shaken girl back to the Maypole.

On the night ride home after Dolly's rescue, Joe and Dolly share charged romantic tension until Hugh intercepts them and Mrs Varden cuts the escort short; back home, Miggs deliberately inflames Tappertit's jealousy by recounting Joe Willet's heroism.

Sir John Chester receives Hugh, reads and burns Dolly's stolen letter meant for Edward, then psychologically subdues Hugh by implicitly threatening to expose his crimes, binding him as a fearful and compliant instrument.

Simon Tappertit visits Sir John Chester in his bedroom to betray the Varden household's role as go-between in Edward's courtship, advising Chester to flatter Mrs Varden and have Joe Willet removed to block the match.

Barnaby's mother travels with Barnaby and Grip to the Warren, where she meets Geoffrey Haredale and Emma to announce she must renounce their financial support and sever all ties for a secret reason she refuses to name, then leaves after promising to receive Haredale the following evening.

Haredale and Gabriel Varden visit the widow Rudge to confront her about harboring a highwayman, but arrive to find Sir John Chester has already bribed her and Barnaby to vanish, dismantling the network secretly aiding Edward and Emma's romance.

Sir John Chester visits the Varden household, charms Mrs Varden with honeyed sophistry, and manipulates her into a secret alliance against her husband and daughter aiding Edward Chester's courtship of Emma Haredale.

Sir John Chester intercepts Dolly Varden's note meant for Emma Haredale (brought by Hugh), extracts intelligence about Edward Chester's failed Maypole visit, and schemes to deliver the note himself while binding Hugh to silence through false promises of protection.

Sir John Chester visits the Maypole, then intercepts Emma Haredale in the Warren and, through calculated lies about Edward's supposed letter breaking off the engagement, destroys her trust in the young man — afterward openly confessing his scheme to a furious Geoffrey Haredale and gloating over the success of their dark compact.

At the Maypole, John Willet humiliates Joe before departing guest Sir John Chester; Joe finally snaps, beats pub-crony Cobb in a rage, barricades himself in his room, and resolves he must leave the Maypole forever.

Joe Willet flees the Maypole at dawn, meets a recruiting sergeant in London, makes a cold farewell visit to Dolly Varden who meets his heartfelt declaration with indifference, then enlists and departs by boat for Chatham—while Simon Tappertit, hidden in the forge, exults that Dolly is now his.

Edward Chester confronts his father Sir John over Emma Haredale's rejection and Sir John's secret meddling, refuses to follow his father's mercenary plans, and is cursed and banished from the house forever.

On a stormy March 19th, Solomon Daisy bursts into the Maypole Inn trembling, claiming he encountered the ghost of a murdered man outside Chigwell church; John Willet and the cronies hear the tale and agree to keep it secret.

John Willet drags Hugh to the Warren at midnight to relay Solomon Daisy's ghost story to Geoffrey Haredale, who is visibly shaken, urges strict secrecy to protect Miss Haredale, while Hugh's insolent toast unsettles everyone and three mysterious horsemen appear as the pair departs.

Lord George Gordon and his fawning secretary Gashford stop at the Maypole Inn after a night ride, where Gashford stokes Gordon's vanity over his anti-Catholic rabble-rousing, while the blunt servant John Grueby warns that the Protestant mob they are inflaming will soon grow uncontrollable and pull London down.

Gashford feigns pious devotion to privately mock the credulous, restless Lord George Gordon while reporting growing Protestant Association numbers and funds, then secretly distributes seditious handbills urging Protestants to rally to Gordon's cause.

Lord George Gordon and his scheming secretary Gashford ride through London stirring "No Popery" crowds, then Gashford recruits hangman Dennis as a procession leader for the coming Catholic Relief Bill protest, just as Hugh arrives at Gordon's house.
Hugh is enrolled into the Protestant Association by Gashford and Dennis, then accompanies Dennis to reconnoitre Parliament and ends the night drinking at The Boot tavern with fellow conspirators.

At The Boot tavern Simon Tappertit and Hugh recognize each other from Maypole days, Hugh is inducted into the United Bulldogs amid drunken anti-Catholic ranting, and on their rowdy walk home Dennis's ghoulish hints about his hangman's trade unsettle Tappertit before the group splits up.

Hugh visits Sir John Chester late at night to report joining the Gordon rioters, while Sir John covertly schemes to use Hugh as a tool to foment anti-Catholic violence and harm Haredale, maintaining public respectability through plausible deniability.

Gabriel Varden works cheerfully at his locksmith shop, Dolly returns home from the Warren with questions about Haredale's secret travels, dinner is disrupted by Mrs Varden and Miggs's Protestant zeal for Lord George Gordon's cause, and Dolly breaks into tears when Gabriel tenderly recalls the absent Joe Willet before marching out in his volunteer militia uniform.

Haredale, haggard and haunted since the night of the March storm, secretly returns to Mrs. Rudge's locked-up house to keep solitary nightly watch, confiding only in bewildered locksmith Gabriel Varden and swearing him to silence.

Geoffrey Haredale, while keeping nightly armed vigil at the old house, encounters Sir John Chester, the renegade secretary Gashford, and Lord George Gordon in Westminster Hall, publicly denounces their No-Popery agitation, is struck by a stone thrown by the roused mob, and is rescued by John Grueby who rows him to safety.
Gashford tracks Hugh and Dennis to their squalid Green Lanes lodgings and secretly commissions them to attack and raze Haredale's house, showing no mercy to its inhabitants.

After five years of quiet rural hiding under false names, Barnaby and his mother are visited by a blind man named Stagg who, once Barnaby is sent away, reveals he acts for an unnamed figure from the widow's past and demands twenty pounds under threat of exposure.

Blind blackmailer Stagg manipulates naive Barnaby while extorting his desperate mother, who surrenders her life savings of six guineas to buy a week before fleeing the cottage at dawn with Barnaby and Grip.

Barnaby and his mother travel toward London with Grip, are humiliated and expelled by a brutal country squire but secretly aided by his wife, while Barnaby grows increasingly fixated on the blind man's promises of gold in the city.

Lord George Gordon and his secretary Gashford recruit the simple-minded Barnaby into the Gordon Riots mob at St George's Fields; Hugh of the Maypole enlists him as standard-bearer, and Simon Tappertit orders the march as Barnaby's desperate mother is thrown to the ground and loses sight of her son.

Three divisions of Gordon Rioters converge on Parliament; Barnaby and Hugh storm the House of Commons lobby alongside Dennis the hangman, are repulsed by the Horse Guards after a standoff, and escape downriver to The Boot tavern.
After the Gordon petition is crushed by parliament and the riot movement collapses, Gashford manipulates Hugh, Barnaby, and Dennis into leading a torch-bearing mob to sack Catholic chapels in London.

Drunk and battered after the Gordon Riots, Simon Tappertit returns to the Varden household, delivers a Lord George Gordon protection letter, then escapes into the night despite Gabriel Varden's attempts to shelter him; Varden tears up the letter and refuses to capitulate to the rioters.

Hugh and Tappertit plan a targeted raid against a Catholic enemy while deceiving Barnaby into standing sentry by falsely claiming Lord George Gordon assigned him the honour; that Sunday night the mob sacks Catholic chapels and homes in Moorfields unchecked, and Gashford urges Hugh to escalate the destruction.

Gashford incites Hugh, Dennis, and Barnaby to lead a riot mob toward Haredale's property to silence him as a witness against the rioters, while Sir John Chester covertly observes and signals his patronage to Hugh from the street.
Hugh leads the Gordon rioters in sacking the Maypole Inn — looting it, binding the stupefied landlord John Willet to his chair — then the mob departs to attack the Warren, Haredale's house.

A catatonic John Willet sits bound in the ruined Maypole bar while a guilt-maddened stranger flees at the sound of an alarm bell; Hugh leads the rioters in the total burning and sacking of the Warren, leaving it a smouldering ruin.

Geoffrey Haredale rides through riot-torn roads to find his house burned to ruins and the Maypole ransacked, then corners and seizes the long-presumed-dead murderer Rudge hiding in the charred turret.

Barnaby keeps lonely guard at The Boot while Grip unearths hidden treasure; Lord George Gordon visits and praises his devotion; soldiers arrive, Barnaby resists and is overpowered, handcuffed, and marched away as a prisoner.

Barnaby is marched under military escort from barracks to Newgate prison, shackled in irons despite rioters' attempts to rescue him, while Grip the raven — seized separately — is quietly thrust into his cell at the end.

After dispersing the rioters from the Warren, Hugh and Simon Tappertit transport the kidnapped Dolly Varden and Emma Haredale by carriage to a London cottage, where Hugh harasses and manhandles the captives while Tappertit ludicrously declares Dolly his destined bride.

After finding The Boot seized by soldiers and learning Barnaby has been captured and taken to Newgate, Hugh and his companions rally rioters at Fleet Market and swear to storm and burn Newgate the following night.

Geoffrey Haredale escorts his bound prisoner (his brother's murderer) through riot-torn London, is refused help by the cowardly Lord Mayor, and finally secures the man's committal to Newgate via Sir John Fielding.

In his prison cell, the elder Rudge confesses the murder to the blind man Stagg, who devises a blackmail scheme using Barnaby as leverage against Mrs. Rudge to procure false exculpatory testimony; the chapter ends with Barnaby and his father encountering each other in the prison yard, Grip circling them as Barnaby recognizes the man he called a robber as his father.

Rioters led by Hugh and Simon Tappertit storm Gabriel Varden's locksmith shop, overpower him despite his armed resistance and refusal to comply, and march him captive to Newgate prison to force him to pick the jail's locks for the attack.

The Gordon Riots mob besieges Newgate Prison demanding release of rioter prisoners; Gabriel Varden defiantly refuses under beatings and death threats to pick the lock, while Hugh leads the crowd in building a bonfire against the gates until the doors burn down and the prison is breached.

Rioters storm and burn Newgate Prison: the terror-stricken murderer is dragged out and reunited with Barnaby, while hangman Dennis cynically locks condemned men in their cells to preserve them for the gallows, until Hugh forces him aside and the four prisoners are finally freed.

Exhausted Geoffrey Haredale searches London all day for his missing niece Emma, is refused shelter everywhere, collapses near Newgate as the mob storms and burns it, and is rescued by a sympathetic vintner and John Grueby while rioters also destroy Lord Mansfield's house and much of London.

At the peak night of the Gordon Riots, Hugh leads massed rioters in arson and attacks across London while soldiers fire on crowds; Geoffrey Haredale and a vintner, discovered on a rooftop by Hugh's mob, are rescued through cellar passages by Edward Chester and Joe Willet.

After escaping Newgate, Barnaby knocks off his and his father's irons in Smithfield, hides the old man in a rural shed, then re-enters the burning city to find Hugh, drags the wounded and drunken rioter away from the catastrophic final night of the Gordon Riots, and leads him back to safety in the countryside.
Dennis betrays Barnaby, his murderer-father, and Hugh to soldiers at their hiding place; the blind man Stagg is shot dead fleeing, and all three are arrested and marched toward London.

Dennis visits the house where Dolly and Miss Haredale are confined, and exploiting Miggs's jealousy of Dolly, conspires with her to arrange Dolly's forced abduction and smuggling out of London so the women cannot testify against him.

Emma Haredale and Dolly, held captive with the treacherous Miggs, nearly yield to Gashford's false-rescuer ruse before Geoffrey Haredale, Edward Chester, Gabriel Varden, and Joe Willet storm in and free them; Simon Tappertit is found among the captors, broken and gravely wounded.

After rescue from the riots, the group reconvenes at the Black Lion, where old John Willet slowly comprehends Joe's lost arm while Dolly and Joe share a bittersweet farewell, Joe confessing enduring love but resigning himself to poverty and separation.

As London quiets after the riots, Barnaby sits chained in his cell with Grip while his mother reveals his father's murderous guilt and pleads with the unrepentant father to confess; Lord George Gordon, abandoned by all followers, is arrested and imprisoned alone in the Tower.
