Dennis the hangman is committed to Newgate after trial—with Gabriel Varden's testimony against him—and is locked in a cell with Hugh, whom he betrayed; Hugh confronts and nearly attacks him but lapses into bitter resignation, revealing his mother was hanged at Tyburn and he expects the same fate.

Gabriel Varden visits Sir John Chester to relay the hangman Dennis's deathbed revelation that Hugh — condemned to hang at dawn — is Sir John's illegitimate son, born of a gypsy woman Sir John abandoned; Sir John listens with icy composure and dismisses the plea entirely, privately acknowledging the truth only after Gabriel leaves.

On the eve of execution, Gabriel Varden leaves Sir John Chester's chambers despairing for Barnaby's life; in the prison yard Barnaby, Hugh, and the craven hangman Dennis each face death differently, until Barnaby's mother is forcibly dragged away and Barnaby lies down to await the clock.

Hugh faces execution at Newgate with fierce defiance and tenderness toward Barnaby, curses his unknown father, while a serene Barnaby is carted separately to Bloomsbury Square for hanging and Dennis collapses in abject terror as the crowd watches the scaffold.

Joe Willet, home maimed from the American war, tells his father he plans to work for Edward Chester abroad, whereupon Dolly Varden rushes in weeping to confess her lifelong love and pledge herself as his wife, while old Mr Willet watches in stupefied silence.

Geoffrey Haredale forgives Edward Chester and formally gives Emma to him, while Gabriel Varden escorts the last-minute pardoned Barnaby home in triumph; the chapter closes on Edward attending the midnight burial of his unacknowledged half-brother in an unmarked grave.

The Varden household celebrates Dolly's reunion with Joe Willet over a festive tea, until the dismissed servant Miggs barges back uninvited, is firmly turned away by Mrs Varden, and flounces out in a bitter torrent of spite and tears.

Geoffrey Haredale encounters Sir John Chester at the burned Warren, their lifetime enmity explodes into a fatal duel in which Haredale kills Chester, then flees England to a monastery; the closing epilogue sketches the post-riot fates of Barnaby, Dolly Varden, Simon Tappertit, Lord George Gordon, Grip, and the other survivors.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Bleak_House/Chapt.plot: Chapter 1 immerses the reader in fog-drenched, mud-thick London and the Court of Chancery, using the endless Jarndyce and Jarndyce suit as a symbol of systemic legal corruption and human ruin, closing with the Chancellor briefly noting two young wards to be placed with a relative.

Tulkinghorn visits Lady Dedlock in London to read new Chancery affidavits in the Jarndyce case, and she inexplicably faints upon noticing the handwriting on the legal papers, hinting at a secret past.

Esther Summerson narrates her childhood under severe godmother Miss Barbary, the birthday revelation of her shameful origins, godmother's death and lawyer Kenge's disclosure of the Jarndyce suit, six years at Greenleaf school, and her arrival in London where she meets Ada Clare and Richard Carstone before the Lord Chancellor, who approves their placement under John Jarndyce's guardianship at Bleak House.

Esther, Ada, and Richard lodge overnight at Mrs. Jellyby's chaotic London house, where the philanthropist mother ignores her filthy, neglected children while obsessively dictating African charity correspondence, and her eldest daughter Caddy breaks down in a late-night confession of misery to Esther.

Esther, Ada, Richard, and Miss Jellyby take a morning walk and are drawn by an eccentric Chancery suitor into Krook's chaotic rag-and-bottle shop, where the illiterate landlord reveals the names in the Jarndyce suit and recounts Tom Jarndyce's suicide, before the party returns to the Jellyby household and departs.

Esther, Ada, and Richard arrive at Bleak House and are warmly welcomed by Jarndyce; they meet the charming, debt-ridden Harold Skimpole, who is arrested and whose bill Esther and Richard quietly pay, provoking Jarndyce's fond exasperation when he learns of it.

At rain-soaked Chesney Wold, housekeeper Mrs. Rouncewell hosts grandson Watt and two London lawyers (Guppy), who tour the house; Guppy is inexplicably transfixed by Lady Dedlock's portrait, and Mrs. Rouncewell narrates the Ghost's Walk legend—a wronged Dedlock ancestress who vowed to haunt the terrace whenever disgrace or calamity threatens the family.

Esther settles into Bleak House, hears Jarndyce explain the ruinous Chancery suit and Richard's uncertain future, then joins the overbearing Mrs Pardiggle on a visit to a brickmaker's hovel where a baby dies, throwing the contrast between mechanical charity and genuine compassion into sharp relief.

Esther observes Richard and Ada falling quietly in love at Bleak House while old friend Boythorn arrives raging against Sir Leicester Dedlock over a right-of-way dispute; solicitor's clerk Guppy then makes an awkward marriage proposal to Esther, which she firmly rejects.

Tulkinghorn traces the anonymous law-writer "Nemo" via law-stationer Snagsby to a foul garret at Krook's rag-and-bottle shop, where he discovers the man apparently dead or insensible on a bed amid opium fumes.

Mr Tulkinghorn and Krook discover the law-writer Nemo dead of an opium overdose; a coroner's inquest at the Sol's Arms rejects Jo the crossing-sweeper as a witness for ignorance, and Nemo is buried in a pestilential pauper's churchyard that Jo silently sweeps clean at night.

Sir Leicester and Lady Dedlock return from Paris to Chesney Wold for a fashionable winter gathering; Mr Tulkinghorn finally arrives and privately reveals to Lady Dedlock that the mysterious law-writer whose handwriting had stirred her curiosity has been found dead in poverty, leaving both characters watching each other with mutual suspicion.

Richard chooses surgery as his profession and is placed with Mr. Bayham Badger in London, while Ada confesses her love for Richard to Esther, and John Jarndyce gives the young couple his cautious blessing.

Richard departs for his new career while Esther escorts Caddy Jellyby to the Turveydrop dancing academy—where the vain, idle elder Turveydrop exploits his hardworking son—before the group visits Miss Flite, whose landlord Krook ominously names her caged birds (Hope, Ruin, Death, Madness, and more) and shadows Mr. Jarndyce with watchful unease.

Jarndyce, Esther, Ada, and Skimpole visit the Bell Yard lodgings of the recently dead debt-collector Neckett, discovering his three orphaned children kept by thirteen-year-old Charley through washing work, and encounter the furious Gridley, the ruined "man from Shropshire," who denounces the Court of Chancery for destroying his life.

Lady Dedlock, veiled and disguised as a servant, seeks out Jo the crossing-sweeper and pays him to guide her to the places associated with the dead Nemo—his lodgings at Krook's and his pauper grave—while Mr Tulkinghorn broods in his chambers and Sir Leicester languishes with gout at Chesney Wold.

Richard abandons his medical training to pursue law (hoping to watch over the Chancery suit), Jarndyce privately discloses to Esther the scant facts of her birth and unknown aunt, and Allan Woodcourt departs on a long sea voyage leaving flowers anonymously for Esther.

Esther's party travels to Boythorn's Lincolnshire estate; at Sunday church in Chesney Wold park Esther is struck by an inexplicable, unsettling sense of recognition when Lady Dedlock's eyes meet hers, and the feeling recurs when Lady Dedlock unexpectedly takes shelter with them in a keeper's lodge during a storm, ending with Mademoiselle Hortense walking barefoot through wet grass in wounded pride.

Jo the crossing-sweeper is arrested for refusing to "move on" and brought to Snagsby's shop, where his account of a veiled lady who paid him to show her Nemo's haunts is interrogated by Guppy during a tea gathering with the pompous preacher Chadband, culminating in Mrs. Chadband's revelation that she once had charge of Esther Summerson.

Guppy arranges for his financially ruined friend Jobling, under the false name Weevle, to lodge secretly at Krook's rag-and-bottle shop, with the covert aim of investigating the enigmatic old landlord.

Trooper Mr. George visits the miserly Smallweed family to pay two months' interest on a loan, reveals he once knew the missing Captain Hawdon (whom he believes drowned), then returns to his shooting gallery where he sleeps alongside his scarred assistant Phil.

Tulkinghorn dispatches Inspector Bucket and Snagsby to the slum Tom-all-Alone's to retrieve Jo, who is then brought to Tulkinghorn's chambers and asked to identify a veiled woman; Jo confirms the dress matches the mysterious lady but not the hands or voice, revealing the figure is Hortense impersonating Lady Dedlock.

Esther holds a frank London conversation with the debt-ridden, Chancery-obsessed Richard who resolves to join the army instead of finishing his legal articles; then accompanies Caddy to secure old Mr Turveydrop's theatrical blessing and Mrs Jellyby's placid indifference to the engagement; and returns to Bleak House to find John Jarndyce has given her the orphan girl Charley as a personal maid.

Richard obtains his army commission and Jarndyce dissolves his informal engagement to Ada before departure; Richard and Esther then witness the absurd Chancery proceedings and follow Mr George to his shooting gallery, where Inspector Bucket—disguised as a physician—reveals himself to arrest the fugitive Gridley, who dies on the spot.

Tormented by guilt over his secret involvement with Jo and Mr. Bucket, Mr. Snagsby endures his jealous wife's surveillance and a hypocritical sermon by Chadband — who uses Jo as preaching fodder — while Mrs. Snagsby has a hysterical fit convinced Jo is her husband's illegitimate son; Snagsby slips Jo money and urges him to stay silent about "the lady."

Grandfather Smallweed visits Mr. George's shooting gallery and, after much evasion, pressures him to produce a handwriting sample of the deceased Captain Hawdon for a mysterious lawyer's inquiry; George reluctantly agrees to accompany Smallweed to meet the lawyer, taking a paper from his cupboard.

Smallweed brings trooper Mr. George to Tulkinghorn, who tries to obtain a specimen of dead Captain Hawdon's handwriting; George refuses, consults the sensible Mrs. Bagnet, then returns to confirm his refusal, and Tulkinghorn dismisses him angrily, branding him associate of the dangerous Gridley.

Ironmaster Rouncewell visits Chesney Wold to propose that his son court Rosa (Lady Dedlock's protégée) on condition she leave service there, sparking a sharp clash between Sir Leicester's aristocratic pride and the industrialist's self-made values, while Lady Dedlock privately reveals a tender, melancholy attachment to the girl.

Guppy visits Lady Dedlock to reveal he has uncovered Esther Summerson's real name is Hawdon, that a dead law-writer named Hawdon visited Lady Dedlock's past, and that a disguised noblewoman visited Hawdon's grave—evidence pointing to Esther as Lady Dedlock's secret daughter, leaving Lady Dedlock shattered and crying "O my child!"

Esther hosts the scheming Mrs Woodcourt, who subtly steers her away from any hope regarding Allan Woodcourt, then Esther helps Caddy Jellyby prepare her trousseau and witnesses Caddy's wedding to Prince Turveydrop, while Mrs Jellyby remains indifferent to her own daughter's marriage.

Esther finds the gravely ill Jo at a brickmaker's cottage and brings him to Bleak House over Skimpole's callous objections; after Jo vanishes in the night, Charley falls ill with his fever, Esther nurses her back from near-death while keeping Ada away, then contracts the illness herself and ends the chapter blind.
Weevle and Guppy meet at midnight to retrieve Hawdon's letters from Krook, but descend to find only greasy ash where the old man stood — Krook has been destroyed by spontaneous combustion.

After Krook's death by spontaneous combustion the Smallweed family descends to claim his estate as next of kin with Tulkinghorn as solicitor, shutting out Guppy who had hoped to seize Krook's papers; Guppy then visits Lady Dedlock to report the letters implicating her are destroyed, and Tulkinghorn witnesses the meeting.

Smallweed calls in a debt that threatens to ruin George's guarantor Bagnet; George and Bagnet are ejected by Smallweed and then negotiate with Tulkinghorn, who agrees to shield Bagnet legally only after George surrenders a private letter Tulkinghorn has long wanted.

Esther convalesces from a disfiguring illness, keeping Ada at bay; Jarndyce visits and laments Richard's Chancery-warped estrangement; eccentric Miss Flite dines with Esther, recounts Chancery's destruction of her own family, and reveals Woodcourt's heroism in a shipwreck—prompting Esther to silently release any hope of his love.

Esther, convalescing at Chesney Wold, confronts her scarred face in the mirror and accepts her changed appearance; Lady Dedlock then seeks her out in the park woods and reveals herself as Esther's mother, demanding they never meet again and confessing dread of Tulkinghorn's suspicions, before Ada arrives and reunites with Esther in tearful joy.

Richard secretly visits Esther and Ada at Boythorn's estate with Skimpole in tow, insists Jarndyce is an interested party in the suit and refuses all counsel to abandon it, then abruptly departs with his new solicitor Vholes when Jarndyce and Jarndyce is called into the Chancellor's paper.

Esther, restored to health, visits Caddy Jellyby's busy dancing household in London and then calls on Mr. Guppy to formally persuade him to abandon any inquiry into her origins, extracting his sworn promise to leave the matter alone.

Richard Carstone, financially and morally eroding, meets with his parasitic lawyer Vholes after another fruitless Chancery session and deepens his resentment of Jarndyce, while Guppy and Weevle retrieve belongings from Krook's former shop and encounter Tulkinghorn, who obliquely hints he knows of Guppy's secret connection to Lady Dedlock.

Tulkinghorn arrives at Chesney Wold during election season, reports Sir Leicester's political losses including Rouncewell's damaging opposition, then tells a thinly veiled allegorical story of a great lady who concealed an illegitimate child — a clear covert threat aimed at Lady Dedlock, who listens in rigid, silent terror.

Lady Dedlock confronts Tulkinghorn in his turret room demanding to know who he has told her secret, then attempts to flee Chesney Wold; Tulkinghorn stops her by threatening to raise the alarm, and forces her to maintain her public façade while he decides what to do, leaving her trapped under his absolute control.
Mademoiselle Hortense confronts Tulkinghorn in his chambers demanding employment or revenge against Lady Dedlock; he threatens her with imprisonment and orders her never to return.

Jarndyce takes Esther and Ada to Skimpole's dilapidated Somers Town home to caution him against draining Richard's money; Sir Leicester Dedlock then pays an unexpected visit to Bleak House, which finally compels Esther to confess to Jarndyce that Lady Dedlock is her mother.

Jarndyce writes Esther a marriage proposal letter asking her to become mistress of Bleak House; after a week of reflection, burning keepsake flowers, and tearful self-examination, Esther accepts him in person.

Esther travels to Deal after Vholes warns Jarndyce of Richard's debts; she delivers Ada's letter offering her inheritance to save him, but Richard—selling his army commission to fund the Chancery suit—refuses all dissuasion, and on leaving Esther unexpectedly meets Allan Woodcourt and enlists him as Richard's friend and guardian.

At dawn in Tom-all-Alone's, Allan Woodcourt treats a brickmaker's wife's injury, then chases down the fugitive Jo and learns that Jo was forcibly removed from Esther's house by a mysterious powerful man—having unknowingly infected her—and now drifts toward death.
Allan Woodcourt shelters the gravely ill Jo at Mr. George's shooting gallery, where Jo makes his dying "will" asking forgiveness and burial beside Nemo, then dies reciting the Lord's Prayer.

Lady Dedlock dismisses her maid Rosa to protect her from the shame of her own secret, but Tulkinghorn declares their non-disclosure agreement void and threatens imminent exposure of Lady Dedlock to Sir Leicester — and is found shot dead in his chambers before morning.

Inspector Bucket attends the Bagnet family's birthday celebration under a pretence of sociability, then manoeuvres trooper George alone and arrests him as a suspect in the murder of Mr. Tulkinghorn, for which Sir Leicester Dedlock has posted a reward.

Esther nurses the ailing Caddy Jellyby in London while confiding her engagement to Jarndyce, but notices Ada growing quietly sorrowful and self-deceivingly concludes Ada grieves for her sake, missing whatever Ada truly conceals.

Esther visits Richard at Symond's Inn, where Ada reveals she has secretly married Richard and will not return home; Richard's haggard decline under the Chancery suit is starkly visible, and John Jarndyce receives the news with sorrowful blessing.

Esther, Jarndyce, and Woodcourt visit imprisoned Mr. George — accused of murdering Tulkinghorn — who stubbornly refuses legal counsel, while George's mention of a cloaked figure at the murder scene shocks Esther into suspecting her mother Lady Dedlock, and Mrs. Bagnet sets off for Lincolnshire to fetch George's long-lost mother as potential leverage.

Inspector Bucket attends Tulkinghorn's elaborate funeral in disguise, collects multiple anonymous letters naming Lady Dedlock, reports cryptically to Sir Leicester that the case is nearly complete, and covertly confirms from a footman that Lady Dedlock was walking outside alone on the night of the murder — closing the net around her as prime suspect.

Inspector Bucket discloses Lady Dedlock's secret past to a devastated Sir Leicester, neutralizes a gang of blackmailers (Smallweed, Chadband, Mrs. Snagsby), then arrests Mademoiselle Hortense for the murder of Tulkinghorn, producing pistol and forged letters as proof gathered through his wife's covert surveillance.

Mrs. Rouncewell and Mrs. Bagnet travel to London to reunite Mrs. Rouncewell with her imprisoned son George (accused of Tulkinghorn's murder); Mrs. Rouncewell then confronts Lady Dedlock with a letter branding her "murderess," Guppy warns Lady Dedlock her compromising secrets are exposed, and Lady Dedlock writes a farewell to Sir Leicester declaring innocence of the murder and flees.

Sir Leicester suffers a paralytic stroke on learning Lady Dedlock has fled; Inspector Bucket is commissioned to find her, searches her rooms, discovers Esther Summerson's handkerchief, then enlists Esther—waking John Jarndyce—to accompany him on the urgent nighttime pursuit.

Inspector Bucket and Esther race through a winter night searching for the fugitive Lady Dedlock, gathering clues from brickmakers and roadside informants—while Bucket exposes Skimpole's paid betrayal of Jo—before reversing course back toward London when Bucket deduces Lady Dedlock has swapped identities with Jenny the brickmaker's wife.

Gravely ill Sir Leicester Dedlock waits through a wintry day and night for the absent Lady Dedlock to return, while London gossip swirls around her disgrace; attended by the newly returned George Rouncewell, he formally declares before witnesses his unaltered love and forgiveness toward her, but she does not come.

Esther Summerson and Inspector Bucket race through pre-dawn London, recover Lady Dedlock's farewell letter from the Snagsbys' epileptic servant Guster, and follow her trail to a squalid burial ground where Esther lifts the face of the woman lying dead at the iron gate and recognises her own mother.

Recovered Esther resumes her place beside guardian Jarndyce, who plans a Yorkshire medical post for Woodcourt; she visits Richard and Ada daily, watching Richard waste away under Vholes and Chancery's grip, until Ada confesses her steadfast love and reveals she is pregnant, fearing Richard may not live to see the child.

Esther confronts Skimpole to stop visiting the ailing Richard and Ada; he agrees for purely selfish reasons and shamelessly justifies accepting Bucket's bribe to betray Jo; that same evening Woodcourt confesses his love to Esther, who gently refuses him as already committed, yet is deeply moved and resolves to be worthier of his devotion.

Inspector Bucket brings moneylender Smallweed to Bleak House to surrender a newly discovered Jarndyce will (found in Krook's papers); Jarndyce and Esther deliver it to solicitor Kenge, who reveals it materially advances Richard Carstone and Ada Clare's interests — all while Jarndyce and Esther have privately agreed she will become mistress of Bleak House next month.

George the trooper travels to his ironmaster brother Rouncewell's factory in the industrial north, where the two reconcile joyfully; George declines to join the business, choosing instead to return and serve the ailing Sir Leicester Dedlock at Chesney Wold, and sends a formal letter to Esther Summerson clarifying his past role in delivering a letter on instructions from abroad.

Jarndyce brings Esther to a cottage he has secretly prepared and named Bleak House as a gift for Woodcourt, releases her from their engagement so she may marry Woodcourt instead, and then Guppy arrives to comically renew his marriage proposal, which Jarndyce firmly rejects on Esther's behalf.
The Jarndyce and Jarndyce suit ends having consumed the entire estate in costs, and the news breaks Richard Carstone, who dies reconciled with John Jarndyce and cradled in Ada's arms.
After Lady Dedlock's death, Chesney Wold falls into gloomy emptiness while the aged, near-blind Sir Leicester silently pays tribute at her mausoleum and the estate decays around him.

Seven years on, Esther closes her narrative by recounting the peaceful domestic life she, husband Allan, guardian Jarndyce, and Ada with her infant son Richard now share, marking full recovery from sorrow and the resolution of all major relationships.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/David_Copperfield.plot: David narrates his own birth on a Friday night at Blunderstone, introducing his posthumous existence as son of a dead father and a fragile young widow, while the domineering great-aunt Betsey Trotwood arrives expecting a girl to champion, then storms out in contempt upon learning the newborn is a boy.

Young David recalls earliest memories of home with his mother and Peggotty, while the dark Mr. Murdstone begins courting the widowed Mrs. Copperfield, stirring in David instinctive jealousy and dread, before Peggotty arranges a trip to Yarmouth.

David travels to Yarmouth with Peggotty, stays in Mr Peggotty's converted boat-house, bonds with Little Em'ly in a childhood idyll, then returns home to learn his mother has secretly married Mr Murdstone.

After Miss Murdstone arrives and seizes control of the household, David fails his lessons under the Murdstones' oppressive watch, bites Murdstone's hand during a brutal beating, is locked in his room for five days, and is finally sent away to boarding school.

David travels alone by cart and coach from Blunderstone to Salem House school, is swindled by a waiter in Yarmouth, and arrives during the empty holiday term to spend his days in desolate isolation wearing a "HE BITES" placard — punishment for biting Murdstone — while Steerforth's name carved on the playground door foreshadows future encounters.

David, still wearing his humiliating placard at Salem House, is summoned by the bullying headmaster Creakle and then taken under the wing of the dominant older boy Steerforth, who appropriates David's money to host a clandestine midnight feast and appoints himself David's protector.

David endures Mr. Creakle's brutal flogging regime at Salem House, earns Steerforth's protection by entertaining him with nightly stories, then watches Steerforth publicly expose teacher Mr. Mell's poverty and cause his dismissal, before Mr. Peggotty and Ham arrive with a surprise visit bearing shellfish and news from home.

David returns home for school holidays, shares one tender fireside evening with his mother and Peggotty (revealing Barkis's courtship of Peggotty), then suffers weeks of suffocating constraint under the Murdstones before departing with a haunting final image of his fragile mother holding his infant brother at the garden gate.
David learns on his birthday that his mother has died, returns home from Salem House for the funeral, and hears Peggotty recount his mother's final days and dying words.

After his mother's death David is coldly neglected by the Murdstones; he accompanies Peggotty to Yarmouth where she secretly marries Mr. Barkis, then returns home only to be dispatched by Murdstone to earn his keep at the Murdstone and Grinby warehouse in London.

Ten-year-old David begins labouring at Murdstone and Grinby's warehouse and lodges with the perpetually insolvent Micawber family, enduring secret misery while Micawber is arrested for debt and imprisoned, yet David persists alone in his degrading existence without revealing his suffering to anyone.

After Micawber is discharged from debtor's prison and the family departs for Plymouth, David—facing renewed isolation at Murdstone and Grinby's—resolves to run away to his aunt Betsey Trotwood near Dover, but a dishonest carter steals his half-guinea and luggage, leaving him penniless and alone on the road to Greenwich.

Penniless David walks six days from London to Dover, selling clothes to survive and enduring trampers and a mad shopkeeper, until he reaches Aunt Betsey Trotwood's cottage, reveals himself as her nephew, breaks down weeping, and is taken in, bathed, and put to bed.

Betsey Trotwood deliberates David's fate, then fiercely confronts Murdstone when he arrives to reclaim the boy, rejects his authority, and resolves to keep David as her ward under the new name Trotwood Copperfield.

Betsey Trotwood drives David to Canterbury to find him a school, visits lawyer Wickfield who offers to board David in his house, and David meets the unsettling Uriah Heep and the serene Agnes Wickfield for the first time.

David enrolls at Doctor Strong's school and settles into the Wickfield household, has his first extended encounter with the obsequiously "umble" Uriah Heep, and witnesses Jack Maldon's India farewell party, where Annie Strong's swoon and anguished expression hint at a secret attachment to her departing cousin.

David, settled at Doctor Strong's, exchanges letters with Peggotty and hosts Mr. Dick's Wednesday visits; during tea at the Heep household Uriah and his mother worm confidences about Wickfield and Agnes out of him, then Micawber unexpectedly walks in, befriends Uriah, and departs Canterbury with a melodramatic debt-confession letter after a jovial farewell dinner.

David retrospectively surveys his Canterbury school years through two failed crushes (Miss Shepherd and Miss Larkins) and a losing fight with a butcher, tracing his gradual growth from boy to head-boy while Agnes serves as steady companion and confidante.

David leaves school, bids farewell to Agnes and the Wickfields in Canterbury (where he notices Wickfield's dark suspicion about Annie Strong and the returning Jack Maldon), then travels to London and unexpectedly reunites with his old idol Steerforth at the Golden Cross hotel.

David accompanies Steerforth to his Highgate home, where he meets Steerforth's proud mother and the caustic Rosa Dartle, witnesses Steerforth's casual class contempt toward working people like Peggotty's family, and secures Steerforth's promise to travel with him to Suffolk.

David and Steerforth travel to Yarmouth, where David joyfully reunites with Peggotty and Mr Barkis, then surprises Mr Peggotty's household to discover that Em'ly and Ham have just announced their engagement, while Steerforth's charismatic ease with the fishing family hints at the predatory interest he is concealing.

David and Steerforth linger near Yarmouth—David revisiting Blunderstone graves while Steerforth buys a boat renamed "Little Em'ly" and suffers a dark crisis of conscience—then the chapter closes with fallen woman Martha Endell appealing to Emily for money to flee to London, leaving Emily in guilty tears in Peggotty's arms.

David returns from Yarmouth with Steerforth, consults him about becoming a proctor at Doctors' Commons, reunites with Aunt Betsey who pays off a mysterious threatening stranger, then visits Spenlow and Jorkins to arrange his articles and secures his first independent chambers in the Adelphi.

David hosts a raucous dinner party in his new bachelor rooms with Steerforth and two Oxford friends, drinks to excess, stumbles to the theatre where he humiliatingly encounters Agnes, and wakes the next day consumed by remorse and shame.

Agnes warns David that Steerforth is his "bad angel" and that Uriah has gained coercive power over her father; at a Waterbrook dinner party obsessed with aristocratic "Blood," David encounters Uriah again, who later confesses his calculated scheme to exploit Mr. Wickfield's weakness and win Agnes as his wife.

David, troubled by fears for Agnes under Uriah Heep's shadow, accompanies Mr. Spenlow to his Norwood home where he instantly and helplessly falls in love with Dora Spenlow, while Miss Murdstone—Dora's unwelcome companion—resurfaces from David's childhood.

David visits old schoolfellow Traddles in his cramped Camden Town room, learns of his legal struggles and long engagement, and discovers the perpetually debt-ridden Micawbers are Traddles's landlords.

David hosts a chaotic dinner for the Micawbers and Traddles; Mrs. Micawber urges Micawber to "throw down the gauntlet" to society via newspaper advertisement, but a post-party letter reveals he is crushed by debt and has already signed Traddles's name to a bill; Steerforth then arrives unexpectedly bearing a letter from Peggotty reporting that Barkis is dying, and persuades David to delay a Yarmouth visit by one day.

David visits Steerforth at his Highgate home, where Rosa Dartle's jealous surveillance and cryptic interrogation expose her obsessive feelings for Steerforth; after dinner she plays harp under his persuasion but violently rejects his embrace, and the chapter closes with a tender, ominous farewell between David and Steerforth as the narrator laments they will never again meet in friendship.

David arrives in Yarmouth, learns Barkis is dying; after a conversation with Mr. Omer about Emily's unsettled attachment to her uncle, he joins Peggotty and Mr. Peggotty at the deathbed, where Barkis revives briefly to say "Barkis is willin'" and dies with the ebbing tide.
After settling Barkis's will and attending his funeral, David learns at the Peggotty boathouse that Little Emily has eloped with Steerforth, shattering Mr. Peggotty and Ham.

After Little Emily's elopement with Steerforth, Mr Peggotty resolves to search the world for her; he and David travel to London, confront a cold Mrs Steerforth who refuses any marriage, while Miss Mowcher visits David to confess her unwitting complicity, and the chapter closes with Mr Peggotty departing alone on his open-ended quest.

David escorts Peggotty through her legal affairs (where Murdstone briefly appears collecting a marriage licence), then attends Dora's birthday picnic, declares his love, and the two become secretly engaged through the mediation of Miss Mills.

Betsey Trotwood arrives unannounced at David's London chambers with all her belongings and announces she is completely ruined, urging David to face misfortune with courage; meanwhile Traddles recounts Micawber's debt troubles and enlists Peggotty to recover Sophy's flower-pot from a broker's shop.

After Betsey Trotwood's ruin forces David to confront poverty and a failed attempt to cancel his legal articles, Agnes Wickfield arrives in London, secures him a secretarial post with Doctor Strong, and exposes Uriah Heep's suffocating grip over her father—while David's anxious obsession with Dora colours his every despairing thought.

Spurred by financial ruin into furious industry, David secures extra work assisting Dr. Strong's dictionary, resolves to master shorthand, arranges copying employment for the troubled Mr. Dick, and learns from the departing Micawbers that Micawber has taken a clerical post under Uriah Heep in Canterbury.

David confesses his ruin to Dora and urges her toward practical housekeeping, but she recoils from all talk of hardship, revealing her charming yet wholly impractical nature, while Peggotty departs and Betsey Trotwood settles firmly into Buckingham Street.

Miss Murdstone discovers David's love letters to Dora and exposes the secret courtship to Mr. Spenlow, who confronts David and orders the romance abandoned; days later Spenlow dies suddenly in his carriage, leaving his affairs in chaos and Dora penniless, while David suffers helpless anguish as she mourns her father.

David visits Canterbury, finds Micawber clerking for Heep, confides in Agnes about Dora, then witnesses Uriah's suffocating surveillance of the household, his brazen declaration of intent to marry Agnes, and Mr. Wickfield's anguished breakdown revealing how Heep has systematically destroyed him.

On a snowy London night David encounters Mr Peggotty, who recounts his months-long quest across France, Italy, and Switzerland for Little Emily, shares her remorseful letters begging forgiveness, and resolves to set out again at dawn following a postal clue to the Upper Rhine.

David and Traddles visit Dora's maiden aunts (the Misses Spenlow) to seek formal permission to court Dora; the aunts grant conditional visiting rights under strict terms, and David is briefly reunited with Dora, who is treated as a charming plaything by everyone around her, including David himself.

Uriah Heep forces a confrontation in which he and Mr. Wickfield expose Doctor Strong to long-suppressed suspicions about his young wife Annie's attachment to Jack Maldon, wounding the Doctor deeply; meanwhile Agnes visits and immediately bonds with Dora, and a letter from Mrs. Micawber alerts David that Micawber has become disturbingly secretive under Uriah's employ.

David, now 21 and earning income as parliamentary reporter and writer, marries Dora Spenlow in a dreamlike ceremony attended by Betsey Trotwood, Agnes Wickfield, and Peggotty, while Mr Peggotty is glimpsed haunting dark streets in search of Emily.

Newly married David and Dora bungle housekeeping and cycle through incompetent servants; Betsey Trotwood counsels patience and refuses to interfere; Dora asks David to always think of her as his "child-wife," accepting her limitations.

Mr. Dick engineers a meeting that prompts Annie Strong to kneel before her husband and deliver a full confession of her suppressed secret—Maldon's dishonorable conduct and her own silence—restoring trust and reconciling the estranged couple, while David finally reveals what he witnessed that earlier night.

David is summoned by Miss Dartle, who has Littimer recount how Steerforth abandoned Emily in Italy and she escaped; David then brings the news to the grieving Mr Peggotty, and together they set out through London to find Martha, hoping she can lead them to the missing Emily.

David and Mr. Peggotty intercept Martha on the Thames riverbank as she contemplates suicide, persuade her to search for Little Emily instead, and on returning home David discovers Betsey Trotwood secretly paying off her estranged, still-living husband.

David narrates domestic chaos with a thieving page, his failed project to "form" Dora's mind, his resignation to loving her as she is, and the ominous onset of Dora's physical decline as Betsey Trotwood nurses her.

Micawber sends David a cryptic letter arranging a secret meeting near the King's Bench Prison, then at Betsey Trotwood's Highgate house breaks down and dramatically reveals that his employer Uriah Heep is a villain guilty of fraud and deception, vowing to expose him at a Canterbury gathering the following week.

Martha leads David to a London lodging house where Rosa Dartle savagely confronts and humiliates the fallen Emily, but Mr Peggotty arrives in time, and carries his unconscious niece away, his long dream of finding her at last fulfilled.

Mr Peggotty tells David and Betsey Trotwood the full story of Emily's flight, fever, and rescue by Martha; they then travel to Yarmouth for farewell, where Ham asks David to carry a message of forgiveness to Emily, and Mrs Gummidge unexpectedly begs to join the Australia emigration, winning Mr Peggotty's consent.

Micawber confronts Uriah Heep at the Wickfield office, reading aloud a letter that catalogues Heep's years of forgery and fraud against Mr. Wickfield, forcing Heep to surrender incriminating documents; the chapter ends with Betsey Trotwood proposing that the Micawbers emigrate to Australia as reward for their service.

David keeps vigil at dying Dora's bedside through three remembered scenes; Dora confesses she was too young for marriage and asks to see Agnes alone, then Jip dies at David's feet and Agnes's mute, upraised gesture signals Dora has also died.

In the aftermath of Uriah Heep's exposure, Traddles reports that Betsey Trotwood's embezzled money is recovered, Mr. Wickfield's accounts are cleared, and the Micawber family are financed to emigrate; meanwhile Betsey reveals her estranged husband has died in hospital, closing that long-hidden wound.

David travels to Yarmouth during a catastrophic storm to deliver Emily's farewell letter to Ham; Ham dies heroically trying to swim out to a wrecked ship, and Steerforth's body washes ashore as the sole casualty from the wreck.

David brings Steerforth's drowned corpse to his mother's house at Highgate, where Rosa Dartle erupts in a frenzied tirade blaming Mrs. Steerforth for her son's ruinous upbringing and confessing her own obsessive love for him, while the mother sits rigid and speechless with shock.

David conceals a recent catastrophe from Mr Peggotty and sees the emigrant party — the Micawbers, Mr Peggotty, Little Emily, and Martha — off to Australia, with Micawber arrested twice and released before the ship sails at sunset.

David wanders Europe for three years after Dora's death, descending into despair, until Agnes's letter reaches him in Switzerland and reignites his will to work — while he silently realises he loves her but resolves the feeling is too late and must be renounced.

David returns to England after years abroad, joyfully reunites with the newly married Traddles in Gray's Inn, learns from Dr. Chillip that Murdstone's religious tyranny has broken his new wife, then travels to Dover where Betsey Trotwood, Peggotty, and Mr. Dick welcome him with open arms.

David returns to Canterbury and reunites with Agnes, who calms his lingering grief; her father reveals the tragic story of Agnes's mother, while David wrestles silently with his suppressed love for Agnes, vowing to revere her as his lifelong spiritual guide.

David and Traddles visit Creakle's model prison and discover that the celebrated model penitents Numbers Twenty Seven and Twenty Eight are the unreformed villains Uriah Heep and Littimer, whose pious performances David sees through as cynical self-interest.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Little_Dorrit/Cha.plot: Arthur Clennam follows Amy Dorrit to the Marshalsea, meets her father William (the self-styled "Father of the Marshalsea") and uncle Frederick, witnesses Amy's self-sacrificing care, is accidentally locked in overnight, and lies awake haunted by the suspicion that his mother deliberately kept William Dorrit imprisoned as a form of self-exculpatory justice.

Arthur Clennam arranges to meet Amy Dorrit outside the Marshalsea, walks with her to the Iron Bridge where she defends her father and reveals the family's circumstances, then accompanies her back to the prison gate where they encounter Maggy, the childlike woman who calls Amy "little mother."

Clennam navigates the Circumlocution Office's deliberate obstructions while inquiring about Dorrit's debt, then meets Mr Meagles dragging out Daniel Doyce, an engineer whose decade-long invention has been endlessly stonewalled by the same system.

Rigaud, a wife-murderer acquitted and notorious in Marseilles, arrives exhausted at a French roadside inn under the alias Lagnier, discovers his former prison companion Cavalletto asleep there, coerces him into keeping silent about his true identity, and forces him to travel together toward Paris and England — prompting Cavalletto to flee at dawn.

Arthur Clennam visits Bleeding Heart Yard (site of Daniel Doyce's factory), meets the impoverished Plornish family to gather intelligence on the Dorrits, then anonymously pays off Tip Dorrit's debt through Plornish as intermediary to secure his release from prison.

Clennam visits the fraudulently benevolent patriarch Casby and his former love Flora—now the voluble, changed Mrs Finching—is disillusioned, dines with her and rent-agent Pancks, then returns home to brood on his wasted life until an unseen visitor whispers "Little Dorrit."

Amy Dorrit visits Arthur Clennam late at night to express wordless gratitude for freeing her brother and to beg him never to lend money to her father, then she and Maggy are locked out of the Marshalsea and spend the freezing night wandering London until dawn — this bleak vigil is bitterly named her "party."

Mistress Affery, half-asleep, overhears a tense argument in which Flintwinch accuses Mrs Clennam of failing to clear Arthur's father's name; meanwhile Affery grows increasingly terrified by mysterious noises in the decaying house, and the chapter closes as Little Dorrit and then Arthur briefly arrive.

Clennam walks to Twickenham, meets Doyce en route and learns of his need for a business partner, visits the Meagles family, internally resolves not to fall in love with Pet, and privately proposes himself to Mr Meagles as Doyce's prospective partner.

Arthur Clennam meets Henry Gowan at the Meagles home, learns from Daniel Doyce that Gowan has long been courting Pet while her parents disapprove, and ends the day in silent anguish over a love he insists he has renounced.

Young John Chivery, the turnkey's son hopelessly devoted to Amy, visits William Dorrit at the Marshalsea then finds Amy on the Iron Bridge where she gently but firmly rejects his unspoken declaration, leaving him heartbroken.

William Dorrit parades his authority as Father of the Marshalsea, then collapses in self-pitying breakdown before Amy, who tends him through the night while he oscillates between grandiosity and despair over his twenty-three years of captivity.

Amy Dorrit visits sister Fanny at the theatre then accompanies her to Mrs Merdle's Harley Street mansion, where Mrs Merdle recounts how she paid Fanny (with bracelet and dressmaker gifts) to rebuff her son's romantic pursuit; Amy's distress at Fanny accepting the bribe triggers a bitter argument about family honour, pride, and who truly sacrifices for the Dorrits.

At a grand Harley Street dinner, Society magnates fawn over the immensely wealthy Mr Merdle and solicit his influence, while a physician privately discloses he can find nothing physically wrong with Merdle despite the financier's vague but ominous sense of complaint.

Mrs Chivery reveals her son John proposed to Amy Dorrit and was refused; Clennam then meets Amy on the Iron Bridge, intercepts begging letters from her father and brother, and is left puzzling over Amy's hidden feelings and whether she secretly loves someone out of reach.

Clennam and Doyce formalise their business partnership at Bleeding Heart Yard; Flora Finching pays a comic visit and offers to employ Little Dorrit; Pancks then returns alone to secretly probe Clennam for everything he knows about the Dorrit family, striking a mutual-information bargain and hinting at undisclosed research into their affairs.

Amy Dorrit begins working as companion to Flora Finching, who rambles about her old romance with Arthur Clennam; Mr Pancks reads Amy's palm, cryptically promises a future revelation, and starts shadowing her at the Marshalsea — while Amy retreats inward and tells Maggy an allegory of a tiny woman who guards a shadow of lost love until death.

Mr Pancks orchestrates a covert investigation with Mr Rugg and Young John Chivery, distributing research tasks across England to trace a hidden inheritance, while separately befriending the cheerful Italian immigrant Cavalletto in Bleeding Heart Yard.

Clennam, suppressing his love for Pet Meagles and calling it "nobody's state of mind," accompanies Henry Gowan to dine with Gowan's aristocratic mother at Hampton Court, where he endures her class contempt and her conviction that the Meagles family are scheming to catch her son.

Clennam learns from Mr Meagles that Tattycoram has fled to Miss Wade; they track her to a dingy Grosvenor-area lodging and appeal for her return, but Tattycoram defiantly refuses, while Miss Wade claims solidarity with her on grounds of shared nameless birth.

Arthur Clennam walks to the Meagles cottage where Pet confides she is to marry Gowan; Clennam suppresses his own love, blesses her, and finally surrenders his last hope by floating her roses down the moonlit river.

Mr Pancks visits and is curtly dismissed by Mrs Clennam, who then questions Amy Dorrit about him and surprises everyone by kissing her forehead; outside in a storm, a sinister foreign traveller (Rigaud) climbs through a window to let Affery back in, then waits ominously in the house while she fetches Mr Flintwinch.

Blandois — revealed as Rigaud in disguise — arrives at the Clennam house with a letter of credit, tours the premises, probes Mrs Clennam and Flintwinch for secrets, then abruptly departs to the Continent, leaving an ominous promise to return.

Amy escorts Old Nandy (a workhouse pauper) into the Marshalsea, shaming William Dorrit whose wounded "Spirit" erupts in reproach; Clennam then visits and Tip publicly accuses him of refusing a loan, sparking a second quarrel over dignity that ends with Tip and Fanny storming out.

Arthur Clennam visits Amy Dorrit at Marshalsea and confides he has renounced romantic love, unknowingly wounding her, before Pancks bursts in to reveal he has discovered the Dorrit family's unclaimed fortune.

Mrs Gowan visits Mrs Merdle to extract social validation for her grudging consent to son Henry's marriage below their station, staging elaborate hypocrisy; then Mr Merdle returns home and is rebuked by his wife for visibly carrying business anxieties into Society, after which he wanders his mansion alone and extinguished.

Pet Meagles marries Henry Gowan at a wedding swarmed by Barnacle family members epitomising Circumlocution Office corruption, while Clennam attends to honour his promise and observes Gowan's cynical self-pity and Mr Meagles's bittersweet pride; Daniel Doyce declines the invitation to avoid fraternising with the officials who obstructed him.

Mr Pancks reveals to Clennam that William Dorrit is heir to a vast forgotten estate; Clennam tells Amy at Flora Finching's house (she faints), then they go to the Marshalsea and deliver the news to William Dorrit, who learns he will soon walk free and wealthy.

William Dorrit stages a grand ceremonial departure from the Marshalsea, distributing money and condescension to fellow prisoners, but Amy is left behind and found fainted by Arthur Clennam, who carries her out to the carriage.
Chapter_40 is the title-only divider marking the start of Book the Second ("Riches") with no narrative content or characters present.

The Dorrit family and other travellers shelter overnight at the Great Saint Bernard convent during an Alpine crossing; Amy secretly visits the injured Mrs Gowan and passes her a note, while the sinister Rigaud (signing as Blandois) spots the Dorrit name in the guest book and declares he too is bound for Italy.

Mrs General's backstory is narrated — a widow of rigid propriety who earns living "forming minds" of wealthy daughters — and William Dorrit hires her as companion and chaperon for his girls after inheriting his fortune.

The Dorrit family descends from the Great Saint Bernard and travels through Switzerland and Italy to Venice; Amy is rebuked for befriending Mrs Gowan and for old humble habits, Mr Dorrit erupts at an innkeeper over a room occupied by Mrs Merdle, Blandois/Rigaud watches ominously as they depart, and Amy drifts through the entire journey in a dreamlike state unable to shed her Marshalsea identity.

From Venice, Amy Dorrit writes Clennam a heartfelt letter confessing her inability to adapt to new wealth and grandeur, her persistent longing for old friends and the Marshalsea past, and begging him to remember her unchanged as the same poor girl he once sheltered.

William Dorrit, coached by Mrs General, rebukes Amy for failing to adopt aristocratic surface manners and forget the Marshalsea; Uncle Frederick dramatically protests against the family's pride and ingratitude toward Amy, then shuffles out, and the scene is conspired to be kept from her.

Amy and Fanny visit Mrs Gowan's Venice studio where Gowan's dog Lion lunges at Blandois/Rigaud; Fanny then orchestrates Mr Sparkler's courtship at dinner and the opera, and Blandois closes the chapter revealing that Lion has been poisoned.

Fanny warns Amy that Mrs General is scheming to marry their father; Rigaud (Blandois) pays a farewell visit in Venice during which Mrs Gowan secretly tells Amy he poisoned the dog; the family moves to Rome where Amy observes suffocating social performance and William Dorrit's growing obsession with meeting the financier Mr Merdle.

Clennam renews the fight with the Circumlocution Office on Doyce's behalf while the snobbish Dowager Mrs Gowan visits the Meagles and provokes a tense confrontation, insisting that marriages between people of differing social standing "never does."

Clennam spots Tattycoram in London with a suspicious foreign man (Rigaud), follows them to the Casby house where they rendezvous with Miss Wade, then interrogates Flora and Pancks and learns that Miss Wade is a woman of entirely unknown parentage, receiving covert payments from Casby and dangerous enough to be feared by anyone who crosses her.

Arthur Clennam visits his mother's house and encounters Blandois (Rigaud), who forces entry, exchanges knowing familiarity with Flintwinch, unsettles Mrs Clennam under her controlled facade, drops veiled threats about silencing inconvenient witnesses, and has Arthur dismissed while Affery refuses to explain what is happening.

Amy Dorrit writes Arthur Clennam from Rome reporting on Pet Gowan's lonely, neglected marriage, her own recurring dreams of childhood poverty, and her deep homesickness, closing with affectionate greetings including one for Mr Pancks.

Mr Merdle hosts a lavish dinner for Lord Decimus, the Barnacles, and other establishment figures to secure Edmund Sparkler's appointment to the Circumlocution Office; William Dorrit is mentioned as a former debtor whose sudden inheritance caused bureaucratic chaos for the Office.

Mr Pancks collects rents in Bleeding Heart Yard where every defaulter invokes Merdle's name as excuse, then dines with Arthur Clennam and urges him to invest in Merdle's schemes, while Cavalletto arrives in terror having spotted a dangerous man in the street.
Fanny confides in Amy her contempt for Mrs Merdle and her deliberate plan to marry Mr Sparkler not for love but as an act of social revenge, then announces the engagement to Amy.

Fanny Dorrit's engagement to Mr Sparkler is formally negotiated between William Dorrit and Mrs Merdle, the wedding is celebrated in Rome with great pomp, and Amy is left behind with Mrs General while Mr Dorrit presses her to seek her own eligible marriage.

Mr Merdle visits William Dorrit at his London hotel, offers to invest his fortune and escorts him through the City in his grand carriage, leaving Dorrit intoxicated by the social prestige of the association.

Flora Finching visits William Dorrit to beg him to search for the vanished Blandois (Rigaud) on his return to Italy, then Dorrit himself goes to Mrs Clennam's gloomy house to investigate but is stonewalled by the tight-lipped Mrs Clennam and Flintwinch, leaving with nothing but unsettling suspicions.

William Dorrit, humiliated by Young John Chivery's unexpected visit which recalls his Marshalsea imprisonment, pays him off and flees England, then travels toward Rome while obsessively daydreaming of marriage and buying jewellery gifts in Paris.

William Dorrit returns to Rome visibly deteriorating, publicly collapses at Mrs Merdle's dinner address­ing guests as if welcoming them to the Marshalsea, is brought home by Amy, and dies bedridden a few days later—his mind never leaving the prison—with Frederick dying beside him moments after.

Clennam travels to Calais and questions the hostile Miss Wade about the missing Blandois, learns she hired him as a spy in Italy but knows nothing of his fate, witnesses a bitter clash between Miss Wade and Tattycoram over loyalty, and returns to London carrying Miss Wade's written account of her life.

Miss Wade narrates her autobiography, recounting a lifelong pattern of perceiving condescension and persecution in everyone around her—school friend Charlotte, governess employers, her fiancé, and Mr Gowan—culminating in her taking in a companion girl who shares her rebellious resentment of patronage.

Clennam bids farewell to Doyce departing on a foreign engineering commission, then Cavalletto reveals that the sinister stranger who visited Mrs Clennam's house is the same man formerly known as Rigaud—a convicted assassin from Marseilles—prompting Clennam to send Cavalletto to track him down.

Arthur Clennam visits his mother to warn her of Rigaud's murderous past and to extract secrets from Affery, but Mrs Clennam deflects all his warnings and Affery, terrorised by Flintwinch, refuses to reveal the house's mysteries unless Arthur first defeats "the two clever ones" himself.

Mr Merdle pays a strangely distracted evening call on Fanny Sparkler, borrows a penknife before leaving — an ominous act foreshadowing his imminent suicide — while Fanny complains of boredom, laments her curtailed social life, and mourns her father William Dorrit.

Mr Merdle is found dead by self-inflicted throat wound at the warm-baths; Physician delivers the news to Mrs Merdle and Bar, and London erupts in panic as Merdle's crimes—massive forgery and theft—are exposed, devastating thousands of investors.

After the Merdle financial crash destroys the firm, Arthur Clennam and Pancks grieve together; Clennam publicly exonerates absent partner Doyce, surrenders all assets to creditors, and accepts arrest — ending imprisoned in the Marshalsea, weeping for Little Dorrit.

Newly imprisoned for debt in the Marshalsea, Arthur Clennam receives the devoted attention of Young John Chivery, who reveals that Amy Dorrit loves Arthur, forcing him to confront his own long-suppressed feelings for her while resigning himself to separation.

Rigaud (Blandois) is tracked down and delivered to Arthur Clennam's Marshalsea cell by Pancks and Cavalletto; he brazenly reveals he has been extorting Mrs Clennam, writes her a letter setting a one-week deadline for capitulation, and departs undefeated while the helpless Arthur is left more wretched than before.

Ill and despairing in the Marshalsea, Arthur Clennam is visited by Amy Dorrit who offers him her entire fortune; he refuses to let her sacrifice herself, confesses his long-suppressed love too late, and bids her not to return, while John Chivery afterward delivers her message of undying love.

Rigaud confronts Mrs Clennam, demanding two thousand pounds to suppress documents proving she withheld a codicil and that Arthur is not her biological son; when she refuses full payment, he reveals he has left copies at the Marshalsea for Amy Dorrit to hand Arthur at nightfall, forcing Mrs Clennam to confess the entire history before rushing out to reclaim them.

Mrs Clennam, risen from her chair after years, goes to the Marshalsea to reclaim a damning packet from Little Dorrit, confesses her wrongs and begs silence until death, then both rush back to confront Rigaud at the Clennam house, which collapses and kills Rigaud while leaving Mrs Clennam permanently paralyzed and mute.

Mr Pancks, tormented by guilt over the Merdle investment disaster, publicly exposes landlord Casby as the true exploiter of Bleeding Heart Yard, delivers a furious oration denouncing him as a sham patriarch, then shears off his iconic white locks and cuts down his hat before fleeing the scene to the crowd's laughter.

Tattycoram, repentant after years under Miss Wade's influence, secretly steals Rigaud's iron box of incriminating papers from Calais and delivers it to the Marshalsea, reuniting with the Meagleses, while Mr Meagles departs again to fetch Daniel Doyce and free the ailing Arthur Clennam.

Amy Dorrit reveals she is utterly penniless after Merdle's collapse wiped out her family's fortune, declares her love and refuses separation; Daniel Doyce then arrives to restore the partnership and free Clennam from the Marshalsea, and Amy and Arthur are married at St George's Church before walking out together into a quiet life of usefulness.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Martin_Chuzzlewit.plot: The narrator mock-seriously traces the Chuzzlewit family's fictional ancient lineage, satirizing aristocratic pride, dubious genealogical claims, and the vanity of noble descent.

Seth Pecksniff, a fraudulently pious architect, is introduced with his daughters; his former pupil John Westlock departs after exposing Pecksniff's financial swindles, while loyal Tom Pinch — whom Westlock reveals is systematically exploited — defends Pecksniff to the last and bids his friend farewell.

Old Martin Chuzzlewit falls ill at the Blue Dragon inn where his young companion Mary Graham nurses him; landlady Mrs Lupin summons Pecksniff, who recognises his wealthy cousin and listens to a bitter confession that riches corrupt all who surround him, then departs after urging Martin to remember his grandson in his will.

Pecksniff meets the shabby swindler Montague Tigg (proxy for cousin Chevy Slyme) while eavesdropping on Old Martin at the Blue Dragon; the entire Chuzzlewit clan descends to scheme over the old man's will, convenes in chaotic council at Pecksniff's house, erupts in mutual recrimination, and is humiliated when Old Martin quietly slips away during the meeting.

Tom Pinch drives to Salisbury to collect Pecksniff's new pupil, meets Mark Tapley on the road debating trades that would test his cheerfulness, finds Martin Chuzzlewit waiting at a tavern, and returns with him to Pecksniff's house where Pecksniff stages an effusive welcome feast for the new arrival.

Pecksniff departs for London leaving Martin and Tom Pinch alone, whereupon Martin confides his disinheritance by his grandfather and his secret love for a dependent young woman, revealing she is the mysterious church visitor Tom had mentioned the night before.

Montague Tigg arrives at Pecksniff's to extract payment for his stranded companion Chevy Slyme's inn bill; Martin and Tom guarantee the debt and are introduced to the drunken, boastful Slyme; Tigg then swindles Tom's last coin as a personal loan; meanwhile Mark Tapley bids farewell to Mrs Lupin and the Blue Dragon and sets off for London.

Pecksniff travels by night coach to London with his daughters, shares the journey with Anthony Chuzzlewit and Jonas (who trade barbs on hypocrisy and money-grubbing), and on arrival in foggy London installs the family at Mrs Todgers's dingy commercial boarding house.

Pecksniff and his daughters stay at Todgers's London boarding house, pay a patronising visit to Tom Pinch's sister Ruth (a governess), are ejected from her employer's grand house, then attend a boisterous Sunday dinner at Todgers's where Pecksniff becomes helplessly drunk and must be locked in his room.

Old Martin Chuzzlewit arrives secretly at Todgers's to forge an alliance with Pecksniff, revealing that young Martin has concealed a secret engagement, and orders Pecksniff to expel him while hinting at rewarding Pecksniff's loyalty.

Jonas Chuzzlewit courts Charity Pecksniff during a visit to Anthony's grim counting-house, while Anthony and Pecksniff tacitly broker the match; the chapter closes with the Pecksniff family departing Todgers's amid a mournful commercial-boarders serenade.

Tom Pinch and Martin dine with former pupil John Westlock in Salisbury, who praises Tom, condemns Pecksniff, and returns Tigg's borrowed money; on their return Pecksniff coldly snubs Martin and formally expels him, whereupon Martin resolves to emigrate to America.

Expelled from Pecksniff's, Martin walks penniless to London, spends five weeks in deepening poverty pawning possessions and fruitlessly seeking passage to America (encountering Tigg at the pawnbroker), receives a mysterious anonymous £20 note, and is then found by Mark Tapley, who volunteers to emigrate with him and reveals that Mary Graham and Old Martin are staying in London.

Martin and Mary Graham meet secretly at dawn in St. James's Park for a clandestine farewell before Martin and Mark Tapley sail to America, during which Martin reads aloud a letter entrusting Tom Pinch with Mary's welfare, while the narrator quietly exposes Martin's fundamental egotism.

Martin and Mark Tapley endure the Atlantic crossing in steerage aboard the ship Screw — Mark cheerfully helps fellow poor emigrants while Martin sulks in his berth hiding class shame — until they arrive at New York.

Martin arrives in New York aboard the Screw, is taken up by Colonel Diver (editor of the Rowdy Journal) and his war correspondent Jefferson Brick, dines at the Pawkins boarding house among a company of hollow American boosters, and is ultimately offered a rare candid critique of American society by an honest fellow guest.

In New York, Martin and Mark are befriended by the candid Mr. Bevan, who takes them to visit the respectable Norris family, where Martin is socially humiliated when General Fladdock reveals he crossed in steerage, exposing the Norrises' shallow class pretensions and their hollow abolitionism, leaving Martin despondent about his prospects in America.

Anthony Chuzzlewit collapses in a fit while Jonas secretly reads the will confirming himself sole heir; Pecksniff, summoned to London by Anthony's cryptic letter about the Jonas–Mercy match, stays as witness through the night as the old miser hovers between life and death.

Pecksniff fetches nurse-and-layer-out Mrs Gamp on Jonas's orders; Anthony Chuzzlewit's lavish funeral proceeds with Jonas, Pecksniff, the undertaker Mould, and the doctor all performing grief cynically for profit or reputation, while only old clerk Chuffey mourns with genuine anguish.

Jonas Chuzzlewit negotiates a dowry with Pecksniff during their coach journey home, then shocks everyone by proposing to younger daughter Merry instead of Cherry, throwing the household into uproar at the very moment Tom Pinch announces the unannounced arrival of Old Martin Chuzzlewit and Mary Graham at the door.

Martin and Mark Tapley travel by train through America, where Martin buys a lot in the sham Eden settlement from the shifty agent Scadder (with Mark as new business partner), then witnesses the Watertoast Sympathisers' meeting collapse in fury when they discover their Irish hero advocates abolition.

After buying land in Eden, Martin is mobbed as a celebrity "lion" by the Watertoast community, endures a chaotic public reception and the insufferable Mrs Hominy, and boards a steamboat for Eden—just as Mark learns from Captain Kedgick that no one who goes to Eden ever returns alive.

Martin and Mark arrive at Eden to find a disease-ridden, desolate swamp utterly unlike what was promised; Martin collapses in despair and falls ill while Mark, with desperate cheerfulness, makes the wretched cabin habitable and resolves to hold firm.

Old Martin visits Pecksniff's house with Mary Graham, Jonas confronts Tom Pinch on the road and is struck down in a scuffle, Charity secretly thanks Tom for it, and old Martin questions Merry about her joyless engagement to Jonas while Jonas privately vows revenge after marriage.

Mrs Gamp negotiates with undertaker Mould to take a night-nursing job at a Holborn inn, then spends the night beside a delirious fever patient who cries out the name of Jonas Chuzzlewit in his ravings.

Poll Sweedlepipe and the precocious Bailey escort Mrs Gamp to Jonas Chuzzlewit's house to collect her belongings after being replaced by his new bride Merry, whose arrival is greeted by old Chuffey's ominous cry of woe upon the wicked house.

Montague Tigg, now grandly styled Tigg Montague and chairing the fraudulent Anglo-Bengalee Disinterested Loan and Life Assurance Company, lures Jonas Chuzzlewit into becoming a complicit investor by openly boasting of its swindling mechanics, then secretly commissions the spy Nadgett to dig up information on Jonas.

Jonas dines at Montague Tigg's opulent Pall Mall lodgings, is flattered and drawn deeper into the fraudulent insurance scheme, then is brought home drunk by Bailey and physically strikes his wife Merry.

Sairey Gamp visits Poll Sweedlepipe's barber shop then helps transport the gravely ill Lewsome to a country-bound coach; Lewsome cryptically hints to John Westlock of a dreadful secret he helped perpetrate, while undertaker Mould gleefully eyes the wasted man as a future client.

Pecksniff negotiates Charity's departure to Mrs Todgers's, manoeuvres Old Martin into moving into his house, then corners Mary Graham alone and proposes marriage while threatening that refusal will ruin young Martin's prospects.

Pecksniff eavesdrops from a church pew as Mary Graham reveals his coercive marriage proposal to Tom Pinch, then dismisses Tom on a fabricated charge of making improper advances to Mary, with Old Martin as unwitting witness to the deception.

Charity Pecksniff returns to Todgers's boarding house and, coaching herself on Mrs Todgers's advice, deliberately maneuvers the lovesick Moddle—who has been pining for her married sister Merry—into a tearful betrothal with herself.

Martin and Mark Tapley both nearly die of fever in the wretched Eden settlement; nursing each other through illness, Martin undergoes a moral reckoning with his own selfishness, and they eventually receive money from Mr Bevan and escape Eden to return to England.

Martin and Mark, sailing home from Eden, meet pompous Congressman Elijah Pogram on the steamboat, endure his jingoistic rhetoric and a levee at the National Hotel, then secure return passage to England through Mark's ingenuity as ship's cook, funded by their generous friend Mr Bevan.
Martin and Mark return to England penniless and witness a public stone-laying ceremony where Pecksniff receives civic honours for a grammar-school design Martin recognises as his own stolen work.

Dismissed by Pecksniff, Tom Pinch coaches to London, reunites with John Westlock, confronts his sister Ruth's condescending employer and extracts her from service, then the two siblings find cheap lodgings in Islington to start life afresh together.

Tom Pinch wanders lost in London, stumbles on Charity Pecksniff near the Monument, is brought to Todgers's where he has a tearful reconciliation with the unhappy Mercy (now Jonass wife), promises to relay her penitent message to old Mr Chuzzlewit, then reunites briefly with John Westlock before returning to his sister at Islington.

Nadgett delivers his secret dossier on Jonas Chuzzlewit to Montague Tigg, who uses the damning intelligence to blackmail Jonas into compliance and strong-arm him into recruiting Pecksniff into the fraudulent Anglo-Bengalee scheme.

Tom Pinch and sister Ruth enjoy cheerful London domesticity while John Westlock brings word of a mysterious offer: an unnamed employer, acting through the enigmatic Mr Fips, installs Tom as secretary-librarian in dusty Temple chambers to catalogue a vast collection of books, the patron's identity kept wholly secret.

Tom Pinch, at a steamboat wharf, unwittingly delivers a mysterious letter to Jonas Chuzzlewit that aborts Jonas's planned escape abroad; Montague Tigg then appears and leads Jonas away, exposing Jonas as a man trapped under his control, while Mrs Gamp and a distraught Merry are also swept up in the scene.

Trapped by Montague Tigg's knowledge of a damning secret and unable to flee, Jonas capitulates and agrees to travel with Tigg that night to lure Pecksniff into investing in the fraudulent Anglo-Bengalee company; a dark interlude with a doctor and a lancet foreshadows murderous intent.

Jonas and Montague travel by carriage through a violent storm toward Pecksniff's, during which Jonas nearly kills Montague when rampaging horses throw their carriage and young Bailey is mortally injured; at the Salisbury inn Montague is tormented by a nightmare of Jonas as murderous threat, then wakes to find Jonas standing over him through a door left suspiciously open.

Martin and Mark return to England from America, reunite with Mrs Lupin at the Blue Dragon, then confront Old Martin at Pecksniff's house where Martin seeks forgiveness, but Pecksniff intercepts every appeal and manipulates the feeble old man into rejecting his grandson, while Martin manages a brief whispered reunion with Mary before being expelled.

Jonas brings Pecksniff to dine with Montague Tigg, who persuades Pecksniff to invest nearly his entire savings in the fraudulent Anglo-Bengalee Assurance company, after which Tigg notes he can now manage Pecksniff alone.

Tom Pinch and his sister Ruth spend a cheerful afternoon with John Westlock — dining at his Temple chambers, enjoying music and easy company — while Tom recounts the mysterious wharf errand involving Mrs. Gamp, prompting John to suspect dark dealings and urge Tom to distance himself from the affair.

Tom Pinch and Ruth visit the battered Merry at Jonas's house where Chuffey's senile mutterings about "foul play" and death unsettle the gathering; Jonas returns and violently drives Tom out before he can reveal Nadgett's name, then enlists Mrs Gamp to silence Chuffey and slips out in secret disguise at night to commit a murder.

Jonas Chuzzlewit ambushes and murders Montague Tigg in a secluded wood after Tigg parts from Pecksniff at a country stile, then flees back to London and slips home, gripped by paranoid dread but utterly without remorse.

Martin Chuzzlewit and Mark Tapley return to London and reunite with Tom Pinch; at John Westlock's rooms they hear Lewsome confess he supplied drugs to Jonas Chuzzlewit to poison old Anthony, and the group resolves to reach the clerk Chuffey through Sairey Gamp to build a case against Jonas.

Mrs Gamp hosts Betsey Prig for tea to discuss nursing old Chuffey, but the evening explodes in a furious quarrel when Betsey denies Mrs Harris exists, inadvertently revealing to the watching Martin Chuzzlewit and John Westlock that Chuffey holds dangerous secrets about Jonas Chuzzlewit.

Martin Chuzzlewit confronts Tom Pinch with an accusation of betrayal and leaves without hearing Tom's defense; afterward Ruth reveals she has discovered Tom's secret unrequited love, and the two siblings share a tender, honest conversation in which Tom accepts his hopeless attachment with dignified calm.

Old Martin Chuzzlewit reveals himself as Tom Pinch's secret employer, disclosing he has long feigned frailty under Pecksniff's roof to gather evidence, and now declares the time for reckoning has come.

Old Martin arrives with Chuffey, Lewsome, and the spy Nadgett to confront Jonas: Chuffey reveals Anthony was never actually poisoned by Jonas, but Nadgett then produces evidence of Tigg's murder and has Jonas arrested; Jonas bribes his escort Slyme for a few minutes alone and poisons himself in the coach, dying before he can be brought to trial.

Old Martin reveals and executes his long-hidden scheme: he assembles family and friends, publicly exposes and physically strikes down the hypocritical Pecksniff, reconciles with grandson Martin, blesses Martin's union with Mary Graham, and dismisses both Pecksniff and Mrs Gamp, turning the tables completely.

John Westlock declares love to Ruth Pinch at the Temple Fountain and they become engaged; Old Martin gifts both brides jewels and plays paternal host at a joyful dinner where Mark Tapley serves, Tom is embraced by all, and the chapter closes in unanimous domestic happiness.

On Cherry Pecksniff's wedding morning, Old Martin rescues the grieving Merry from Todgers's and asks her forgiveness, while Augustus Moddle sends a letter fleeing to sea and abandoning Cherry at the altar; the chapter closes with a lyrical epilogue on Tom Pinch's tranquil life and the fallen Pecksniff's degradation.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Nicholas_Nickleby.plot: Chapter 1 narrates the Nickleby family backstory: grandfather Godfrey inherits a modest fortune, his elder son Ralph becomes a ruthless London moneylender obsessed with wealth, while younger son Nicholas (the protagonist's father) squanders the family farm on a stock speculation, loses everything, and dies broken, leaving his widow and two young children destitute.

Ralph Nickleby, a cold-eyed moneylender who exploits his destitute clerk Newman Noggs for pittance wages, attends a farcical public meeting for the fraudulent United Metropolitan Improved Hot Muffin and Crumpet Baking Company, where manipulative speeches drive the crowd to inflate worthless shares.

Ralph Nickleby learns of his brother's death from Newman Noggs, visits the destitute widow and children in London, treats them with cold contempt, and maneuvers Nicholas into accepting a poorly-paid teaching post at Squeers's Yorkshire school by promising to support the family in his absence.

Ralph Nickleby brings Nicholas to the Saracen's Head Inn to meet Yorkshire schoolmaster Wackford Squeers, whose cruelty to pupils is laid bare, and negotiates Nicholas's appointment as assistant master at Dotheboys Hall, after which Nicholas delivers papers to Ralph's eccentric clerk Newman Noggs.

Nicholas tearfully leaves his mother and Kate, joins Squeers and his starved pupils on the Yorkshire coach, receives a secret letter from Newman Noggs as Ralph looks on, and endures a brutal winter journey that ends when the coach overturns on the road.

After a coach overturn strands Nicholas, Squeers, and passengers at a roadside inn, two gentlemen trade embedded tales — the elegiac "Five Sisters of York" (sisters resist monastic pressure; youngest Alice dies young, memorialized in stained glass) and the darkly comic "Baron of Grogzwig" (a despairing baron is talked out of suicide by the Genius of Despair) — before the journey resumes to Greta Bridge.
Nicholas arrives at the squalid Dotheboys Hall, meets Mrs. Squeers and the wretched Smike, and discovers a secret letter of warning and friendship from Newman Noggs.

Nicholas witnesses Dotheboys Hall's brutal daily routine—medicinal fraud, starvation meals, sham lessons, corporal punishment—then has a compassionate exchange with the broken Smike, who despairs of hope or home.

Miss Squeers develops a one-sided infatuation with Nicholas after a brief schoolroom encounter, arranges a tea party to pursue him, but the evening collapses into rivalry and tears between her and her friend Miss Price, while Nicholas retreats to his dismal dormitory reflecting bitterly on his captivity at Dotheboys Hall.

Ralph Nickleby arranges Kate's employment at Madame Mantalini's dressmaking establishment and promises her rent-free lodging in his own property, providing for his niece with calculated coldness rather than genuine warmth.

Newman Noggs escorts Kate Nickleby and her mother to their bleak new lodgings in Thames Street—a gloomy, decaying house arranged by Ralph Nickleby—where Newman has secretly furnished basic comforts without taking any credit.

Fanny Squeers reconciles with Matilda Price after their quarrel and learns of Matilda's coming marriage, then engineers a meeting with Nicholas who bluntly rejects her romantic delusions; humiliated, Fanny redirects her spite onto Smike, who meanwhile clings to Nicholas as his sole protector and begs him not to leave Dotheboys Hall.

Smike flees Dotheboys Hall but is recaptured; when Squeers attempts a public flogging, Nicholas intervenes, beats Squeers unconscious, and quits the school—with Smike secretly following him on the road to London.

Newman Noggs attends the Kenwigs family's wedding anniversary party, where lower-class neighbors gather around the esteemed water-rate collector uncle Lillyvick, until Newman is abruptly summoned away by two mysterious mud-soaked visitors.

Nicholas and Smike arrive exhausted at Newman Noggs's London garret; Newman reads aloud Fanny Squeers's accusatory letter about the Dotheboys Hall assault; Nicholas resolves to confront Ralph Nickleby but is persuaded to wait; he incidentally rescues the Kenwigs baby from a nursemaid's fire, winning the admiration of the party downstairs.

Nicholas searches London for work, witnesses a satirical parliamentary confrontation at corrupt MP Gregsbury's lodging before declining his inadequate secretary post, then accepts Newman Noggs's arranged French-tutoring job for the Kenwigs family as his only available income.

Kate Nickleby endures her first day at Madame Mantalini's millinery, suffering condescension from Miss Knag and open insolence from a wealthy customer, then walks home to her daydreaming mother while privately mourning and clinging to Nicholas's letter as consolation.

Miss Knag at Madame Mantalini's millinery feigns sisterly affection for Kate for three days, but when aristocratic customers single out Kate's beauty and dismiss Miss Knag from the showroom, her friendship instantly turns to furious hatred and public denunciation.

Ralph Nickleby uses Kate as social bait at a dinner for his dissolute business clients, where Sir Mulberry Hawk harasses her shamelessly while Ralph looks on, and Kate flees in tears; Ralph then reveals—when confronted—that he brought her deliberately as a lure for Lord Frederick Verisopht, though Kate's distress momentarily pierces even his mercenary shell.
Nicholas returns to London, confronts Ralph at his mother's house, refutes the theft and assault charges, then leaves his family in Ralph's hands while pledging to journey on together with Smike.

Bailiffs arrive at Mantalini's millinery with a writ of execution, Mantalini stages a farcical fake suicide, the business collapses into bankruptcy, Kate is dismissed, and Ralph (who secretly engineered the failure) steers her toward a companion post with the affected socialite Mrs. Wititterly of Cadogan Place.

Nicholas and Smike depart London penniless for Portsmouth seeking work, bid farewell to Newman Noggs on the road, and at a roadside inn meet theatrical manager Vincent Crummles, who recruits them both to join his travelling theatre company.

Nicholas and Smike arrive in Portsmouth with the Crummles troupe, are introduced to the eccentric theatrical company and Mrs. Crummles, witness a rehearsal of the Indian Savage ballet (including the famously age-frozen "infant phenomenon"), and Nicholas is pressed to translate a French play and take on multiple acting roles by Monday.

Nicholas helps Miss Snevellicci canvass local patrons for her bespeak benefit night, then makes a triumphant first stage appearance in his own adapted piece, winning thunderous audience applause alongside the Crummles company.
