Fanny retreats to her East room wrestling with doubts about refusing to act; Edmund visits to announce he will take the role of Anhalt himself to prevent an outsider joining the theatricals, and Fanny inwardly attributes his capitulation to Mary Crawford's influence.

Edmund capitulates and agrees to act in the theatricals, to the triumph of the play's organizers and the distress of Fanny and Julia, who both suffer in isolation—Fanny from jealousy over Edmund's admiration of Mary Crawford, Julia from Henry Crawford's open preference for Maria.

Fanny endures painful rehearsals — watching Edmund and Mary Crawford act a love scene together, being coaxed by all into reading Mrs. Grant's absent part — until Julia bursts in announcing Sir Thomas Bertram has just arrived home.

Sir Thomas Bertram returns unexpectedly from Antigua, throwing the household into panic; he discovers the makeshift theatre in his study, receives Mr. Yates with icy civility, and silently reproaches Edmund with a look that Fanny, trembling in the corner, witnesses with anguish.

Sir Thomas returns to dismantle all traces of the theatricals, hears Edmund praise Fanny's steadfast judgment, rebukes Mrs. Norris who deflects with flattery, then watches Henry Crawford depart without declaring himself, crushing Maria's hopes while Fanny quietly rejoices.

Sir Thomas questions Maria about her cold feelings toward Rushworth and offers to break the engagement, but Maria—driven by wounded pride over Crawford's departure rather than love—reaffirms it, and the marriage proceeds, freeing her from Mansfield's restraint.

Fanny's status rises after her cousins leave; she begins visiting Mary Crawford at the Parsonage, and during one such visit Edmund joins them, prompting a sharp exchange between him and Mary over wealth, ambition, and honour, while Fanny silently observes their mutual attraction with unease before Edmund walks her home.

Fanny is invited to dine at the Parsonage; after Mrs Norris belittles her, Sir Thomas insists on sending the carriage; at dinner Henry Crawford arrives unexpectedly, reminisces about the theatricals, and Mary Crawford learns with suppressed anger that Edmund is soon to take holy orders.

Henry Crawford confesses to Mary his plan to make Fanny fall in love with him for sport; meanwhile Fanny's joy at brother William's return from sea inadvertently deepens Crawford's fascination with her, prompting him to extend his stay at Mansfield indefinitely.

At an evening card party at the Parsonage, Henry Crawford seats himself beside Fanny during speculation to court her attention, proposes grandiose improvements for Edmund's future living at Thornton Lacey, and Sir Thomas—observing Crawford's marked attentions—hears Edmund firmly declare his intent to reside among his parishioners rather than let Crawford rent the house.

Sir Thomas announces a ball for William and Fanny; Fanny frets over what to wear; Mary Crawford gives her a gold necklace — originally Henry Crawford's gift — to hang her amber cross on, leaving Fanny grateful but uneasy and suspicious of a hidden design.
Edmund gives Fanny a gold chain for William's cross and then confides growing doubts about Mary Crawford's moral character, while Fanny silently suppresses her love for him on the eve of the ball.

Fanny opens the Mansfield ball with Henry Crawford at Sir Thomas's insistence, endures Henry's attentive pursuit with discomfort, dances her cherished two dances with a fatigued Edmund who finds peace in her silence, and ends the night aware that Sir Thomas now suspects Crawford is in love with her.

After William's departure leaves Fanny in post-ball melancholy, Mary Crawford—consumed by jealousy over Edmund's prolonged absence and fear he may court the Miss Owens—visits Mansfield Park under pretense of casual chat to extract news of him from Fanny.

Henry Crawford confesses to his sister Mary that he is firmly resolved to marry Fanny Price, and the two debate Fanny's virtues, the social advantages of the match, and Henry's plans to settle near Mansfield.

Henry Crawford delivers news of William Price's naval promotion then immediately proposes to Fanny, who refuses him despite gratitude for his help, while Mary Crawford's congratulatory note and Mrs Norris's petty remarks compound Fanny's distress.

Sir Thomas visits Fanny in the East room to convey Henry Crawford's formal marriage proposal and pressures her to accept, but Fanny firmly refuses; Sir Thomas rebukes her for ingratitude and willfulness, Crawford departs graciously, and the chapter ends with Fanny summoned alone to face Crawford directly.

Crawford refuses to accept Fanny's repeated rejection of his proposal; Sir Thomas, approving the match, informs Mrs Norris and Lady Bertram, both of whom react with displeasure or superficial approval, leaving Fanny trapped between family pressure and her firm refusal.

Edmund returns to Mansfield Park, learns from Sir Thomas of Fanny's refusal of Crawford, and that evening Crawford captivates a reluctant Fanny with his Shakespeare reading, then persistently presses his romantic suit until the arrival of tea relieves her.

Edmund, urged by Sir Thomas, walks with Fanny in the shrubbery and validates her refusal of Crawford while pressing her to reconsider, revealing his own entanglement with Mary Crawford as he praises both siblings.

Mary Crawford visits Fanny for a private farewell, reminisces about the theatrical rehearsals in the East room, presses Fanny to accept Henry's courtship by invoking his devotion and William's commission, then departs with Henry the following morning.

Sir Thomas arranges Fanny's visit to Portsmouth with William, partly to cure her of Crawford's loss; Fanny is secretly relieved to escape Edmund's intimacy and Mary Crawford's shadow, Mrs Norris nearly joins them but backs out for selfish reasons, and Edmund delays his London trip to propose to Mary while Fanny departs Mansfield in tears.

Fanny arrives at Portsmouth with William, who immediately departs for his ship the Thrush; Fanny finds the cramped, chaotic Price household a painful contrast to Mansfield's order, feeling overlooked by her father and unsettled by her family's indifference.

Fanny arrives at Portsmouth and is rapidly disillusioned — William departs early, her father proves coarse and negligent, her mother indifferent and chaotic, and the noisy disorder of the Price household makes her long desperately for the order and peace of Mansfield Park.

Fanny, exiled in Portsmouth, receives a letter from Mary Crawford hinting at Edmund's movements toward London, while finding consolation in bonding with her sister Susan — guiding her reading and mediating household conflicts.

Henry Crawford visits Fanny at Portsmouth, escorts her and Susan on a walk to the dockyard, reveals he came solely to see Fanny, and attempts to win her approval by describing his reformed conduct at Everingham, while Fanny remains resistant yet grudgingly acknowledges his improvement.

Henry Crawford joins the Price family on their Sunday walk along the Portsmouth ramparts, expresses concern for Fanny's declining health, offers to retrieve her early from Portsmouth via Mary, and departs leaving Fanny dejected and enviously aware he will soon be with Edmund and Mary in town.

Fanny reads Mary Crawford's letter describing Henry's Portsmouth visits and hinting at Edmund's London appearances, leaving Fanny in anxious suspense about Edmund's romantic prospects while she finds solace mentoring her sister Susan.

Edmund writes Fanny a long letter revealing his faltering hopes of winning Mary Crawford, then Lady Bertram writes to report Tom Bertram's dangerous fever after a fall at Newmarket, prompting Edmund to rush to his bedside while Fanny anxiously follows events through a stream of letters.

Fanny, stranded in Portsmouth while Tom Bertram hovers near death, receives a calculating letter from Mary Crawford fishing for news of the heir's decline and offering an escort home, which Fanny indignantly declines, deferring to Sir Thomas's authority and seeing through Mary's cold ambition for Edmund to inherit.

Fanny receives a cryptic warning from Mary Crawford, then discovers via newspaper and Edmund's letter that Henry Crawford has eloped with the married Maria Bertram (Mrs. Rushworth), after which Edmund arrives at Portsmouth to escort Fanny and Susan back to a shattered Mansfield Park.

Edmund confides to Fanny his final, disillusioning meeting with Mary Crawford, whose callous dismissal of the Maria–Henry scandal as mere imprudence rather than vice destroys his love for her, while Mansfield Park mourns Maria's elopement and Julia's clandestine marriage.

The narrator wraps up all consequences: Maria Bertram and Henry Crawford's affair ends in ruin and divorce, Mrs Norris exiles herself with Maria, Sir Thomas reflects on his failures as a father, and Edmund gradually transfers his affections to Fanny, who becomes his wife and the daughter Sir Thomas truly values.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Northanger_Abbey/C.plot: Austen's prefatory advertisement explains the novel was completed in 1803, sold to a bookseller but never published, and warns readers that thirteen years of social and cultural change have rendered some parts obsolete.

Narrator ironically presents Catherine Morland as an unlikely heroine — plain, tomboyish, unremarkable — then traces her growth to seventeen and her invitation to Bath with the Allens, where adventure may finally find her.

Catherine and Mrs. Allen arrive in Bath and attend their first ball at the Upper Rooms, where Catherine knows no one, fails to get a dance partner, and leaves only mildly satisfied after two strangers call her pretty.

Catherine meets Henry Tilney at the Lower Rooms, they dance and exchange witty banter about journals, letter-writing, and muslins, and Catherine parts with a strong desire to continue the acquaintance.

Catherine goes to the pump-room hoping to find Tilney but he is absent; Mrs. Allen reunites with old schoolfellow Mrs. Thorpe, and Catherine is introduced to Isabella Thorpe, with whom she rapidly forms an intimate friendship.

Catherine and Isabella deepen their friendship while Catherine fruitlessly searches Bath for the vanished Henry Tilney; the narrator interrupts to defend novel-reading against the social stigma that dismisses it as trivial.
Catherine and Isabella gossip in the pump-room about Gothic novels (chiefly Udolpho) and men, then rush out pretending to flee two young men while actually pursuing them.

Catherine and Isabella unexpectedly meet James Morland and John Thorpe on the street; Thorpe boasts about his gig and horse, dismisses novels while bungling Udolpho's authorship, and the group walks to Mrs. Thorpe's lodgings, where Thorpe flatters Catherine into accepting a dance engagement despite her private dislike of him.

At the Upper Rooms ball Catherine is abandoned by John Thorpe, must refuse Henry Tilney's dance invitation because she is already engaged to Thorpe, meets Eleanor Tilney, and ends the evening disappointed as Henry dances with someone else.

John Thorpe takes Catherine on a carriage drive to Claverton Down, boring her with endless self-aggrandizing talk, while Mrs. Allen happens to meet the Tilneys at the Crescent; returning home, Catherine regrets having gone out and begins to find Thorpe disagreeable.

Catherine meets Eleanor Tilney at the pump-room, then at the cotillion ball dances with Henry Tilney (evading John Thorpe), during which Henry draws an extended analogy between dancing and marriage, and the evening ends with Catherine glimpsing General Tilney and arranging a country walk with the Tilney siblings.

Thorpe lies that the Tilneys have left Bath, pressuring Catherine into an aborted carriage excursion toward Blaize Castle; she spots the Tilneys on foot as they drive past and cannot stop, then returns home to learn they had called for her.

Catherine is snubbed when she calls on Eleanor (General Tilney forced the denial), but at the theater that evening Henry visits her box, explains the incident, and John Thorpe reveals he has been conversing with General Tilney, who greatly admires Catherine.

Catherine refuses to break her walking engagement with Miss Tilney despite intense pressure from Isabella, John Thorpe, and her brother James; after Thorpe fabricates an excuse to Miss Tilney on Catherine's behalf, Catherine runs to the Tilneys to set the record straight, is warmly received by General Tilney, and is later validated by Mr. Allen's approval of her conduct.

Catherine walks to Beechen Cliff with Henry and Eleanor Tilney; they debate novels versus history and women's understanding, Henry tutors Catherine in picturesque landscape theory, and a comic misunderstanding erupts when Eleanor mistakes Catherine's mention of a shocking new novel for news of a political riot in London.

Isabella Thorpe announces her engagement to Catherine's brother James, who rides to Fullerton for parental consent; consent arrives by letter sparking family celebration; John Thorpe departs for London after clumsily hinting he intends to court Catherine.

Catherine endures a disappointing visit to the Tilneys at Milsom Street, then at the evening rooms dances with Henry while Captain Tilney pursues Isabella (who feigns reluctance yet complies); the chapter closes on James Morland's modest financial settlement being revealed, with Isabella's thinly veiled dissatisfaction exposing mercenary motives beneath her professed indifference to money.
General Tilney invites Catherine to visit Northanger Abbey; she accepts ecstatically, her parents consent, and she indulges fantasies of gothic ruins and her growing attachment to Henry Tilney.

Isabella informs Catherine that John Thorpe claims to have made her an offer of marriage; Catherine firmly denies any encouragement, but leaves the pump-room disturbed after witnessing Isabella flirt openly with Captain Tilney despite her engagement to James.

Catherine confronts Henry Tilney about Captain Tilney's pursuit of the engaged Isabella, and Henry gently argues that Isabella's flirtation, not his brother's attentions, is the real problem, reassuring Catherine until she reluctantly accepts his reasoning.

Catherine departs Bath with the Tilneys, travels to Northanger Abbey in Henry's curricle while he teases her with playful gothic horror scenarios, and upon arrival she finds the abbey disappointingly modern rather than atmospherically sinister.

Catherine arrives at her Northanger Abbey bedroom, investigates a mysterious old chest (finds only a counterpane) and then a locked black cabinet where she discovers a hidden manuscript, but snuffs her candle before she can read it and lies terrified through a violent storm all night.

Catherine discovers the mysterious manuscript is mundane laundry bills, suffers humiliation; during a tour of Northanger's abbey and gardens with General Tilney and Eleanor, Eleanor reveals her mother's favourite walk, prompting Catherine to suspect the General of past cruelty toward his late wife.

General Tilney leads Catherine on a tour of Northanger Abbey, but his abrupt blocking of a forbidden wing—and Eleanor's whispered revelation that their mother died suddenly while Eleanor was absent—ignites Catherine's lurid Gothic suspicion that the General murdered or secretly imprisoned his wife.

Catherine secretly enters Mrs. Tilney's room expecting gothic evidence of the General's guilt, finds only a cheerful ordinary apartment, and is caught by the early-returning Henry, who gently but firmly rebukes her gothic suspicions about his father and his mother's death.

Catherine recovers from her gothic delusions and, after nine days without news, receives a letter from her brother James revealing Isabella has abandoned him for Captain Tilney, prompting her and the Tilney siblings to discuss Isabella's inconstancy and mercenary ambition.

General Tilney arranges a visit to Henry's Woodston parsonage; Catherine tours it with growing delight, and the General's pointed remarks about furnishing the drawing-room "for a lady's taste" signal his approval of a match between her and Henry.

Catherine receives Isabella's shallow, self-serving letter begging her to intercede with James, sees through its falsehood, reads it aloud to Henry and Eleanor, and resolves never to answer it or think of Isabella again.

General Tilney returns unexpectedly from London and orders Catherine ejected from Northanger Abbey the next morning without explanation or proper escort; Eleanor delivers the distressing news, comforts her, and lends her money for the journey home.

Expelled by General Tilney, Catherine travels home alone to Fullerton, is warmly received by her family, writes a brief letter to Eleanor Tilney, visits the Allens, and grieves over Henry while her family puzzles over the General's inexplicable cruelty.

Henry Tilney visits Catherine at Fullerton, declares his love and proposes despite his father's orders, then reveals that General Tilney expelled Catherine after John Thorpe—having earlier inflated the Morlands' wealth to court the General's favour—spitefully contradicted himself and exposed her as poor.

Eleanor Tilney's marriage to a wealthy viscount softens General Tilney's pride, leading him to grant consent for Henry and Catherine's marriage, which follows swiftly and ends the novel in "perfect felicity."

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Persuasion/Chapter.plot: Sir Walter Elliot, vain baronet obsessed with rank and appearance, faces growing debt he cannot address without compromising his pride, while his eldest daughter Elizabeth nurses disappointment over the heir Mr Elliot's rejection of the family, and younger Anne is dismissed as worthless by both father and sister.

Lady Russell and Anne devise a retrenchment plan for Sir Walter's debts, but Sir Walter rejects economy measures and decides to quit Kellynch Hall for Bath, overriding Anne's wishes for a modest local home.
Mr Shepherd persuades a reluctant Sir Walter to allow Admiral Croft to rent Kellynch Hall, while Anne privately sighs at learning the Admiral's wife is sister to Captain Wentworth.

Anne Elliot's brief engagement to young Captain Wentworth eight years earlier is recounted: their mutual love, opposition from Sir Walter and Lady Russell, Anne's persuaded renunciation, Wentworth's subsequent rise to fortune, and Anne's lingering regret as news of the Crofts taking Kellynch revives old pain.

Crofts finalize lease of Kellynch Hall; Sir Walter and Elizabeth depart to Bath with scheming Mrs Clay; Anne stays behind due to Mary's illness and settles at Uppercross Cottage, where she encounters the Musgrove family.

Anne settles at Uppercross, mediates petty quarrels between Mary and the Musgroves, and is emotionally jolted when the visiting Crofts reveal that their brother Captain Wentworth is about to return to the neighbourhood.

Anne stays behind to nurse an injured child while Mary and Charles dine at Uppercross, allowing Captain Wentworth's first visit to Kellynch to be a brief, stilted bow; he later tells others she is so altered he would not have known her, privately resolving she is his only exception among women he would now pursue.

Anne and Wentworth meet repeatedly at Uppercross gatherings, exchange only cold civilities while inwardly haunted by their past engagement, as lively naval conversation and dancing highlight their painful distance.

Captain Wentworth becomes a daily fixture at Uppercross, disrupting Charles Hayter's courtship of Henrietta Musgrove, while Anne—avoiding Wentworth—is left overwhelmed when he silently removes a troublesome child from her back in a brief charged encounter at the Cottage.

Anne overhears Wentworth praise Louisa's decisiveness and learns from her that Lady Russell persuaded Anne to refuse Charles Musgrove; the walk ends with Wentworth silently handing the exhausted Anne into the Crofts' carriage, revealing residual care beneath his resentment.

The Uppercross party travels to Lyme to visit Captain Wentworth's wounded friend Harville, where Anne meets the bereaved Captain Benwick and, in a private evening conversation, counsels him to read prose moralists rather than melancholy poetry — while privately reflecting that her own conduct under grief would not bear examination.

Louisa Musgrove falls and is knocked unconscious jumping from the Cobb steps; Anne takes command amid the chaos, Wentworth is distraught, and the group discovers the admiring stranger was Mr Elliot — heir to Sir Walter — before dispersing, with Anne ultimately displaced by Mary as Louisa's nurse.

Anne wraps up her time at Uppercross by organizing the Musgroves' departure to Lyme, then returns to Lady Russell at Kellynch Lodge, where a visit to the Crofts at Kellynch Hall forces her to navigate painful memories of home and awkward conversation about Captain Wentworth's presumed attachment to Louisa.

Charles and Mary report Captain Benwick's growing admiration for Anne, Lady Russell weighs his character cautiously, Captain Wentworth departs for Shropshire as Louisa recovers, and Anne arrives reluctantly in Bath where Elizabeth's letter reveals Mr. Elliot has begun seeking the family's acquaintance.

Anne arrives at the family's Bath lodgings to find Sir Walter and Elizabeth happily absorbed in social triumphs and fully reconciled with the long-estranged heir Mr Elliot, who calls that evening and makes a surprisingly agreeable impression on Anne.

Back in Bath, Anne watches Sir Walter and Elizabeth fawn over noble cousins the Dalrymples while worrying about Mrs Clay's hold on her father; Lady Russell warms to Mr Elliot, and he debates with Anne the meaning of "good company," revealing their differing values around rank.

Anne renews friendship with impoverished invalid Mrs Smith against her father's contemptuous objections, while Lady Russell urges her to consider Mr Elliot as a suitor — a prospect Anne inwardly rejects, distrusting his polished but guarded character.

Anne learns via Mary's letter — confirmed by Admiral Croft in a chance street encounter — that Captain Benwick and Louisa Musgrove are engaged, leaving Anne secretly joyful at the thought of Captain Wentworth now unattached.

Anne unexpectedly encounters Captain Wentworth in Bath, endures Elizabeth's cold snub of him and Lady Russell's oblivious non-recognition, then pins her hopes on an upcoming concert as the next chance to speak with him properly.

At a Bath concert, Anne and Wentworth share a charged conversation revealing his fading attachment to Louisa and implicit longing for Anne, but Mr Elliot's persistent attentions provoke Wentworth's jealousy and he leaves abruptly, leaving Anne to wrestle with how the truth of her feelings can ever reach him.

Anne visits Mrs Smith, who exposes Mr Elliot's true character as a cold-blooded, self-serving schemer who engineered the ruin of her husband and refused to act as executor, revealing also his calculated motives for reconciling with the Elliot family.

Anne learns Mr Elliot's true character from Mrs Smith, meets the Musgrove party in Bath where Captain Wentworth reappears and exchanges charged words with her, and discovers Mrs Clay secretly meeting Mr Elliot despite his claimed absence.

After overhearing Anne and Harville debate whether men or women love more faithfully, Wentworth slips Anne a secret letter declaring undying love, and the two reunite and exchange promises during a walk through Bath, ending years of estrangement.

Anne and Wentworth's engagement wins cold acceptance from Sir Walter and Elizabeth, forces Lady Russell to admit her past errors in judging character, exposes Mr Elliot's double game as he flees with Mrs Clay, and ends with Anne joyfully settled as a sailor's wife shadowed only by dread of future war.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Pride_and_Prejudic.plot: Mrs. Bennet excitedly tells Mr. Bennet that wealthy bachelor Bingley has taken Netherfield Park, and pressures him to call on the newcomer so one of their five daughters may marry him.
Mr. Bennet reveals he has already paid a visit to Mr. Bingley, having kept the family in suspense by pretending he would not go, causing Mrs. Bennet's resentment to dissolve into delight.

At the local assembly ball, Mr Bingley wins universal admiration while Mr Darcy's haughty refusal to dance and his dismissal of Elizabeth as merely "tolerable" turns the neighborhood—and Elizabeth herself—against him.
Jane and Elizabeth privately discuss Bingley after the ball; narrator then contrasts Bingley's warm character with Darcy's haughty reserve, and sketches the Bingley sisters' wealth and pride.

Morning after Netherfield ball: Charlotte Lucas visits Longbourn; she, Elizabeth, Jane, and Mrs Bennet dissect Mr Bingley's preference for Jane and debate whether Mr Darcy's pride is justified, with Mary delivering a pedantic distinction between pride and vanity.

Darcy's opinion of Elizabeth shifts from indifference to attraction while Charlotte advises Elizabeth that Jane should show more affection to secure Bingley, and a social evening at the Lucases ends with Darcy privately admitting to Miss Bingley that Elizabeth is the object of his admiration.

Mrs Bennet engineers Jane's visit to Netherfield on horseback so rain forces her to stay overnight; Jane falls ill, and Elizabeth walks three miles alone to nurse her, ending up invited to remain at Netherfield.

While Jane remains ill at Netherfield, Elizabeth endures Miss Bingley and Mrs Hurst's catty mockery of her manners and low connections, observes Darcy's covert admiration, and joins a drawing-room debate on what truly constitutes an accomplished woman.

Mrs Bennet visits Jane at Netherfield with Lydia and younger daughters, embarrasses Elizabeth with tactless boasting and country-vs-town squabbling before Darcy, while Lydia extracts a ball promise from Bingley.

At Netherfield, Elizabeth observes and engages in sharp debate with Darcy and Bingley about humility and yielding to persuasion, while Darcy grows bewitched by her and Miss Bingley jealously schemes to provoke his dislike of Elizabeth by mocking a supposed marriage between them.

At Netherfield, Miss Bingley vies for Darcy's attention while he and Elizabeth spar over pride, vanity, and personal faults, ending as Darcy privately acknowledges the danger of being too attentive to Elizabeth.

Elizabeth and Jane leave Netherfield; Darcy deliberately suppresses all signs of admiration for Elizabeth, while Miss Bingley feigns warmth; back at Longbourn the family receives them coolly, and Lydia brings gossip from the regiment.

Mr Collins arrives at Longbourn, having written a letter announcing his visit and citing Lady Catherine de Bourgh's patronage and his intention to make amends to his cousins for inheriting the entailed estate, and he proves pompous and sycophantic upon arrival.

Mr Collins holds forth at dinner praising Lady Catherine's condescension, then attempts to read Fordyce's Sermons aloud but is cut short by Lydia's interruption, after which he retreats to play backgammon with Mr Bennet.

Mr Collins shifts his matrimonial target from Jane to Elizabeth after Mrs Bennet warns him off Jane; on a walk to Meryton the group meets the charming newcomer Mr Wickham, and a charged, silent exchange between Wickham and Darcy puzzles Elizabeth.

At a Meryton evening party, Wickham wins Elizabeth's admiration and trust by recounting how Darcy denied him the church living promised by Darcy's late father, revealing Lady Catherine as Darcy's aunt and hinting at a planned match between Darcy and Miss de Bourgh.

Elizabeth tells Jane about Wickham's account of Darcy's cruelty; Bingley arrives to personally invite the Bennets to the Netherfield ball; Mr Collins claims Elizabeth's first two dances, thwarting her plan to dance with Wickham, and Elizabeth begins to suspect he intends to propose to her.

At the Netherfield ball Elizabeth dances with a contemptuous Mr Darcy while Wickham is absent, clashes with Miss Bingley over Wickham's character, endures Mr Collins's obsequious introduction to Darcy, and suffers acute embarrassment as her mother loudly proclaims Jane's coming marriage to Bingley within Darcy's earshot.
Mr Collins formally proposes to Elizabeth, who refuses him clearly and repeatedly, but Collins persists in misreading her rejections as coquetry and vows to try again.

After Elizabeth refuses Mr Collins, Mrs Bennet pressures husband and daughter to reverse the decision, but Mr Bennet sides with Elizabeth, leaving Mrs Bennet to complain fruitlessly while Mr Collins withdraws his suit with pompous self-justification.

Caroline Bingley's letter reveals the Netherfield party has left for London with no plans to return, hinting Bingley should marry Georgiana Darcy; Elizabeth sees through the manipulation and reassures Jane that Bingley's affection is genuine.
Charlotte Lucas secretly accepts Mr Collins's proposal for financial security, then tells Elizabeth, who is shocked and dismayed that her friend has sacrificed happiness for worldly advantage.

Sir William Lucas announces Charlotte's engagement to Mr Collins, provoking Mrs Bennet's fury and Elizabeth's private sense of betrayal, while Bingley's unexplained absence deepens Jane's distress and Elizabeth's fears about Darcy's interference.

Miss Bingley's letter confirms Bingley has permanently left Hertfordshire, dashing Jane's hopes; Elizabeth and Jane debate whether Bingley acted from weakness or design, while Wickham's public grievances against Darcy spread through the neighbourhood.
Gardiners arrive at Longbourn for Christmas; Mrs Gardiner proposes Jane visit London for change of scene after Bingley's withdrawal, while privately noting Elizabeth's worrying attachment to Wickham.

Mrs Gardiner warns Elizabeth against Wickham for lack of fortune; Charlotte marries Collins and leaves for Hunsford; Jane writes from London that Miss Bingley has turned cold; and Wickham shifts his attentions to a wealthier woman, which Elizabeth accepts with clear-eyed equanimity.
Elizabeth departs for Hunsford, stops in London to visit Jane and the Gardiners, debates Wickham's mercenary pursuit of Miss King with her aunt, and eagerly accepts an invitation to tour the Lakes.

Elizabeth arrives at Hunsford Parsonage, observes Charlotte's cheerful management of Mr Collins, and gets her first glimpse of the sickly Miss De Bourgh at the garden gate, ending with an invitation to dine at Rosings.

Elizabeth and the Collins party dine at Rosings for the first time, where Lady Catherine dominates conversation with intrusive questions and imperious opinions, but Elizabeth alone resists her authority with calm wit and refuses to be intimidated.

Elizabeth settles into Hunsford routine observing Charlotte's tactical management of Mr Collins and Lady Catherine's domineering visits, then Darcy arrives at Rosings with Colonel Fitzwilliam and calls at the Parsonage, where Elizabeth pointedly asks whether he has seen Jane in London.

At Rosings on Easter evening, Elizabeth plays pianoforte while Colonel Fitzwilliam and Darcy attend; she and Darcy trade pointed witticisms about his aloofness with strangers and her lack of practice, as Lady Catherine repeatedly interrupts to criticise Elizabeth's playing and praise her own daughter Anne.

Darcy visits Elizabeth alone at the Parsonage, their conversation is tense and guarded, and Charlotte begins to suspect he is in love with Elizabeth, while both Darcy and Fitzwilliam continue to call frequently, leaving Elizabeth and Charlotte puzzled about Darcy's motives.
Elizabeth learns from Colonel Fitzwilliam that Darcy boasted of separating a friend from an imprudent match, realizes he broke off Bingley and Jane, and retreats to her room in indignant grief.
Darcy visits Elizabeth and declares his love, but she rejects him, citing his arrogant manner, his role in separating Bingley from Jane, and his alleged cruelty to Wickham.

Darcy delivers a letter to Elizabeth in which he defends his separation of Bingley and Jane on grounds of Jane's apparent indifference and the Bennet family's impropriety, and exposes Wickham's dissolute past and his attempted elopement with Darcy's sister Georgiana for her fortune.
Elizabeth re-reads Darcy's letter and, through painful reflection, is forced to acknowledge Wickham's dishonesty and her own vanity and prejudice.

Elizabeth spends her final days at Rosings processing Darcy's letter—alternating between indignation and self-reproach—while Lady Catherine dominates farewell interactions with commanding opinions on travel, and Elizabeth privately grieves over her family's impropriety and Jane's lost happiness with Bingley.

Elizabeth and Mr Collins exchange farewell civilities at Hunsford parsonage; Elizabeth departs with private pity for Charlotte's resigned domestic life, travels to London, briefly reunites with Jane, and privately wrestles with whether to reveal Darcy's proposal.

Elizabeth, Jane, and Maria return from Hunsford and reunite with Lydia and Kitty at an inn; Lydia dominates the journey home with gossip about Wickham's broken pursuit of Mary King and army pranks, while Elizabeth privately dreads further encounters with Wickham and opposes the family's Brighton scheme.

Elizabeth tells Jane the truth about Darcy's proposal and Wickham's villainy, they debate whether to expose Wickham publicly, and Elizabeth observes Jane's lingering unhappiness over Bingley while Mrs Bennet complains about the Collinses and Netherfield.

Elizabeth fails to persuade her father to prevent Lydia from joining the regiment at Brighton, then has a final tense exchange with Wickham in which she signals she now sees through both him and Darcy more clearly, before Lydia departs noisily with Mrs Forster.

Elizabeth reflects on her parents' miserable marriage, mourns the curtailed Lakes tour redirected to Derbyshire, then secretly confirms Darcy is absent from Pemberley before agreeing to visit his estate.

Elizabeth visits Pemberley with the Gardiners, hears housekeeper Mrs Reynolds praise Darcy's generous character, and unexpectedly meets Darcy himself, who behaves with striking civility and asks to introduce his sister to her.

Darcy and Georgiana visit Elizabeth at Lambton inn, Bingley joins; Elizabeth observes Darcy's transformed manners and, lying awake that night, realises her feelings for him have shifted from dislike to gratitude and nascent love.
At Pemberley, Miss Bingley's jealous attacks on Elizabeth's looks backfire when Darcy openly declares Elizabeth one of the handsomest women of his acquaintance, leaving Miss Bingley mortified.
Elizabeth receives Jane's letters revealing Lydia has eloped with Wickham and is not married; she breaks the news to Darcy who appears unexpectedly, then departs with the Gardiners to Longbourn.

Elizabeth and the Gardiners return to Longbourn, where Jane shares news of the fruitless search for Lydia and Wickham, Elizabeth blames herself for not exposing Wickham's true character, and Lydia's flippant elopement note is read aloud.

While the Bennet family waits at Longbourn for news, Gardiner's London search reveals Wickham has no traceable relations and massive gambling debts; Collins sends a pompous condolence letter endorsing the family's disgrace; Mr Bennet returns home guilt-ridden; and Elizabeth privately admits her feelings for Darcy make Lydia's scandal doubly painful.

Mr Gardiner's letter reveals Lydia and Wickham found but not yet married; he proposes terms requiring Mr Bennet to settle money on Lydia and pay Wickham's debts, and Elizabeth and Jane immediately suspect their uncle secretly subsidised the match far beyond the stated sum.

After Lydia's elopement is settled at Gardiner's expense, Mr. Bennet grudgingly consents to Wickham leaving the militia and to a brief Longbourn visit, while Elizabeth privately grieves her lost chance with Darcy and recognises too late how well-suited they were.

Lydia and Wickham return home as a married couple, unembarrassed; Lydia inadvertently lets slip that Darcy was present at their wedding, shocking Elizabeth into writing urgently to her aunt for an explanation.

Elizabeth reads Mrs Gardiner's letter revealing Darcy secretly arranged Lydia and Wickham's marriage by paying Wickham's debts and purchasing his commission, then confronts Wickham with veiled irony when he intercepts her in the garden.

Wickham and Lydia depart for Newcastle; news of Bingley's return to Netherfield revives Mrs. Bennet's matchmaking schemes; Bingley arrives accompanied by Darcy, and their visit to Longbourn leaves both Jane and Elizabeth painfully unsettled — Jane struggling to hide her feelings for Bingley, Elizabeth tormented by Darcy's reserved manner and her mother's mortifying behaviour toward him.

At a dinner party at Longbourn, Bingley gravitates back toward Jane while Elizabeth watches Darcy from a distance, frustrated by his cold reserve and her own inability to exchange more than a few stilted words with him.
Bingley proposes to Jane Bennet; the engagement is joyfully accepted, with Mrs Bennet's machinations finally succeeding and the whole Longbourn family celebrating.
Lady Catherine de Bourgh arrives uninvited at Longbourn and demands Elizabeth renounce any intention of marrying Darcy, but Elizabeth refuses to be intimidated and gives no promise.

After Lady Catherine's visit, Elizabeth anxiously wonders if Darcy will be deterred from proposing; her father then mockingly reads her a letter from Mr Collins warning against an alleged engagement between Elizabeth and Darcy, leaving Elizabeth distressed while forced to laugh along.

Darcy renews his proposal to Elizabeth during a walk; she accepts gratefully, they confess how each changed the other, and Darcy reveals he also confessed to Bingley about concealing Jane's presence in London, clearing the way for the Bingley-Jane engagement.

Elizabeth reveals her engagement to Darcy first to Jane, then obtains her father's reluctant but warm consent by disclosing Darcy's role in Lydia's marriage, and finally tells her mother, whose reaction is mercenary rapture.

Elizabeth and Darcy playfully dissect the origins of their love, then exchange letters announcing their engagement to Lady Catherine, Mr Collins, and the Gardiners, while Charlotte and Collins arrive at Lucas Lodge after Lady Catherine's furious reaction to Darcy's news.

The epilogue traces the post-marriage fates of all principal characters: Elizabeth and Darcy thrive at Pemberley, Jane and Bingley move to Derbyshire, Kitty improves away from Lydia's influence, Lydia and Wickham drift into debt and indifference, Lady Catherine eventually reconciles with Darcy, and the Gardiners remain cherished friends.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Sense_and_Sensibil.plot: After the entailed Norland estate passes to John Dashwood and his infant son, widow Mrs. Dashwood and daughters are left nearly penniless; the selfish Mrs. John Dashwood seizes the house while Elinor's cool judgment steadies the grief-consumed family.
Fanny Dashwood systematically talks her husband John down from a £3000 bequest to nothing, convincing him that his dying father's request to help his widow and daughters requires no money at all.

Mrs. Dashwood observes growing attachment between Elinor and Edward Ferrars, quickly anticipates their marriage, while Marianne critiques Edward's lack of sensibility and passion as unworthy of her romantic ideal.

Elinor and Marianne debate Edward Ferrars's merits and Elinor's guarded feelings for him; Fanny's veiled warnings about Edward's expectations prompt Mrs. Dashwood to accept Sir John Middleton's offer of Barton Cottage in Devonshire, resolving to quit Norland.

Mrs. Dashwood announces the move to Barton Cottage, disposes of Norland effects under Elinor's prudent guidance, and the family departs for Devonshire while Marianne bids a passionate farewell to beloved Norland.

The Dashwood women arrive at modest Barton Cottage, settle in despite comparing it unfavorably to Norland, and receive warm hospitality from landlord Sir John Middleton and his reserved wife Lady Middleton.
Dashwood women dine at Barton Park with the Middletons, Mrs. Jennings, and the silent Colonel Brandon, where Marianne performs music and grudgingly respects Brandon as the only attentive listener.

Mrs. Jennings proclaims Colonel Brandon in love with Marianne; Marianne scoffs at him as too old for true feeling, while also fretting that Edward Ferrars's absence from Barton signals illness — exposing the sisters' contrasting views on love and self-command.

Marianne sprains her ankle fleeing a storm on the downs and is carried home by the dashing John Willoughby, whose handsome appearance and gallant manner instantly captivate the Dashwood women; Sir John reveals Willoughby is heir to Allenham and teases that Colonel Brandon already has a rival.

Willoughby visits daily and rapidly forms a deep mutual attachment with Marianne through shared tastes in music, books, and dancing, while Elinor and Mrs. Dashwood observe his charm with approval; Elinor also notices Colonel Brandon's growing but hopeless partiality for Marianne, and defends him against Willoughby and Marianne's contemptuous dismissal of him as dull and unremarkable.

Willoughby and Marianne's open courtship intensifies during Devonshire social gatherings while Elinor, finding companionship only in Colonel Brandon, learns through his halting confession that he has suffered a past disappointed love resembling Marianne's romantic temperament.

Willoughby's gift of a horse to Marianne (declined under Elinor's pressure) and his secret taking of a lock of her hair convince Elinor the two are secretly engaged, while Margaret's teasing hints about Elinor's own admirer cause public embarrassment at a social gathering.

Colonel Brandon abruptly departs on mysterious urgent business, cancelling the Whitwell excursion; Willoughby then takes Marianne alone to Allenham, prompting Elinor to rebuke her sister for the impropriety while Marianne defends it as innocent pleasure.

Mrs. Jennings gossips about Colonel Brandon's abrupt departure while Elinor puzzles over Willoughby and Marianne's silence about their apparent engagement; that evening Willoughby passionately declares his love for Barton Cottage and its inhabitants, hinting at a permanent bond.

Willoughby abruptly announces he must leave for London on Mrs. Smith's orders, bids a strained farewell to the Dashwoods, and Marianne collapses in grief while Elinor and Mrs. Dashwood debate whether a secret engagement explains his suspicious behavior.

After Willoughby's departure Marianne grieves inconsolably, then mistakes an approaching rider for him but is surprised instead by Edward Ferrars, whose cold and distracted manner toward Elinor deepens everyone's unease.

Edward visits Barton Cottage and, while subdued in spirits, joins the Dashwood women in a fireside debate contrasting Marianne's romantic idealism about wealth and love with Elinor's pragmatism, as his evasive reaction to being called "reserved" hints at concealed troubles.

Edward visits the Dashwoods, sparking debate on picturesque taste; Marianne notices a hair-ring on his finger that Elinor silently suspects contains her own hair, hinting at Edward's secret attachment, while mention of Willoughby reveals Marianne's feelings to Edward.

Edward departs Barton after a week's visit despite wishing to stay, citing his lack of independence from his mother; Elinor quietly subdues her grief through occupation while Marianne would have indulged hers; the Palmers arrive as new comic company, with Mr. Palmer's rude indifference contrasting his cheerful wife.

Elinor and Marianne visit the Palmers; Mrs. Palmer chatters about Willoughby's good reputation and reveals she heard from Colonel Brandon in London that Marianne is expected to marry Willoughby, while Elinor quietly gathers what intelligence she can about his character.

The Steele sisters arrive at Barton Park, flatter Lady Middleton shamelessly to win her favour, and Elinor forms a cold opinion of them; the chapter ends with Lucy Steele's casual claim of knowing Edward Ferrars, sharpening Elinor's curiosity and unease.

Lucy Steele shocks Elinor by revealing she has been secretly engaged to Edward Ferrars for four years, confirming it with his miniature portrait and a letter in his hand, while Elinor struggles to conceal her distress.

Elinor privately processes the devastating confirmation that Edward is secretly engaged to Lucy Steele, resolves to conceal her grief from her family, and maneuvers at a social gathering to sit beside Lucy in order to reopen the subject calmly and convince her rival that her own heart is unwounded.

Elinor and Lucy resume their tense private dialogue about Lucy's secret engagement to Edward Ferrars, sparring over his constancy, financial obstacles, and the scheme to secure him a church living, while Elinor privately concludes Lucy keeps Edward bound by self-interest alone.

Mrs. Jennings invites the Dashwood sisters to London; Marianne's barely-concealed eagerness to reunite with Willoughby overrides Elinor's objections, and Mrs. Dashwood insists both accept, so Elinor agrees to go partly to guard her sister and partly because Edward Ferrars will not be in town until February.

Elinor and Marianne arrive in London with Mrs. Jennings; Marianne secretly writes to Willoughby and spends the chapter in feverish anticipation of his visit or reply, only to be repeatedly disappointed, while Colonel Brandon's unexpected appearance instead of Willoughby deepens her distress and Elinor's unease about the mysterious engagement.

Colonel Brandon visits Elinor and reveals that Marianne's engagement to Willoughby is publicly rumoured; he confesses his own love for Marianne and departs in grief, while Elinor — uncertain of the true state of the relationship — withholds full disclosure and grows increasingly anxious about Willoughby's intentions.

At a crowded party Marianne encounters Willoughby, who deliberately cold-shoulders her; his cold, formal manner makes clear he has abandoned her, leaving Marianne devastated and forcing Elinor to rush her home.

Marianne receives Willoughby's coldly formal letter breaking off their unacknowledged attachment and returning her letters and lock of hair, while Elinor reads the correspondence and comforts her devastated sister.

Marianne is devastated by news of Willoughby's imminent marriage to wealthy Miss Grey; Elinor manages Mrs. Jennings's well-meaning but clumsy sympathy, then learns from Colonel Brandon—who overheard the news in a shop—that Willoughby's engagement is confirmed, and the two discuss Willoughby's deceit and Marianne's suffering.

Colonel Brandon visits Elinor and reveals Willoughby's past seduction and abandonment of his ward Eliza Williams, including a duel with Willoughby, exposing Willoughby's true dissolute character to give Marianne perspective on her own heartbreak.

Elinor delivers news of Willoughby's marriage to a devastated Marianne, while Mrs. Dashwood urges the sisters to remain in London; the Steele sisters then reappear, with Lucy resuming veiled provocations at Elinor.

Elinor and Marianne encounter their half-brother John Dashwood in a jeweller's shop, and he reveals his mercenary priorities by urging Elinor to pursue Colonel Brandon for his fortune, hinting at Edward Ferrars's planned marriage to the wealthy Miss Morton, and calculating potential inheritances from Mrs. Jennings, all while complaining of his own expenses.

At the Harley Street dinner Mrs. Ferrars coldly snubs Elinor while warmly favouring Lucy Steele — unaware Lucy is secretly engaged to her son Edward — until Marianne, outraged by the slight, defends her sister aloud and collapses in tears, prompting Colonel Brandon's visible concern.

Lucy visits Elinor to gloat over Mrs. Ferrars's apparent approval, Edward arrives unexpectedly creating an excruciating three-way scene, and Elinor maintains heroic composure while Marianne inadvertently praises Edward's conscience, all three trapped by the secret Lucy and Elinor share.

Elinor and Marianne are pushed into daily visits at the Middletons' alongside Lucy Steele; at a musical party Elinor meets the conceited Robert Ferrars; Fanny Dashwood, to dodge hosting her sisters-in-law, invites the Miss Steeles to Harley Street instead, unwittingly advancing Lucy's scheme to be near Edward.

Mrs. Jennings brings news that Edward Ferrars's secret engagement to Lucy Steele has been exposed at the Dashwood house; Elinor reveals to a horrified Marianne that she has borne this knowledge for four months, and John Dashwood reports that Edward refused to break the engagement despite Mrs. Ferrars's threats and has been disinherited in favour of his brother Robert.

Anne Steele reveals to Elinor (via eavesdropped conversation) that Edward stood firm by Lucy despite disinheritance, plans to take orders, and Lucy then writes Elinor a letter confirming the engagement holds and soliciting help securing a living.
Colonel Brandon offers Edward Ferrars the living at Delaford through Elinor, while Mrs. Jennings comically misreads their window conversation as a marriage proposal to Elinor.

Colonel Brandon offers Edward Ferrars the living of Delaford through Elinor, who delivers the news to Edward in person amid mutual embarrassment, while Mrs. Jennings comically misreads the situation as a marriage proposal to Elinor before the confusion is cleared up.

Elinor visits John Dashwood, who marvels at Colonel Brandon's gift of the Delaford living to Edward; Robert Ferrars then ridicules Edward's clerical fate and his engagement to Lucy, exposing the Ferrars family's hypocrisy and class prejudice.

The Dashwood sisters leave London and arrive at Cleveland, where Marianne's obsessive grief over Willoughby drives her to reckless wet-weather rambles that bring on a violent cold, while Colonel Brandon briefs Elinor on Edward Ferrars's parsonage at Delaford and reveals his unspoken devotion to Marianne through anxious looks.

Marianne's illness deteriorates into near-fatal crisis at Cleveland; Elinor nurses her through a terrifying night while Colonel Brandon rides to fetch their mother; Marianne recovers, but the chapter ends with the shock entrance of Willoughby instead of Mrs. Dashwood.

Willoughby arrives at Cleveland to confess to Elinor his selfish motives for courting Marianne, explaining how financial necessity and vanity led him to abandon her and marry Miss Grey, and begging Elinor to relay his remorse and penitence to her sister.

After Willoughby departs, Elinor processes complex pity for him while Mrs. Dashwood arrives with Colonel Brandon and privately reveals to Elinor that Colonel Brandon has declared his love for Marianne, urging hope for their eventual marriage.

Recovering from illness, Marianne returns home with Elinor, confronts memories of Willoughby at the spot where they met, delivers a heartfelt confession of past selfishness and vows moral reformation, then learns Willoughby's apology from Elinor and weeps in private grief.

After Marianne reaches painful closure on Willoughby's selfishness through Elinor's cool analysis, a servant's report that Edward Ferrars has married Lucy Steele shocks the household and forces Mrs. Dashwood to recognize how much she has overlooked Elinor's silent, long-suppressed grief.

Edward Ferrars arrives unexpectedly at Barton Cottage and reveals that Lucy Steele married his brother Robert instead of him, releasing Elinor from her long-suppressed anguish and sending her from the room in tears of joy.

Edward Ferrars, freed from his engagement to Lucy Steele (who secretly married his brother Robert), arrives at Barton Cottage and proposes to Elinor Dashwood, who joyfully accepts, while Colonel Brandon also visits and the two men bond as the newly engaged couple plans reconciliation with Mrs. Ferrars.

The final chapter resolves all fates: Edward and Elinor marry and settle at Delaford parsonage with Colonel Brandon's help; Marianne overcomes her romantic idealism and marries Colonel Brandon; Lucy Steele's calculated flattery wins Mrs. Ferrars's favour over Edward; and Willoughby lives comfortably but always regards Marianne as his secret standard of perfection.

Testi/Wilde/Atomized/009_The_Picture_of_.plot: Wilde's Preface declares his aesthetic manifesto: art exists solely to create beauty, has no moral purpose, and all art is quite useless.

Basil confesses to Lord Henry his obsessive artistic idolatry of Dorian Gray and refuses to exhibit the portrait because it exposes his soul; despite Basil's reluctance to introduce them, Dorian arrives at the studio as the chapter ends.

While Basil completes Dorian's portrait, Lord Henry mesmerizes Dorian with his philosophy of hedonism and the brevity of youth; upon seeing the finished painting, Dorian wishes his soul away so the picture ages in his place, speaking the fatal wish that sets the novel's central curse in motion.

Lord Henry visits his uncle to uncover Dorian's tragic family history, then dazzles guests at a society lunch where Dorian is present, while privately resolving to dominate the young man's soul as Basil's portrait dominates his image.
Dorian tells Lord Henry of his passionate love for actress Sibyl Vane, discovered performing Shakespeare in a dingy theatre; the chapter ends with Dorian's telegram announcing he is engaged to her.

Sibyl Vane declares her love for the mysterious Prince Charming (Dorian Gray) to her mother and departing brother James, who distrusts the gentleman; when Dorian passes them briefly in the park, James swears to kill him if he wrongs Sibyl, then wrings from their mother the admission that he is illegitimate.

At a private dinner, Dorian announces his engagement to actress Sibyl Vane; Basil worries about the mismatch while Lord Henry philosophizes on marriage, pleasure, and morality, and the three men then head to the theatre to watch Sibyl perform.

Dorian brings Basil and Lord Henry to watch Sibyl Vane perform Juliet, but she acts badly because real love has eclipsed art for her; Dorian cruelly rejects her, and returning home notices the portrait has taken on a cruel expression — the first sign his wish is taking effect.

Dorian learns from Lord Henry that Sibyl Vane has died; after brief guilt he examines the altered portrait and resolves to let it bear the burden of his sins while he pursues a life of eternal youth and pleasure.

Morning after Sibyl's death: Basil confronts Dorian's shocking coldness, confesses his obsessive idolisation of Dorian as the soul of his art, and Dorian — having kept Basil from seeing the portrait — resolves to hide it permanently.

Dorian has the portrait secretly moved to his locked childhood schoolroom, reads the decadent "yellow book" sent by Lord Henry with fascination, and coldly dismisses the newspaper inquest report announcing Sibyl Vane's death before meeting Lord Henry at the club.

Dorian Gray, consumed by the yellow book Lord Henry gave him, spends years obsessively pursuing aesthetic experiences — perfumes, exotic music, jewels, embroideries, vestments — while his youth stays intact and the hidden portrait silently bears the corruption of his dissolute secret life.
Basil confronts Dorian with rumors of moral ruin and ruined associates; Dorian, stung, seizes a lamp and leads him upstairs to see the portrait itself as his answer.
Dorian reveals the corrupted portrait to Basil, then in a sudden rage stabs him to death and calmly engineers an alibi through his valet.
Dorian, haunted by Basil Hallward's corpse, summons scientist Alan Campbell and blackmails him into chemically destroying the body with nitric acid, eliminating all evidence of the murder.

Dorian performs social normality at Lady Narborough's dinner with Lord Henry, then returns home to burn Basil Hallward's remaining belongings, and finally yields to opium craving and sneaks out toward the river den.

Dorian flees to an opium den to blot out guilt; James Vane corners him at gunpoint to avenge Sibyl's death, but Dorian's unchangingly youthful face convinces him he has the wrong man — until a woman confirms the terrible truth that Dorian has not aged in eighteen years.

At Selby Royal, Dorian and Lord Henry engage in sparkling wit with the Duchess of Monmouth, but Dorian collapses in a faint when he glimpses James Vane's face pressed against the conservatory window, watching him.
Dorian, consumed by terror that James Vane is hunting him, discovers after a shooting accident that the sailor killed in the hunt is Vane himself, and rides home with tears of relief at being safe.

Dorian dines with Lord Henry and declares intent to reform, while they debate Basil's mysterious disappearance; Dorian obliquely confesses to killing Basil (dismissed as posturing by Lord Henry), and their exchange circles around the soul, corruption, and the secret behind Dorian's unchanging youth.

Tormented by guilt and the worsening portrait, Dorian resolves to destroy it — stabbing it with Basil's murder knife — and is found dead, aged and hideous, while the portrait reverts to its youthful beauty.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/David_Copperfield.plot: David rides to Canterbury, confesses his long-suppressed love to Agnes, discovers she has loved him all her life, and they marry within a fortnight; Agnes then reveals that Dora herself, on her deathbed, had asked Agnes to take her place.

Mr. Peggotty visits David and Agnes in London after years in Australia, recounting Emily's quiet redemption, Martha's marriage, Micawber's triumph as a colonial magistrate, and closing with a visit to Ham's grave to gather earth for Emily.

In this closing retrospect David surveys the faces of his past — Agnes at his side, Aunt Betsey and Peggotty in old age, Micawber still whimsically hopeful, Traddles prosperously settled — before dismissing all shadows and ending his written story with a rapturous apostrophe to Agnes as his guiding, heavenly presence.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Dombey_and_Son/Ch.plot: Paul Dombey sits triumphant beside his dying wife who has just delivered a male heir, fixating entirely on the boy as the future of his firm while barely acknowledging his daughter Florence.

Paul Dombey Jr. is christened in a cold, formal ceremony presided over by his pride-driven father, with Florence and Susan Nipper in attendance, while hints of the infant's fragility shadow the occasion.
Paul is dispatched to Mrs. Pipchin's bleak Brighton establishment, attended by Florence and Susan Nipper, marking his second painful uprooting from home and deepening his physical decline.
Paul Dombey grows into an odd, old-fashioned child at Mrs. Pipchin's establishment, develops deep dependence on Florence, and poses his father the famous question about what money can and cannot do.
Solomon Gills faces bankruptcy at the Wooden Midshipman shop; Captain Cuttle and Walter Gay scramble to raise money and save him, with Walter turning to the Dombey firm for help.

After Sol Gills vanishes to search for the shipwrecked Walter Gay, Captain Cuttle takes charge of the Wooden Midshipman shop and receives a grieving Florence Dombey, who arrives with Susan Nipper seeking news of Walter.
Paul Dombey is brought to Doctor Blimber's academy in Brighton, accompanied by Florence and Susan Nipper, marking his entry into formal schooling away from home.
Paul endures the relentless academic regime at Dr. Blimber's school while Florence and Susan visit him, revealing his deteriorating health and the deep bond between the siblings.
Paul Dombey grows ever more old-fashioned at school while Captain Cuttle devises an artful scheme tied to shipping news, opening a new pursuit for Walter Gay amid the business of Dombey's firm.

Young Paul Dombey dies peacefully at home, comforted by Florence at his bedside, as he drifts toward death murmuring about waves and visions of his dead mother, while Walter Gay is summoned to his side.
Captain Cuttle visits Solomon Gills's shop to discuss Walter Gay's forced posting to Barbados and pawns his own valuables to raise money on the young people's behalf.
After little Paul's death, Florence seeks her father's love and comfort, but Mr. Dombey coldly rebuffs her every approach, leaving her more isolated than before.
Walter Gay says farewell to his uncle Sol Gills, Captain Cuttle, Florence Dombey, and Susan Nipper before sailing to Barbados on orders engineered by Dombey to remove him from Florence's orbit.

Mr. Dombey travels to Leamington with Major Bagstock, who engineers an introduction to the proud, beautiful widow Edith Granger and her scheming mother Mrs. Skewton, planting the seed of Dombey's second marriage.

Major Bagstock engineers an introduction between Mr. Dombey and the beautiful widow Edith Granger (with her scheming mother Mrs. Skewton) at a Leamington spa resort, planting the seed of Dombey's second marriage.
Carker exploits his managerial authority to coerce the disgraced Rob the Grinder into becoming his personal spy and dependent, exposing his predatory, scheming nature.
Florence grows ever more solitary in her father's cold house while, at the Wooden Midshipman, Solomon Gills vanishes without explanation and Captain Cuttle keeps a lonely vigil in his absence.

Florence, isolated and ignored by her father after Paul's death, throws herself into diligent study hoping to earn Mr. Dombey's love, while quietly pining for the absent Walter Gay, with only Susan Nipper as her companion.

Solomon Gills, distressed by Walter Gay's forced posting to the West Indies, vanishes from the instrument shop, leaving Captain Cuttle to hold the fort while Florence and Susan Nipper arrive to bid Walter farewell.

Florence endures her father's continued coldness as shadows of dead Paul haunt the household while Dombey advances his courtship of Edith Granger, with Carker and Major Bagstock lurking in the social machinery around the match.

In the Dombey household after the marriage, Mr. Dombey and Edith maintain a proud, icy coexistence while Florence remains invisible to her father and Carker's scheming influence deepens the gloom over all.

Mr. Dombey has the family house extensively refurbished in preparation for his marriage to Edith Granger, while Florence silently witnesses alterations that further erase her presence in the household and Carker maneuvers himself into the new domestic order.

Mrs Chick discovers that her longtime friend Miss Tox had secretly nursed matrimonial hopes for Mr Dombey, and, outraged by this perceived betrayal, she coldly severs their friendship in the wake of Dombey's marriage to Edith Granger.

In the days before Dombey's wedding to Edith, Florence hopes Edith will be a true mother to her, Edith privately shows Florence genuine tenderness while entering a cold mercenary union, Carker insinuates himself as useful go-between, and Dombey's pride remains the engine driving the whole arrangement.
Mr. Dombey and Edith Granger are wed in a formal, joyless ceremony witnessed by Florence, Major Bagstock, Carker, and Susan Nipper — a union of pride and social calculation with no trace of love.

Florence Dombey, struck by her father and fleeing his house, arrives with Susan Nipper at the Wooden Midshipman shop, where Captain Cuttle has kept a lonely vigil during Sol Gills's absence, and the neglected shop's deterioration mirrors the collapse of every surrounding relationship.

Chapter juxtaposes Florence's lonely, neglected life in the frigid Dombey mansion against warmer domestic scenes elsewhere, while Edith's proud coldness toward her husband and Carker's creeping influence deepen the household's moral divide.

Edith Granger and her scheming mother Mrs. Skewton receive James Carker, whose flattery of the mother and probing attention to Edith expose the hollow, mercenary foundation of Edith's arranged marriage to Dombey and deepen her bitter, silent resistance.

Dombey and Edith Granger are married in an outwardly splendid ceremony that exposes the cold, transactional nature of their union, while Florence, Carker, and Major Bagstock observe the hollow spectacle of the "happy pair."

Dombey and his new wife Edith host a lavish housewarming party that showcases their wealth while exposing the frigid emptiness of the marriage, as Carker maneuvers himself into Edith's orbit and Florence remains on the household's periphery.
Florence observes Edith's veiled warnings about Carker's treacherous nature while Carker ingratiates himself further into the Dombey household, multiplying omens of the domestic catastrophe to come.

Miss Tox, shut out from the Dombey household since his remarriage, renews her acquaintance with the Toodle family as a surrogate link to the world—and the people, chiefly Florence—she can no longer reach.

Captain Cuttle takes in the fleeing Florence Dombey at Solomon Gills's deserted instrument shop, improvises domestic care for her, and Susan Nipper joins to serve as companion while Cuttle keeps the shop and waits for news of Walter Gay.

In the Dombey household after the marriage, Mr. Dombey continues to coldly ignore Florence while Edith, though proud and constrained herself, shows unexpected warmth toward her stepdaughter, and Carker insinuates himself as Dombey's trusted agent amid the household's brittle domestic arrangements.

Florence Dombey, haunted by the death of little Paul and the disappearance of Walter Gay, hears new voices in the waves that merge Paul's remembered words with her anguish for Walter, while Captain Cuttle and Solomon Gills anxiously wait for news of their lost boy.

Carker meets privately with Edith to relay Dombey's expectations in his role as calculating go-between, while Florence accidentally intrudes on the charged encounter, exposing the household's web of coercion and false intimacy.

Florence Dombey keeps lonely night vigil in the cold Dombey mansion while Captain Cuttle maintains watch at the Wooden Midshipman, both waiting anxiously for news of the missing Walter Gay and the absent Solomon Gills.

Edith flees the Dombey household alongside Carker, and Mr. Dombey discovers his wife's departure while Florence and Susan Nipper witness the collapse of the marriage and the fury of Dombey's wounded pride.

Carker visits Edith as Dombey's self-appointed trusty agent and delivers his master's cold, domineering instructions, exposing both Dombey's tyrannical hold over his wife and Carker's own sinister, double-dealing influence over the household.

Florence reflects on her deep attachment to Edith and her fruitless longing for her father's affection while Major Bagstock and Susan Nipper hover at the edges of a Dombey household poised on the brink of crisis.
Edith elopes with Carker, and when the devastated Mr. Dombey violently rejects Florence's attempt to comfort him, she flees the Dombey house accompanied by Susan Nipper.
After being struck by her grief-maddened father following Edith's elopement with Carker, Florence flees the Dombey house and takes shelter with Captain Cuttle at the Wooden Midshipman.
After fleeing her father's house, Florence Dombey arrives at the Wooden Midshipman where Captain Cuttle discovers her and takes her in.
Mr Toots visits the Midshipman and pours out his lovesick complaint about Florence to Captain Cuttle and Susan Nipper, who receive his comic, heartfelt confession of unrequited devotion.

After Edith's elopement with Carker becomes public scandal, Mr. Dombey endures the world's contempt alone, his rigid pride preventing him from showing grief while fair-weather allies like Major Bagstock quietly withdraw.
News of Edith's flight with Carker spreads through society via Major Bagstock's gossiping, while Florence shelters with Captain Cuttle at the Wooden Midshipman and Susan Nipper rejoins her there.
Captain Cuttle receives further intelligence about Carker's elopement with Edith while Florence Dombey, having fled her father after he struck her, arrives at the Wooden Midshipman seeking shelter.
Florence flees her father's house after he strikes her and takes shelter with Captain Cuttle, while Edith and Carker are simultaneously fugitives having eloped together.

Rob the Grinder, left without employment after Carker's flight, arrives at Captain Cuttle's instrument shop—where Florence is sheltering—seeking help, while Carker's absence exposes Rob's role as a spy.
Walter Gay returns safely from sea, filling Captain Cuttle, Sol Gills, and Florence with joy, while the Game Chicken is disgusted by his patron Toots's romantic preoccupations.
Florence Dombey and Walter Gay marry in a quiet ceremony witnessed by Captain Cuttle and Susan Nipper, while the long-absent Solomon Gills unexpectedly returns to complete the family reunion.
After a long lapse of time, Solomon Gills returns to the Wooden Midshipman and is joyfully reunited with Captain Cuttle, while Florence and Walter Gay find quiet domestic peace together.

Edith reveals to Carker she never intended to become his mistress but used him as instrument of revenge against Dombey; Carker flees in horror and is struck dead by a train while being hunted by Dombey.

Florence Dombey and Walter Gay, now married, reunite with the returned Solomon Gills and Captain Cuttle at the Wooden Midshipman, while Susan Nipper's marriage to Mr. Toots is also celebrated in a chapter surveying the matrimonial happiness of those who remained loyal.
Broken by financial collapse and left utterly alone, Paul Dombey is visited by Florence, who returns with Walter Gay, and he at last relents, weeping and accepting the daughter he had long rejected.
The unit contains only the heading for the final chapter (LXII) and references to the 1848 and 1867 prefaces, with no narrative text present in the file.
Paul Dombey Sr. exults over the birth of his long-awaited male heir while his wife Fanny, too weak to rally, dies as Florence clings to her.

After his wife Fanny's death, the coldly proud Mr. Dombey hires working-class Polly Toodle as wet nurse for infant Paul, renames her "Richards," and insists the arrangement be purely transactional with no emotional bond formed.

After Mrs. Dombey's funeral, wet-nurse Polly Richards comforts the grieving Florence and, despite Susan Nipper's orders to keep them apart, wins Mr. Dombey's cold permission for Florence to visit baby Paul — exposing Dombey's emotional distance from his daughter.

Walter Gay returns home after his first day at Dombey and Son's firm; uncle Solomon Gills and Captain Cuttle celebrate with the prized Madeira wine, share seafaring tales, and Sol urges Walter to embrace commerce over the sea while hinting at Walter's future prospects tied to the Dombey house.

Little Paul is christened with Miss Tox as godmother in a bleak, cheerless ceremony that mirrors Mr. Dombey's icy pride, while Florence is marginalized by her father's indifference and finds solace only by creeping beside her infant brother, as Susan Nipper secretly plans to escort Richards to see her own child.

Florence is separated from her nurses during street chaos, abducted and stripped of her clothes by the sinister "Good Mrs Brown," then found by Walter Gay who brings her safely to his uncle Solomon Gills's shop before Walter fetches Susan Nipper to return her home to a cold, indifferent Mr Dombey — who dismisses nurse Polly Richards for the unauthorized visit to Staggs's Gardens.

Miss Tox snubs Major Bagstock and lavishes obsessive attention on baby Paul Dombey, nursing secret matrimonial ambitions toward Mr. Dombey while the Major watches from across Princess's Place in bewildered jealousy.

Sickly young Paul Dombey grows up under his cold father's impatient ambition, questions whether money can save lives, is sent to Brighton under the harsh Mrs Pipchin, and begins listening mystically to the sea while clinging to Florence for comfort.

Walter Gay, nursing romantic daydreams about Florence, discovers Uncle Solomon Gills is under a broker's execution for a £370 bond debt, rushes to Captain Cuttle for help, and the two set off for Brighton to petition Mr Dombey for a loan.

Major Bagstock engineers a friendship with Mr Dombey at Brighton, while Walter Gay and Captain Cuttle plead for rescue of Solomon Gills from debt, which Dombey grants by letting young Paul symbolically "lend" the money.

Mr. Dombey enrolls six-year-old Paul at Dr. Blimber's relentlessly rigorous boarding school, where Paul weeps at parting from Florence and is left isolated in the cold, mechanically learned establishment.

Paul Dombey arrives at Doctor Blimber's hothouse school and endures relentless academic grinding, finding his only relief when Florence secretly masters his textbooks and tutors him on Saturday visits, their bond deepening as Paul grows solitary and morbidly contemplative.

Mr Dombey, prompted by Carker the Manager, appoints Walter Gay to a junior post in Barbados; afterward Carker the Junior privately confesses his past embezzlement and social death to Walter, urging him to keep his integrity.

Ailing little Paul Dombey is released from studies at Doctor Blimber's, attends the school's end-of-term party where Florence's singing moves him to tears, bids emotional farewells to all, and is carried home in a feverish and confused state that signals his approaching death.
Walter Gay enlists Captain Cuttle to break news of his forced Barbados posting to Uncle Sol, then encounters Susan Nipper searching for Paul Dombey's old nurse as the dying child asks to see her.

Young Paul Dombey lies dying, comforted ceaselessly by sister Florence, bids farewell to Walter Gay and his grief-stricken father, then slips away peacefully in a vision of a river bearing him to the sea where he glimpses his dead mother.

Captain Cuttle visits Carker at Dombey's offices to sound out Walter Gay's prospects, and is duped by Carker's sly smiling into believing Walter is headed for fortune and romance with Florence, while the narrator flags Carker's cat-like treachery.

After little Paul's funeral, Florence mourns alone while Mr. Dombey shuts himself away; Mr. Toots brings her Paul's dog Diogenes as a keepsake; Florence's nightly vigil at her father's door finally leads to a confrontation in which he coldly repels her, extinguishing her last hope for his affection.

On the eve of Walter Gay's voyage to Barbados, Florence Dombey and Susan Nipper visit Sol Gills's shop to say goodbye; Florence pledges to befriend the lonely old man in Walter's absence, asks Walter to be her brother in memory of dead Paul, and the next morning Captain Cuttle escorts Walter and Sol to the Son and Heir, which then sails away.

Mr. Dombey and Major Bagstock travel by train from London to Leamington; a chance encounter with stoker Toodle (wearing mourning crape for his own dead son) sharpens Dombey's jealous grief over little Paul, while the train journey becomes a sustained meditation on death and Dombey's bitter resentment that Florence survived instead of his son.

At Leamington, Major Bagstock introduces Mr Dombey to the vain Mrs Skewton and her proud widowed daughter Edith Granger; repeated encounters lead to an evening visit where Dombey grows visibly drawn to Edith's beauty and accomplishments.

Carker the Manager recruits the wayward Rob Toodle as a spy to be placed in Sol Gills's shop and report on all visitors—especially a young lady—while coldly dismissing his brother John's plea for reconciliation with their sister Harriet.

Florence, living alone in the desolate Dombey house and longing for her father's love, visits Captain Cuttle and drags him to consult the oracle Bunsby about Walter's overdue ship, while Uncle Sol behaves with unsettling urgency and secrecy that troubles them all.

Florence, staying with the Skettles family at Fulham, obsessively studies children with loving fathers to learn how to win her own father's love, overhears a stranger pity her as a child outcast from a living parent, and ends the chapter with an unsettling roadside encounter with Carker, who offers to carry her message to Mr. Dombey at Leamington and leaves her trembling.

Captain Cuttle discovers Solomon Gills has vanished overnight, leaving him the shop keys and a letter asking him to keep a home for Walter; after a fruitless week searching for the old man's body, Cuttle secretly flees his landlady Mrs MacStinger and installs himself at the Instrument-maker's to await news.

Carker arrives at Leamington and insinuates himself into Major Bagstock's and Dombey's confidence, while Bagstock conspires with Mrs Skewton to push Dombey's courtship of Edith Granger forward; the evening's dinner reveals Carker's hidden predatory ambitions beneath a facade of servility.

Carker joins Dombey, Major Bagstock, Mrs Skewton, and Edith on a day excursion to Warwick Castle, where he covertly observes the cold transactional courtship; that night Edith erupts to her mother in bitter shame, declaring she knows Dombey is buying her but has refused to actively lure him.

Florence returns from the Skettles villa to find the Dombey house gutted by workmen, and her cold father introduces her to Edith — his future wife — who silently embraces Florence and privately begs her to begin by thinking well of her.
Mrs Chick visits Miss Tox to announce Paul Dombey's engagement to Edith, and upon realizing Miss Tox has nursed secret romantic hopes for Dombey herself, furiously severs their long friendship.

In the week before her wedding to Mr. Dombey, Edith brings Florence to stay with her and Mrs. Skewton; Florence endures an awkward dinner reunion with her cold father; and on the wedding eve Edith, consumed by guilt over the mercenary match, orders Florence home to protect her innocence, then breaks down weeping over the sleeping girl.

Mr. Dombey weds Edith Granger in a grand church ceremony attended by Major Bagstock, Carker, Florence, and Captain Cuttle, while Edith's cold compliance and Carker's ominous attentions cast a dark shadow over the union.

Captain Cuttle, sheltering at the Wooden Midshipman, receives confirmation via Mr Toots that Walter Gay's ship the Son and Heir is wrecked and all aboard perished; he grieves, confronts Carker at Dombey's office only to be contemptuously dismissed, then returns to don mourning clothes and privately read the Burial Service for Walter.

Chapter contrasts Carker the Manager's opulent Norwood cottage—where he broods over a portrait resembling Edith—with the poor home of his disgraced siblings Harriet and John Carker, where Harriet receives a mysterious elderly benefactor and then shelters a destitute ex-convict woman with quiet compassion.

Alice Marwood returns from transportation to her squalid mother Good Mrs Brown, bitterly indicts her ruined childhood and unjust conviction, learns her mother has spied on the Dombey household, then discovers she unwittingly accepted charity from Harriet Carker—sister of the man she despises—and flings the money back with violent curses before the chapter closes with a pointed parallel to Edith Dombey and her own scheming mother.

Dombeys return home after honeymoon; the marriage is immediately shown as cold and mercenary, while Florence and Edith form a tender bond, with Edith warning Florence not to seek from her any model of love, even as Florence hopes Edith will help her win her father's affection.

At the Dombeys' housewarming dinner, rival guest factions clash, Cousin Feenix accidentally exposes the mercenary nature of the marriage with a blundering anecdote, and Dombey then publicly rebukes Edith for coldness to his guests—with Carker as witness—only to be crushed by her silent, withering contempt.
