Carker visits Edith and uses veiled knowledge of Florence's past associations to coerce her silence, securing her complicity through subtle blackmail; shortly after, Mrs. Skewton suffers a paralytic stroke, recovers with rose-coloured curtains and renewed vanity, but grows jealously demanding of Edith's affection.

Miss Tox, cut off from the Dombey circle after being snubbed by Louisa Chick, visits the Toodle family to cultivate Polly Richards as an informant on Dombey affairs, while Rob the Grinder's duplicitous character is exposed when he immediately wastes the charitable gift Miss Tox gives him on parting.

Captain Cuttle, living in solitary exile at the instrument shop after Rob the Grinder's treacherous departure, opens Solomon Gills's sealed packet in Bunsby's presence, reads Sol's farewell letter and will, then barely survives a terrifying invasion by his landlady Mrs MacStinger before Bunsby diplomatically escorts her away and retrieves Cuttle's chest.

Mr Dombey demands Edith's total submission and rejects her offered truce, then the household departs for Brighton where Mrs Skewton's mental decline worsens and Edith encounters a beggar-woman who eerily mirrors her own fate of having been sold.

Florence visits Brighton and revisits Dr. Blimber's school with the lovesick Mr. Toots (who confesses his feelings and is gently refused), while Edith tends to her dying mother Mrs. Skewton nearby; the chapter ends with Mrs. Skewton's death and the making of funeral arrangements.

Carker receives Dombey's explicit instructions to demand Edith's submission and suppress her bond with Florence; after Dombey is thrown and injured from his horse, Carker uses the accident as a pretext to visit the house and exercise coercive dominance over Edith, who afterward strikes her own hand in fury and shame.

Florence, tormented by estrangement between her father and Edith, steals to her injured father's bedside at night and silently kisses him as he sleeps, then finds Edith awake in anguished wakefulness, delivering a dark monologue about self-defeating pride and clinging to Florence as her only hope.

Susan Nipper confronts Mr Dombey about his neglect of Florence, is promptly dismissed by Mrs Pipchin on his orders, bids Florence a tearful farewell, and is escorted to her night-coach by the kind-hearted Mr Toots.

Carker visits Edith at night, ostensibly as Dombey's agent, to deliver the threat that her open affection for Florence will be used against the girl, while covertly drawing out Edith's contempt for her husband and tightening his psychological hold over her.

Carker intensifies his scrutiny of Dombey's firm and finances, Rob the Grinder is coerced by the vengeful Mrs Brown and her daughter Alice who despise Carker, Carker quarrels bitterly with his brother John over loyalty to Dombey, and the chapter closes with Carker riding past the Dombey house, brooding on his perilous, manipulative entanglement with the proud and hating Edith.
Edith openly defies Dombey at dinner and demands separation, then elopes overnight with Carker; upon discovering this, Dombey strikes Florence and drives her out of the house.

Florence flees her father's house in desperate grief and takes refuge with Captain Cuttle at Sol Gills's instrument shop, where the Captain hides her, locks the door against pursuit, and keeps tender watch while she sleeps.

Florence, having fled her father's violent household, shelters with Captain Cuttle at the Midshipman, where he tenderly cares for her and then haltingly reveals—through a barely disguised tale of a wrecked ship—that Walter Gay survived the storm and has returned alive, reuniting the two in tearful joy.

Florence, sheltering at the Midshipman after fleeing her father, and Walter—torn between honour and love—finally confess their mutual love and become engaged, while the lovesick Mr Toots volunteers to find the missing Susan Nipper.

After Edith's flight with Carker, a stoic Mr Dombey endures public disgrace in silence while Major Bagstock and Cousin Feenix visit to offer sympathy and hint at vengeance, and the wider household — clerks, servants, and the devoted Miss Tox — all speculate freely about his ruin.

Mr Dombey secretly visits Good Mrs Brown's squalid dwelling, where the old woman manipulates and terrorises Rob the Grinder into revealing that Carker and Edith traveled separately and rendezvoused in Dijon, giving Dombey the intelligence he needs to pursue them.

John Carker is dismissed from Dombey's firm by letter; their secret benefactor Mr Morfin reveals himself and promises help; then Alice Marwood arrives to confess she betrayed James Carker's location at Dijon to the furious Mr Dombey, and now repents, urgently warning Harriet to get word to James to flee before Dombey overtakes him.

Edith, having lured Carker to a midnight Paris apartment under the pretense of elopement, confronts him with a knife and declares the flight was a deliberate trap to shame him and Dombey alike, then escapes through a hidden passage as Dombey's party hammers at the door.

After being humiliated and spurned by Edith, Carker flees in a feverish, guilt-racked delirium by carriage and sea from France back to England, haunted throughout by premonitions of death, until he stumbles onto a railway track and is killed by a train at the moment he comes face to face with Paul Dombey, the man he had wronged.

In the days before Florence Dombey and Walter Gay's wedding, Susan Nipper and Mr Toots return to the Midshipman where Toots gracefully accepts his unrequited love; on the wedding eve, Solomon Gills unexpectedly returns from his long Caribbean search, and Captain Cuttle discovers that Sol's letters never reached him because he had fled Mrs MacStinger's lodgings.

Florence Dombey and Walter Gay marry quietly in a humble city church with Captain Cuttle, Susan Nipper, and Solomon Gills as witnesses, then depart by coach and ship while Sol reads aloud Walter's explanatory letter addressed to Mr Dombey.

A year after Dombey and Son collapses, Harriet Carker secretly enlists Mr. Morfin to channel her inherited fortune back to the ruined Mr. Dombey, while Alice Marwood dies peacefully at Harriet's side after her mother reveals Alice's blood kinship with Edith Dombey.

After Dombey's bankruptcy empties and auctions the great house and all servants depart, Mr Dombey sinks into isolated shame and near-suicidal despair, until Florence returns, kneels before him begging forgiveness, and breaks through his pride to achieve their long-overdue reconciliation.

Two weddings occur — Feeder marries Cornelia Blimber while the hapless Bunsby is dragooned into marrying Mrs MacStinger — then Captain Cuttle and the Tootses (Susan Nipper now Mrs Toots) rush to Florence, learning that she has reconciled with her dying father and brought him home.

Florence nurses her delirious, dying father while Cousin Feenix engineers a surprise meeting with Edith, who tearfully proclaims her innocence of adultery with Carker and bids Florence a final, irrevocable farewell.

In the final chapter, an aged and humbled Paul Dombey Sr. celebrates Walter and Florence's happiness with Captain Cuttle and Sol Gills, while a closing vision of Dombey tenderly caring for his grandchildren by the sea confirms his full redemption.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Great_Expectation.plot: Young orphan Pip, visiting his family's graves on the Kent marshes, is seized by an escaped convict who threatens him into promising to bring food and a file by morning.

Pip, tormented by guilt over his promise to the convict, hides food down his trousers at tea, suffers Mrs Joe's abuse and tar-water punishment, learns about prison hulks, and at dawn secretly steals food and a file from the forge before fleeing to the marshes.

Pip delivers stolen food and a file to the convict on the marshes, accidentally encounters a second escaped convict, and reports this to the first convict, who frantically files his leg-iron to pursue the other man.

On Christmas Day Pip endures a dinner of moral lectures from Mrs Joe, Pumblechook, Wopsle, and the Hubbles while concealing his theft from the pantry; Pumblechook accidentally drinks tar-water Pip substituted for brandy; just as the missing pork pie is about to be discovered, soldiers appear at the door bearing handcuffs.

Soldiers arrive at Joe's forge to repair handcuffs, then Joe and Pip join the marsh hunt and witness Magwitch recaptured after he deliberately drags down the other convict; Magwitch confesses to stealing Joe's food, and Joe responds with unsentimental compassion before Magwitch is rowed back to the prison hulk.

Pip, carried home by Joe after the convict episode, silently resolves not to confess his theft to Joe, fearing loss of Joe's good opinion, while the household invents wild theories about how the convict entered the pantry.

Pip shows Joe a crudely written letter, Joe confesses his own illiteracy and recounts his abusive childhood, then Mrs Joe returns with Uncle Pumblechook announcing Miss Havisham has summoned Pip to her house to play.

Pip is escorted to Satis House where he meets the eerily time-frozen Miss Havisham in her yellowed bridal dress, then plays cards with the scornful Estella, who humiliates him over his coarse hands and common origins, leaving him weeping in the brewery yard and newly ashamed of his social station.
Pip fabricates wild lies about Miss Havisham's to satisfy Mrs. Joe and Pumblechook, then privately confesses the truth to Joe and reveals his shame at being called "common" by Estella.

Pip asks Biddy to teach him, then at the pub encounters a mysterious stranger who secretly shows him a file linked to Magwitch and slips him money, leaving Pip haunted by guilt over his convict connection.

Pip returns to Satis House, is made to walk a morbid Miss Havisham around her cobwebbed wedding-feast room on her forbidden birthday while sycophantic relatives visit, meets a burly stranger on the stairs (Jaggers, unnamed), fights a pale young gentleman (Herbert Pocket, unnamed) in the overgrown garden, and receives a contemptuous kiss from Estella as reward.

Over eight to ten months Pip regularly visits Miss Havisham, pushing her wheelchair and singing for her while Estella remains coldly capricious; the period ends when Miss Havisham tells Pip to bring Joe Gargery so he can be formally apprenticed.

Joe and Pip visit Miss Havisham to sign Pip's indentures; she pays 25 guineas as apprenticeship premium, and Pip is formally bound to Joe's forge trade — leaving him secretly wretched and disillusioned while Pumblechook falsely claims credit at a celebratory dinner.

Pip reflects on his shame of home and forge apprenticeship, contrasting his former innocent belief in both with his current sense of coarseness, haunted by fear Estella will see him at his grimiest and despise him, while crediting Joe's faithfulness alone for keeping him from abandoning his indentures.

Pip takes a half-holiday to visit a cold, dismissive Miss Havisham and learns Estella is abroad beyond his reach; meanwhile Orlick's quarrel with Mrs Joe and his subsequent brawl with Joe foreshadow the chapter's dark close, when Mrs Joe is found savagely struck down by an unknown hand.

Mrs Joe is found brutally attacked with a convict's filed leg-iron; she survives but is left brain-damaged and mute, Biddy joins the household to care for her, and Pip suspects Orlick or the stranger with the file—a suspicion reinforced when Mrs Joe's slate-drawings repeatedly summon Orlick, toward whom she shows fearful submission.
Pip confides to Biddy his obsession with Estella and desire to become a gentleman; Biddy wisely challenges his motives; on the walk home Orlick lurks menacingly behind them.

Lawyer Mr Jaggers arrives at the forge to announce Pip has "great expectations" from a secret patron, cancels his apprenticeship to Joe, and instructs him to come to London to be educated as a gentleman.

Pip burns his apprenticeship indentures, quarrels with Biddy over Joe's manners, shops for gentleman's clothes while discovering money's social power, visits Miss Havisham to say goodbye, and finally departs for London in tears, closing the first stage of his expectations.

Pip arrives in London, wanders near Newgate Prison, waits in Jaggers's grim office, witnesses Jaggers bully clients and expose a witness-tampering attempt, receives his financial arrangements, and is escorted by Wemmick toward Barnard's Inn.

Wemmick escorts Pip to the grim, dilapidated Barnard's Inn, where Pip waits for Herbert Pocket, who arrives late with fruit and they instantly recognise each other as the "prowling boy" and "pale young gentleman" from their childhood fight at Miss Havisham's.

Pip and Herbert Pocket recognize each other as old sparring partners, bond over dinner at Barnard's Inn where Herbert reveals Miss Havisham's backstory — jilted at the altar by a scheming swindler who conspired with her half-brother — and then escorts Pip to the chaotic Pocket household in Hammersmith.

Pip settles into the Pocket household, meeting Mr. Pocket and fellow lodgers Drummle and Startop, and observes the chaotic domestic life where servants wield real authority while Mrs. Pocket neglects her children in favour of obsessing over aristocratic titles.

Pip arranges his studies under Mr. Pocket, visits Jaggers's office to secure twenty pounds for furnishings, and Wemmick shows him the grim death-cast trophies and Jaggers's courtroom dominance, hinting at the lawyer's terrifying power over all around him.

Pip visits Wemmick's eccentric Walworth home — a miniature castle with drawbridge, cannon, and the Aged Parent — and learns that Wemmick keeps his private life rigorously separate from his professional identity at Jaggers's office.

Pip and his companions dine at Mr Jaggers's gloomy Gerrard Street house, where Jaggers manipulates his guests, singles out the brutish Drummle with cryptic approval, and forces his housekeeper Molly to display her scarred, powerful wrists before dismissing her.

Joe visits Pip in London, awkward and out of place; Pip feels ashamed of him; Joe delivers Miss Havisham's message that Estella has come home, then departs with quiet dignity, telling Pip they belong in different worlds.

Pip travels by coach to his hometown, seated beside a convict he recognises from childhood who unknowingly reveals he once delivered Magwitch's two-pound-note gift to Pip; arriving shaken, Pip finds a local newspaper falsely crediting Pumblechook as his earliest patron.

Pip visits Satis House, finds the transformed adult Estella returned from France, walks with her in the ruined garden while she coolly declares she has no heart, dines alongside Mr Jaggers and Miss Havisham, and ends the night haunted by Miss Havisham's frenzied command to love Estella unconditionally.

Back in London, Pip confesses his hopeless adoration of Estella to Herbert, who warns she may bring misery given Miss Havisham's influence, then Herbert reveals his own secret engagement to Clara; the chapter also shows Pip's humiliation by Trabb's boy and his report of Orlick to Jaggers.

Pip and Herbert attend a rowdy, mockery-filled performance of Hamlet starring their acquaintance Wopsle, visit him backstage out of pity, take him to supper, and Pip goes to bed miserably dreaming of Estella and Miss Havisham.
Pip accompanies Wemmick on a visit to Newgate Prison while anxiously awaiting Estella's arrival in London, then feels morally contaminated by the prison atmosphere just as her coach appears.

Pip escorts Estella by carriage from an inn to her new lodgings in Richmond, during which Estella reveals she is being deployed by Miss Havisham to enter society, warns Pip that the Pocket relatives slander him to Miss Havisham, and Pip suffers the ache of knowing Estella attracts him deliberately yet feels nothing for him.
Pip reflects on how his great expectations have corrupted him and Herbert through lavish spending and mounting debt at Barnard's Inn, while the chapter closes with news of Mrs. Joe Gargery's death.

Pip returns to the forge for Mrs Joe's funeral, observes its comic-grotesque ceremony, buries his sister near his parents' graves, then walks with Biddy who gently exposes his hollow promise to visit Joe often, leaving Pip to depart knowing she is right.
On Pip's 21st birthday, Mr Jaggers grants him £500/year from his unnamed benefactor while refusing to reveal the patron's identity, and Wemmick bluntly advises Pip never to invest money in a friend.
Pip visits Wemmick at Walworth Castle, secures his help to secretly fund Herbert Pocket's entry into a shipping partnership via Clarriker, then mentions Estella as the next chapter's subject.

Pip escorts Estella to Satis House where she and Miss Havisham clash bitterly over Estella's trained inability to love; back in London, Pip is tormented by Estella's deliberate encouragement of the brutish Bentley Drummle.

On a stormy night Magwitch, the convict from Pip's childhood, arrives at Pip's London rooms and reveals he is the secret source of Pip's fortune and gentleman status, destroying Pip's illusions about Miss Havisham and leaving him stunned with abhorrence and guilt.

Pip hides Magwitch in his chambers, confirms from Jaggers that Magwitch is his true benefactor, arranges lodgings and a disguise for the fugitive, and swears Herbert Pocket to secrecy upon his return.

Pip reveals Magwitch's identity to Herbert; horrified and indebted, they agree Magwitch must be smuggled out of England before Pip can break free of him, and resolve to ask Magwitch about his past history at breakfast the next morning.

Magwitch recounts his life story to Pip and Herbert — childhood destitution, partnership with swindler Compeyson (including Arthur's dying hallucination of a woman in white), and the trial where class prejudice gave Compeyson a lighter sentence — ending when Herbert silently passes Pip a note identifying Compeyson as Miss Havisham's false lover.

Pip, tormented by shame over harboring Magwitch and jealousy about Estella, travels to find her already gone to Satis House, then endures a bristling confrontation with rival Bentley Drummle at the Blue Boar inn before pressing on to Miss Havisham's.

Pip confronts Miss Havisham about letting him believe she was his benefactor, then declares his love to Estella who coldly announces she will marry Drummle; walking back to London in anguish, Pip receives Wemmick's urgent note warning him not to go home.

After a sleepless night at a Covent Garden inn following Wemmick's warning note, Pip visits Wemmick at Walworth, where Wemmick reveals that Magwitch is being watched and that Herbert has already secretly relocated him to a safer riverside lodging near Limehouse.

Pip navigates to Magwitch's secret riverside lodging at Mill Pond Bank, meets Herbert's sweetheart Clara, relays Wemmick's warnings about being watched, and the three devise a boat-on-Thames scheme to smuggle Magwitch out of England when the moment comes.

Pip, burdened by debt and anxiety over Magwitch's hiding, visits a theatre where Mr. Wopsle reveals he spotted Compeyson sitting directly behind Pip, confirming the enemy is dangerously close and prompting Pip and Herbert to redouble their caution.

Pip dines with Jaggers and Wemmick, recognizes Jaggers's housekeeper Molly as Estella's mother by her distinctive hands and eyes, then Wemmick reveals Molly was acquitted of murder decades earlier through Jaggers's brilliant legal defense.

Pip returns to Satis House, secures £900 from Miss Havisham for Herbert's partnership, learns that Mr Jaggers brought infant Estella to her as an orphan, exchanges mutual forgiveness with a broken Miss Havisham, then saves her when her rotting bridal dress catches fire, burning his own hands in the struggle.

While Herbert tends Pip's fire-injuries, he relays Magwitch's dark past—a jealous woman tried for murder, defended by Jaggers, who then destroyed their child and vanished—leading Pip to the sudden revelation that Magwitch is Estella's father.

Pip confronts Mr Jaggers and Wemmick with the truth of Estella's parentage—Magwitch as father, Molly as mother—and Jaggers, speaking in elaborate hypotheticals while admitting nothing, counsels that the secret must stay buried for everyone's sake.

Pip receives Wemmick's coded letter signalling the time to act, finalises the river-escape plan for Magwitch with Herbert and Startop, then impulsively races alone to the marshes after an anonymous letter threatens to reveal information about "Provis."

Orlick lures Pip to a remote marsh sluice-house, binds him at gunpoint, confesses to attacking Mrs Joe and to spying on Magwitch, and is about to murder him when Herbert Pocket and Startop burst in and drive Orlick off.

Pip, Herbert, and Magwitch row Magwitch down the Thames toward a Hamburg steamer to smuggle him out of England, but a police galley intercepts them; Compeyson is unmasked among the pursuers, both convicts go overboard in a violent struggle, Compeyson drowns, and the badly injured Magwitch is recaptured and manacled—while Pip, whose inherited fortune is now forfeit, resolves to stay at Magwitch's side until death.

While Magwitch is formally committed for trial and Pip's forfeited inheritance proves unrecoverable, Herbert departs for Cairo after offering Pip a clerk's post, and Wemmick secretly marries Miss Skiffins with Pip as best man.

Magwitch lies dying in prison after his death sentence; Pip attends him daily and, at the last moment, reveals that Estella—Magwitch's lost daughter—is alive and beautiful, whereupon Magwitch dies peacefully.

Gravely ill and arrested for debt after Magwitch's death, Pip is nursed back to health by Joe Gargery, who quietly pays off the debt and slips away; recovering, Pip resolves to go to the forge and propose to Biddy.

Ruined Pip returns to his hometown, suffers Pumblechook's smug moralising, discovers Joe and Biddy have just married, begs their forgiveness, then departs abroad to pay his debts and build an honest career with Herbert's trading firm.

Pip returns to England after eleven years, visits Joe and Biddy at the forge, then walks alone to the ruins of Satis House where he unexpectedly meets Estella, and they part as friends, suggesting a hopeful reunion rather than final separation.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Hard_Times/Chapte.plot: Thomas Gradgrind harangues a classroom of children, insisting that facts are the one thing needful and that nothing else has any place in education.

Gradgrind and Bounderby observe a schoolroom drill where Sissy Jupe cannot define a horse by rote facts while Bitzer recites the mechanistic definition perfectly, dramatising the system's crushing of imagination.
Gradgrind and Bounderby catch Louisa and Tom secretly peeping at the circus through a wall gap, exposing the failure of rigid fact-based upbringing to extinguish the children's natural curiosity.
Thomas Gradgrind introduces Sissy Jupe to the boastful self-made banker Josiah Bounderby, who relentlessly brags about his wretched origins while Louisa and Tom look on.

Dickens describes the grim industrial landscape of Coketown and introduces Stephen Blackpool as one of its factory "Hands," contrasting the workers' bleak existence with the wealth of mill-owner Bounderby.

Gradgrind and Bounderby arrive at Sleary's circus, catch Louisa and Tom sneaking a look at the show, then learn that Sissy Jupe's father has vanished and Gradgrind resolves to take Sissy into his household to be educated on Fact.

Mrs Sparsit, formerly of aristocratic Powler lineage but now reduced to keeping house for Bounderby, is introduced as a proud, sharp-eyed dependent who privately looks down on her loud, self-made employer while relying on his patronage.
Gradgrind and Bounderby assess Sissy Jupe's failure to absorb fact-based schooling, illustrating how the utilitarian system systematically extinguishes children's natural capacity for wonder.

Gradgrind reviews Sissy's dismal progress under the Fact-based curriculum, learns she still mourns her missing father, and decides to keep her in the household despite her failure to absorb utilitarian doctrine.
Stephen Blackpool visits Bounderby to ask about divorcing his drunken wife and is told that divorce, easily obtained by the rich, is wholly inaccessible to a man of his station.

Stephen Blackpool visits Bounderby to ask how a working man might escape a ruinous marriage, but Bounderby and Mrs Sparsit make clear that divorce law is the privilege of the wealthy, leaving Stephen with no way out.
An enigmatic old woman (Mrs. Pegler) encounters Stephen Blackpool near Coketown and questions him admiringly about Bounderby, hinting at a hidden connection to him.

Stephen Blackpool endures a night at home with his drunken estranged wife while Rachael nurses her, and narrowly averts disaster when the wife nearly drinks poison, laying bare his trapped domestic condition and his moral bond with Rachael.
Time passes over two years; Bounderby proposes to Louisa, Thomas Gradgrind presents the match as cold fact, Tom selfishly urges acceptance, and Louisa consents with joyless resignation.
Louisa confronts her father Thomas Gradgrind, blaming his cold utilitarian upbringing for leaving her emotionally stunted and driving her to the edge of ruin.
Gradgrind presents Bounderby's marriage proposal to Louisa, who accepts with chilling passivity, unable to express desire or preference after her fact-based upbringing stripped her of feeling.
Chapter 17 ("Effects in the Bank") contains only its heading and page marker in this file — no narrative prose is present, indicating a stub or extraction artifact.

James Harthouse arrives in Coketown, introduced as a cynical gentleman of leisure who takes up the political cause of Gradgrindism purely out of boredom, positioning himself as a dangerous influence in the Bounderby circle.
Harthouse cultivates a cynical friendship with Tom Gradgrind, flattering the selfish young man into drunkenly revealing details about Louisa, whom Harthouse uses Tom to pursue.
Stephen Blackpool refuses to join the workers' union combination, is publicly denounced by orator Slackbridge, and is shunned and isolated by his fellow workers as a result.
Bounderby dismisses Stephen Blackpool after Stephen refuses to join the union and is shunned by his fellow workers, while Harthouse observes the stark divide between masters and men.
Chapter unit contains no narrative body; only the title "Fading Away" is present with no prose, characters, or events.
During a thunderstorm Mrs Sparsit secretly trails Louisa and witnesses her clandestine meeting with Harthouse, watching as Louisa teeters on the brink of moral ruin.
Unit contains only the chapter title "Explosion" with no narrative body; no characters or events are rendered in this fragment.

Mrs. Sparsit, drenched from following Louisa, rushes to Bounderby with news of supposed elopement, but when they confront the matter at Gradgrind's house Louisa is found safely with her father, leaving Mrs. Sparsit exposed and Bounderby furious.

Mrs. Sparsit envisions a metaphorical staircase descending into ruin and watches with obsessive satisfaction as Louisa, drawn ever closer to Harthouse, appears to her to be stepping down it toward disgrace.
Mrs. Sparsit pursues Louisa through a violent storm, convinced she is witnessing Louisa's final descent down the imagined fatal staircase toward elopement with Harthouse.
Louisa flees to her father in the storm and, in a desperate confrontation, indicts his Fact-based system for destroying her capacity for feeling before collapsing broken at his feet.

James Harthouse arrives in Coketown with a letter of introduction to Bounderby, presenting himself as a fashionable idler who adopts the Fact philosophy out of bored cynicism, and is introduced to Louisa.

Sissy Jupe visits James Harthouse at his lodgings and, with quiet but unyielding resolve, demands he leave Coketown forever and relinquish all claim on Louisa; Harthouse, disarmed by her plain earnestness, capitulates and departs.
Chapter file contains only the heading "Very Decided" with no narrative text; no events or characters are rendered in this unit.
Chapter titled "Lost" contains no narrative body in this atomized file — only the chapter heading and title are present, indicating a unit stub with no extractable plot content.
Sissy Jupe confronts James Harthouse at his lodgings and, through quiet moral earnestness, persuades him to abandon his pursuit of Louisa and leave Coketown permanently.
Unit contains only the chapter title "The Starlight" with no narrative prose — file is a stub header with no plot content.
Tom Gradgrind (the "Whelp"), hiding in disguise at the circus, is tracked down and confronted, while Thomas Gradgrind faces the ruin of his system as Sissy Jupe's loyalty helps secure Tom's escape.
Chapter VIII presents no narrative prose; the unit contains only the heading and subtitle "Philosophical," offering no depicted events or characters.

Unit is a list of illustrations only, naming key scenes: Harthouse dining at the Bounderbys', Harthouse conspiring with Tom Gradgrind in the garden, and Stephen Blackpool recovered from the Old Hell Shaft.
Unit contains no narrative content — it is a bare section-title page marking the start of Book the First ("Sowing") with no characters, dialogue, or events.
Thomas Gradgrind delivers his rigid utilitarian creed — Facts above all else — while surveying a bare schoolroom full of children ready to be filled with them.

In Gradgrind's school, a government inspector and Gradgrind interrogate Sissy Jupe about horses and flowers, forbidding all fancy, then introduce teacher M'Choakumchild to begin drilling pupils with pure facts.

Gradgrind catches Louisa and Tom secretly peeping at Sleary's circus and marches them home, repeatedly invoking Bounderby's opinion as moral authority while Louisa confesses she is tired of everything.

Bounderby boasts of his wretched origins to Mrs. Gradgrind on his birthday; when Gradgrind returns with Louisa and Tom caught peeping at the circus, the two men blame idle imagination and resolve to expel Sissy Jupe from the school.

Gradgrind and Bounderby walk through industrial Coketown (depicted as a monotonous triumph of fact suppressing all fancy), encounter Sissy Jupe being chased by Bitzer, and accompany her to her injured father's lodgings.
Gradgrind and Bounderby visit the circus to dismiss Sissy from school, discover her father has already fled, and Gradgrind offers to take Sissy in; she tearfully accepts.

Bounderby breakfasts with Mrs Sparsit and boasts of her aristocratic connections; Gradgrind arrives with Louisa and resolves to take Sissy Jupe into his household at Stone Lodge for strict rational education, silencing her talk of fairy tales.

Louisa and Tom share a twilight fireside talk lamenting their joyless Gradgrind upbringing; Tom reveals he plans to exploit Louisa's influence over Bounderby, while Mrs. Gradgrind interrupts to forbid Louisa from "wondering," embodying the chapter's theme of Never Wonder.

Sissy confides to Louisa about her failures under M'Choakumchild's fact-based schooling and her father's mysterious disappearance, revealing an instinctive empathy that defies utilitarian logic, while Louisa listens with quiet compassion and Tom interrupts only to summon her for Bounderby.

Stephen Blackpool walks home through Coketown after the factory bells ring, briefly accompanies Rachael (keeping cautious distance), then arrives at his lodging to find his estranged drunken wife collapsed on the floor of his room.

Stephen Blackpool visits Bounderby to ask how he can legally divorce his drunken wife and remarry, but Bounderby informs him that divorce is only accessible to the wealthy, leaving Stephen trapped with no way out.

Stephen Blackpool meets a mysterious old woman who makes an annual 40-mile pilgrimage just to glimpse Bounderby, then broods on his own wrecked life — bound to a drunken wife, unable to marry Rachael.

Stephen returns home to find Rachael tending his degraded wife; while he sleeps in tormented dreams, his wife seizes a poison bottle but Rachael wakes in time to wrest it away, and Stephen kneels before Rachael calling her his angel and sole hope.

Time passes in Coketown as Gradgrind dismisses Sissy from school for failing at facts, Tom enters Bounderby's bank, and Tom cryptically hints to Louisa that their father is arranging her marriage to Bounderby.

Thomas Gradgrind presents Bounderby's marriage proposal to Louisa, who accepts with cold resignation after her father reframes love as mere statistical fact, revealing how her utilitarian upbringing has extinguished all emotional life; Sissy watches in silent grief.

Bounderby tells Mrs. Sparsit he is marrying Louisa Gradgrind; she responds with condescending pity and accepts relocation to the Bank, after which the cold, fact-dominated wedding takes place and Book One ends.
This unit is a stub containing only the Book the Second title and subtitle "Reaping," with no narrative content or character action.

James Harthouse, a bored gentleman bearing a letter of introduction to Bounderby from Gradgrind, wanders into the Coketown Bank where Mrs Sparsit—after gossiping with Bitzer about Tom Gradgrind's dissipation—receives him and unwittingly reveals Louisa's youth and Bounderby's address.

James Harthouse, a bored gentleman of no real convictions, arrives in Coketown bearing Thomas Gradgrind's letter of introduction, is received by Bounderby who introduces him to Louisa, and Harthouse—observing her cold reserve crack only at Tom's arrival—silently identifies her brotherly attachment as a lever for future influence.

Harthouse plies Tom with drink and flattery at his hotel, extracting Tom's cynical confession that he pressured Louisa into marrying Bounderby purely to secure his own comfort, revealing Tom's selfishness while Harthouse covertly gathers intelligence about the Bounderby household.

At a Coketown union meeting, orator Slackbridge denounces Stephen Blackpool for refusing to join the workers' association; despite crowd sympathy Stephen stands firm and is collectively shunned, enduring four days of total social isolation before being summoned to Bounderby's house.

Summoned before Bounderby and Harthouse, Stephen Blackpool defends striking workers' integrity despite their ostracism of him, diagnoses the industrial "muddle" as a systemic failure no repression can fix, and is dismissed from his job by Bounderby.

Stephen Blackpool, blacklisted by Bounderby and shunned by fellow workers, receives money from Louisa and a suspicious private instruction from Tom to linger nightly outside the Bank before departing Coketown at dawn — unknowingly being set up as a scapegoat.

Harthouse systematically wins Louisa's trust by feigning concern for Tom's debts and gambling losses, extracts her financial secrets, and simultaneously manipulates Tom into being kinder to his sister — all as calculated steps in his cynical campaign to seduce her.

After Bounderby announces the bank robbery and accuses Stephen Blackpool, Mrs Sparsit installs herself at the house while Harthouse courts Louisa in the garden; that night Louisa goes to Tom's room and begs him to confess, but he stays doggedly silent and, once she leaves, collapses in guilty anguish.

Mrs Sparsit's scheming widens the rift between Louisa and Bounderby while pushing Louisa closer to Harthouse, then Louisa is called to Stone Lodge where she watches her mother die murmuring that something vital—unnamed, not an Ology—was missing from the Gradgrind upbringing.

Mrs Sparsit, lodging at Bounderby's retreat, constructs an allegorical staircase in her mind and obsessively watches Louisa descend it step by step toward ruin as Louisa grows ever closer to Harthouse in secret garden trysts.

Mrs Sparsit covertly trails Louisa, witnesses her secret woodland meeting with Harthouse, then pursues her by train through a thunderstorm back to Coketown, only to lose her in the chaos and cry "I have lost her!"

Louisa returns to her father during a storm and delivers a devastating reckoning: Gradgrind's cold rationalist system robbed her of feeling, forced her into a marriage she never loved, and has now left her on the verge of adultery with Harthouse — she collapses at his feet demanding he save her by means other than his philosophy.
Unit is the title page for Book the Third ("Garnering"), containing no narrative content beyond the book heading.

Louisa wakes bedridden in her childhood room; her remorseful father confesses his utilitarian system has failed and questions head-over-heart wisdom, then Sissy Jupe offers unconditional love and Louisa collapses into her arms begging forgiveness.

Sissy Jupe visits James Harthouse at his hotel and, acting alone on moral conviction, informs him Louisa will never see him again and demands he leave Coketown permanently—which he ultimately agrees to and does.

Bounderby storms Stone Lodge with an ailing Mrs Sparsit, confronts Thomas Gradgrind over Louisa's flight, rejects Gradgrind's plea for patience and reconciliation, and delivers an ultimatum that if Louisa does not return by noon the next day he will send her belongings and resume a bachelor life — which he immediately does.

Bounderby posts a public wanted placard naming Stephen Blackpool as suspected bank robber; Rachael confronts Louisa and Bounderby demanding Stephen be cleared, promises he will return within two days to vindicate himself, but Stephen never appears — having fled after receiving her warning letter — while Tom skulks guiltily at Bounderby's side throughout.

Mrs Sparsit drags Bounderby's hidden mother Mrs Pegler before him, shattering his fabricated rags-to-riches legend, while Sissy and Rachael keep faith in absent Stephen Blackpool and silently suspect Tom Gradgrind of orchestrating his disappearance.

Sissy and Rachael find Stephen Blackpool's hat near the abandoned Old Hell Shaft, organize a rescue, and bring him up mortally injured; Stephen delivers a dying speech condemning industrial negligence and the "muddle" of society, forgives those who wronged him, and asks Gradgrind to clear his name before dying.

After Stephen Blackpool's death exposes Tom as the real bank thief, Sissy secretly engineers Tom's escape to Sleary's circus while Gradgrind, shattered, tells Bounderby the truth and vindicates Stephen's memory.

Sissy and Louisa track Tom Gradgrind to Sleary's Circus where he hides in blackface disguise as a comic servant; Thomas Gradgrind arrives, Tom confesses to the safe robbery and is dressed as a carter for flight to Liverpool, but Bitzer intercepts them and seizes Tom at the door.

Bitzer captures Tom and refuses Gradgrind's pleas by invoking pure self-interest; Sleary secretly engineers Tom's escape via circus animals; then reveals Sissy's father's dog returned and died, implying her father is dead and chose to spare her, prompting Gradgrind to confront a world of love that transcends utilitarian logic.

Bounderby dismisses Mrs Sparsit with a cheque and veiled contempt; the narrator then prophesies each character's future—Bounderby's vainglorious death, Gradgrind's chastened old age, Louisa's childless but compassionate life, and Sissy's joyful, imaginative flourishing.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Little_Dorrit/Cha.plot: Book 1 table of contents lists 36 chapters tracing the Dorrit family's confinement in the Marshalsea debtors' prison alongside figures such as Mr Merdle and Mr Pancks, with threads of social criticism, mystery, and aspirations to move in society.

Unit presents Book Two's chapter list and Dickens' 1857 preface, in which he defends his satirical inventions—especially Mr Merdle as stand-in for real financial fraudsters—and describes revisiting the physical ruins of the Marshalsea Prison where Little Dorrit was born.
This unit is a section-divider heading for Book the First ("Poverty") with no narrative content — no characters appear and no events occur.

In a sweltering Marseilles prison, the menacing Monsieur Rigaud delivers a self-serving account of his wife's fatal fall to fellow-prisoner John Baptist Cavalletto before being escorted out under guard to stand trial.

Released from Marseilles quarantine, Clennam and the Meagles family share a farewell breakfast with fellow travelers; Miss Wade darkly prophesies fated encounters, while Tattycoram's barely-contained rage is coldly observed by her.

Arthur Clennam returns on a grim London Sunday to his mother's dark, stifling house, endures a cold reunion with the bedridden Mrs Clennam and the Flintwinches, broods over his oppressive Puritan childhood, and gets a first glimpse of Little Dorrit.

Affery Flintwinch witnesses her husband Jeremiah secretly meeting his mysterious double at night and handing off an iron box, then is throttled and gaslit into believing she only sleepwalked and dreamed.

Arthur Clennam confronts Mrs Clennam with suspicions that his dead father wronged someone and left guilt unrepaired; she furiously silences him, Flintwinch is made new business partner, Arthur resolves to lodge elsewhere, and his curiosity about the mysterious seamstress Little Dorrit begins to deepen.

William Dorrit enters the Marshalsea as a hapless debtor, his wife gives birth to Amy within its walls, and over decades of passive confinement he transforms into the self-styled "Father of the Marshalsea," living off small tributes from fellow prisoners.

Chapter traces Amy Dorrit's entire childhood and young womanhood inside the Marshalsea—born there, raised by the turnkey as godfather, she becomes sole caretaker of her broken father and idle siblings (Fanny, Tip), managing secret work, pious deceits, and repeated failed attempts to free Tip, until at twenty-two she is glimpsed returning to the prison by Arthur Clennam.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Our_Mutual_Friend.plot: Bradley Headstone, driven by murderous jealousy, stalks Eugene Wrayburn through the night and encounters Rogue Riderhood outside the Temple, recruiting him as a paid informant to track Wrayburn's movements and locate Lizzie Hexam.

The Lammles, bankrupt swindlers, devise a scheme to manipulate Mr Boffin by falsely denouncing his Secretary's mercenary motives, while Sophronia also flatters Fledgeby into supposedly interceding with moneylender Riah — though Fledgeby in fact orders Riah to seize the Lammles' furniture.

Fledgeby uses Riah as a scapegoat front-man, performing false generosity toward Twemlow while secretly directing Riah to press him for full repayment of an old debt; Jenny Wren, watching, denounces Riah as the wolf who will one day sell and betray Lizzie.

Mr Venus secretly warns Boffin about Wegg's blackmail scheme over a discovered will, lets Boffin hide to overhear Wegg's boastful threats, and the two agree to coordinate their response before Mrs Lammle intercepts Boffin with further alarming news.

Boffin publicly humiliates and dismisses Rokesmith (John Harmon) for allegedly courting Bella for money; Bella, appalled, defends him, denounces Boffin as corrupted by wealth, and leaves the house for good.

Bella visits her father R. Wilfer at his Mincing Lane office, where John Rokesmith (John Harmon) follows and proposes; she accepts, renouncing the Boffin household for poverty and love, and the three then walk home to face the Wilfer family together.

As the Lammles face bankruptcy, Mrs Lammle visits Twemlow to enforce his silence and reveals Riah is merely Fledgeby's mask; meanwhile at the Veneerings' wondering dinner Eugene Wrayburn quietly receives Lizzie Hexam's whereabouts from Mr Dolls and slips away.
Unit contains only the section heading "Book the Fourth: A Turning" with no narrative content or character action.

Bradley Headstone, disguised in Riderhood's clothes, stalks Eugene Wrayburn upriver past Plashwater Weir Lock, bribes lock-keeper Riderhood for intelligence, returns blood-spitting and exhausted after confirming Eugene has met Lizzie, then collapses in Riderhood's hut while Riderhood—suspicious the disguise implicates him—secretly unbuttons Bradley's coat to find a counterfeit red neckerchief matching his own, setting up a mutual trap.

Mr Boffin pays off the scheming Lammles £100 for a past service, firmly dismisses them from his household, then intercepts the naive Georgiana Podsnap's cash and necklace offered to help the very people who exploited her friendship.

Silas Wegg, backed by a reluctant Mr Venus, confronts Nicodemus Boffin at the Bower and extorts him into surrendering two-thirds of the Harmon estate under threat of exposing a will, then escorts him home in gleeful contempt.

Bella Wilfer secretly elopes with John Rokesmith (Harmon) at Greenwich church, with only her father Pa as witness, then celebrates the wedding with breakfast and dinner before Pa returns to London, leaving the newlyweds at their Blackheath cottage.

After news of Bella's elopement with John Rokesmith shocks the Wilfer household, Bella's joyful visit disarms her mother's hostility; the chapter then follows the couple's contented Blackheath domestic life — Bella learning housekeeping, mentioning Lizzie Hexam, and finally hinting to John that she is expecting a child.

Eugene meets Lizzie by the river where she pleads with him to leave due to their insurmountable class difference; after she departs, he is ambushed and beaten nearly to death by an unseen assailant, falls into the river, and Lizzie—hearing the attack—rows out alone to pull his broken body from the water and carry him to safety.

After attacking Eugene Wrayburn and throwing him in the river, Bradley Headstone shelters at Riderhood's lock-house and disposes of his bloody clothes, while Riderhood secretly tails him to gather blackmail leverage, and Charley Hexam renounces Headstone entirely for endangering his own social respectability.

Jenny Wren deflects Fledgeby's attempts to extract Lizzie Hexam's whereabouts, then arrives at his Albany chambers to find him thrashed by Lammle; she tends his wounds while secretly sprinkling pepper into the vinegar-and-brown-paper plasters as covert revenge for his tricks.

Jenny Wren visits Riah at Pubsey & Co., confirms Fledgeby's identity and wins Riah his freedom; her drunken father Mr Dolls collapses and dies in the street; Mortimer Lightwood then arrives to escort Jenny to the bedside of the dying Eugene Wrayburn.

Dying Eugene, nursed by Jenny Wren and Mortimer Lightwood, begs Mortimer to let Bradley Headstone go unpunished so Lizzie's reputation is spared, then—after Jenny whispers the key word—asks Mortimer to fetch Lizzie and arrange their deathbed marriage as his final act of reparation.

Bella (as Mrs Rokesmith) travels with Lightwood and the Milveys to witness Eugene Wrayburn and Lizzie Hexam's bedside wedding; at the station Bradley Headstone overhears of the marriage and collapses in a fit, while Eugene and Lizzie exchange vows at dawn, Eugene confessing doubt he deserves to live.

Bella's husband John Rokesmith—suspected as Julius Handford in the Harmon murder—is confronted by Lightwood and escorted by Mr Inspector through a police-station identification scene, while Bella trusts him absolutely; the chapter closes with Mr and Mrs Boffin welcoming them to their new home, signalling the imminent disclosure of John's true identity as John Harmon.

Mrs Boffin reveals to Bella that her husband Rokesmith is truly John Harmon, and Mr Boffin confesses that his miser act was a deliberate scheme to test and correct Bella's greedy tendencies, ending in joyful reunion of the whole household.

Wegg arrives to extort Boffin with a later will, but Venus reveals he secretly sided with Boffin all along, John Harmon exposes the document as worthless, and Sloppy physically ejects Wegg into a scavenger's cart.

Riderhood confronts Bradley Headstone at his school and lock-house with evidence of the Bargeman disguise, extorting money and threatening ruin; Bradley, trapped and despairing, seizes Riderhood on the lock-gate and drags them both into the water, killing them both.

The Harmons settle into their new household—hosting Mrs Wilfer's pompous visit and Jenny Wren's cheerful meeting with Sloppy—while a recovering Eugene Wrayburn tells Lightwood he will stay in England and fight openly for Lizzie's place in society rather than flee abroad.

At a final Veneering dinner, Society mocks and condemns Eugene Wrayburn's marriage to working-class Lizzie Hexam as a mésalliance, but the mild Twemlow silences the table by insisting a gentleman's feelings are sacred, earning Lightwood's quiet gratitude.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Sketches_by_Boz/S.plot: Dickens introduces his earliest sketches in a preface, acknowledging their crudeness and haste as a young writer while explaining he chose not to substantially remodel or expunge them.

Narrator sketches three parish figures — the pompous beadle who lords over paupers and fumbles a fire-engine emergency, the tyrannical workhouse master, and the broken schoolmaster whose life of bad luck, lost inheritance, and abandoned friends ends in pauper obscurity.

Narrator sketches three parish figures: a charismatic curate who captivates parishioners then loses them to a rival clergyman; a pious, orderly old lady admired for quiet charity; and her meddlesome half-pay naval captain neighbour who disrupts her domestic life yet remains her friend.

Four ageing maiden sisters (the Miss Willises) live in rigid uniformity until one marries Mr. Robinson — the neighbourhood never learns which one — and the birth of a baby girl finally resolves the parish's long-running curiosity.

Two parish factions contest election of new beadle after Simmons dies; candidate Bung defeats Spruggins despite Spruggins's larger family, thanks to Captain Purday's campaign tactics and a voter-intimidation scandal that turns the poll.
Narrator introduces Mr. Bung, a cheerful broker's man who has spent his life oscillating between destitution and bare subsistence, setting up his professional anecdotes about parish poverty.

Mr. Bung, a broker's man who enforces debt seizures, narrates three encounters: a wealthy gentleman who bribes him to pose as a waiter during a dinner party; a destitute family in squalor whose mother is driven to madness and dies after her husband is transported; and a dignified gentlewoman who stoically endures a distraint, runs herself ragged raising the debt money, and dies shortly after the execution is lifted.

Dickens satirises competing parish ladies' societies — the child-examination faction led by the Miss Browns and the Bible-distribution faction led by Mrs. Johnson Parker — whose charitable activities are driven entirely by social rivalry, culminating in the distributionists winning popular favour through a barnstorming Exeter Hall orator while the examination society decays.

Narrator riffs on door-knockers as personality indices, then sketches two disruptive lodgers at the neighbour's house, before closing on a widow and her consumptive son who dies in a London lodging, begging to be buried in open fields.
Narrator sketches London streets from pre-dawn stillness through the gradual awakening of laborers, market-workers, servants, clerks, and shopmen until the full bustle of noon.

Narrator surveys London streets at night, moving from cozy suburban domesticity through squalid market districts to a destitute mother singing for pennies, then to post-theatre revelry and a rowdy harmonic-meeting tavern, painting contrasts between comfort and wretchedness across the dark hours.

Narrator tracks single London shop through successive failed tenants — linen-draper, widowed stationer's dying daughter, tobacconist, and others — each cycle showing deeper decay until house reaches ultimate degradation.

Dickens sketches Scotland-Yard as a tight coal-heaver community whose simple customs, tavern rituals, and resistance to change are steadily erased by London's modernisation — new bridge, new shops, new fashions — leaving only one mournful old man watching the vanished past.

Narrator sketches Seven Dials district of London — its labyrinthine streets, overcrowded lodging houses, and inhabitants marked by poverty, idleness, and recurring brawls that end in police intervention.

The narrator wanders Monmouth-street's second-hand clothes shops and, through imaginative projection onto a series of garments, reconstructs one man's entire life arc from pampered boyhood through idle dissipation, domestic violence, and a mother's lonely death to final imprisonment or transportation.

Narrator satirically defends old London hackney-coaches against cabs and modern improvements, sketching vivid street scenes—a grandmother departing, a wedding party pretending to ride in private carriage—then mourns the coach as fallen aristocracy of the road.

Narrator wanders into Doctors' Commons, observes absurd brawling-case trial where Sludberry is excommunicated for insulting Bumple, then visits the Prerogative Office where seekers of wills reveal greed, bewilderment, and human passions recorded in testamentary documents.

Narrator surveys London recreational habits across classes — the city businessman who prizes his garden as status symbol, the retired old couple who tend their garden with quiet devotion and mutual love, and the boisterous Sunday crowd at tea-gardens imitating upper-class pleasures with noisy, cheerful vulgarity.

Narrator surveys Thames river life — bungled amateur boating parties, a chaotic rowing race, and the crowded Gravesend steamboat with its flustered passengers and comic mishaps — as a humorous study of London middle-class leisure.

Narrator visits Astley's amphitheatre, observes a large family's delight at circus acts, describes the riding-master and clown's routines with Miss Woolford, then reflects on the gap between performers' glamorous stage appearance and their shabby off-stage reality.

Narrator sketches Greenwich Fair on Easter Monday — the chaotic road, park games, thimble-rig swindles, Richardson's booth melodrama, wild-beast shows, freak exhibitions, and the Crown and Anchor ballroom — as a riotous annual release valve for London's working classes.

Dickens satirizes London private theatres where working-class young men pay to perform roles in amateur productions, exposing the vanity, squalid backstage conditions, false identities, and commercial exploitation that underlie their theatrical ambitions.

Narrator visits Vauxhall Gardens by daylight for first time (lured by balloon race) and finds the once-magical pleasure garden exposed as tawdry painted boards and dingy ornaments, then witnesses Mr. Green's balloon ascent captivate the daytime crowd.

Narrator satirically chronicles the ordeal of early-morning coach travel in London — the indifferent booking clerks, sleepless night, pre-dawn dressing, frozen streets, and chaotic departure — ending as the coach finally rolls off.

Narrator praises omnibus over stage-coach, then sketches daily Oxford Street–City ride: pushy cad overcrowds vehicle, testy old gentleman feuds with cad at Regent Street stop, rival omnibus poaches passengers, and mixed crowd of regulars and newcomers drift through London in comic tableau.

Narrator sketches two London street characters — an anarchic red cab-driver who courts imprisonment rather than pay fines, and Bill Barker ("Aggerawatin Bill"), a waterman-turned-omnibus-cad notorious for cheating and bullying passengers — as comic emblems of a rough urban world being swept away by modernisation.

Narrator guides reader through chaotic Parliament precincts — corridors, Strangers' gallery, and Bellamy's kitchen — sketching pompous officials, eccentric MPs, veteran butler Nicholas, and waitress Jane to expose the absurdity and theatre of political life.

Dickens satirises the annual charity dinner as comic spectacle: pompous committee bustle, chaotic seating, formulaic speeches, loyal toasts, orphan procession, and mutual self-congratulation among donors, all masking self-interest behind benevolent display.

Narrator laments the disappearance of May-day spring traditions — maypole dancing replaced by sweeps' dinners, mystery of noble-born chimney boys exposed as myth — culminating in witnessing a shabby, imposter May-day parade that ends drunk and miserable, confirming the holiday's total decline.

Narrator surveys London brokers' and marine-store shops, showing how their jumbled secondhand wares reflect the poverty and slow ruin of surrounding neighbourhoods — from theatrical Drury Lane to sailors' Ratcliff Highway to debtors near King's Bench Prison, whose clothing tells of progressive destitution.

Narrator surveys the flashy gin-shops of London's poorest districts, sketches their gaudy interiors and desperate customers, and argues that drunkenness is symptom—not cause—of wretchedness, so gin-palaces will vanish only when poverty is addressed.

Narrator observes a working-class London pawnbroker's shop near Drury Lane, sketching a series of customers—a harried grandmother, a drunken wife-beater, a mother-daughter pair pawning keepsakes, a ruined prostitute, and a slovenly woman—as vignettes of poverty, desperation, and moral decline.

Dickens sketches the Old Bailey criminal courts and Newgate prison, contrasting the bureaucratic coldness of judges and jury with two vivid scenes: a mother reclaiming her wayward son just released from prison, and a streetwise juvenile pickpocket who clowns through his trial before being sentenced to transportation.

Narrator tours Newgate Prison — women's ward, boys' school, men's yards, chapel with its condemned pew, press-room holding men awaiting execution — and closes with an imagined portrait of a condemned felon's agonised final night in his cell before the scaffold.

Narrator observes and sketches three types of solitary London figures — the anonymous city clerk grinding through joyless routine, the wealthy self-made misanthrope luxuriating in his own bitterness, and the cheerful young apprentices parading their finery on a Sunday — contrasting their different relationships to solitude, class, and pleasure.

Dickens sketches the ideal annual Christmas family gathering — feasting, games, songs — culminating in the reconciliation of estranged daughter Margaret and her family, who are welcomed back, dissolving year-long grudges in seasonal goodwill.

Dickens sketches a New Year's Eve quadrille party at the Dobble household, satirising the social climber Tupple through his flattering toasts, then closes with a solemn reflection on the midnight bell as a reminder of human mortality.

Journeyman carpenter Samuel Wilkins takes his sweetheart Jemima Ivins and another couple to the Eagle pleasure gardens, where two flashy strangers flirt with the women, provoking a fight that leaves both young men beaten on the gravel and the women carried home in hysterics.

Narrator stops at old London pub and witnesses self-important red-faced man (Mr. Rogers) hold court in parlour with inflammatory political speeches about liberty and slavery, impressing sycophantic regulars while a greengrocer alone pushes back, until Rogers storms out to general admiration.

A dying battered woman, brought before magistrates at a London hospital to identify her abuser, instead falsely exonerates him out of love and dies moments after whispering her forgiveness and farewell.

Middle-aged widower John Dounce becomes infatuated with a young oyster-shop girl, abandons old friends and alienates his daughters, is coldly rejected by the girl, and ends up henpecked by his cook — a cautionary tale of misplaced attachment.

Miss Amelia Martin, a plain milliner, is flattered into believing she has singing talent by the Jennings Rodolphs at a wedding dinner, abandons her dressmaking business to pursue a stage career, then is hissed off the stage at a White Conduit benefit night and never recovers her former life or good humour.

Young shopman Augustus Cooper joins Signor Billsmethi's dubious dancing academy seeking genteel society, is flattered and ensnared by the Billsmethis, and after a chaotic ball ends up sued for breach of promise to Miss Billsmethi, settling out of his mother's till for twenty pounds and retreating permanently back home.

Narrator observes and defines the "shabby-genteel" type — men of fallen station who haunt London streets and the British Museum Reading Room concealing their destitution behind worn gentlemanly trappings — focusing on one specimen whose slow sartorial disintegration, brief revival via dye, and final resignation illustrate the pathos of poverty masked by pride.

Potter and Smithers, two city clerks and inseparable friends, blow their quarterly wages on a raucous night of drinking and theatre-going, get ejected from the playhouse for disorderly conduct, brawl through the streets, and end up fined at the police court the next morning.

Narrator observes the prisoners' van at Bow Street, watches two sisters — one hardened, one ashamed — loaded into it after sentencing, and reflects on how London streets and a corrupt mother doom such girls to inevitable ruin.

File contains only the chapter heading with no body text; unit opens the boarding-house sketch by introducing the setting of a London lodging house where domestic comedy and social maneuvering among lodgers will unfold.

Mrs. Tibbs opens a London boarding house where three male boarders and a widow with two daughters scheme separately to marry, resulting in a triple simultaneous wedding: Hicks weds Matilda Maplesone, Simpson weds Julia, and Mrs. Maplesone nearly catches Calton — who backs out and is sued for breach of promise — after which all marriages collapse disastrously, leaving Mrs. Tibbs with only her henpecked husband.

Wealthy hypochondriac widow Mrs. Bloss joins Mrs. Tibbs's boarding house; mischief-maker Evenson lures Mrs. Tibbs into a midnight spying expedition that exposes her husband's drunken flirtation with servant Agnes, triggering a chain of revelations—O'Bleary's scheme, Gobler's surprise proposal to Mrs. Bloss—that unravels the entire household and ends in the Tibbs's legal separation and auction of their home.

Fastidious bachelor Minns, who loathes dogs and children, is pestered by boorish cousin Budden into a wretched suburban dinner party, misses the last coach home, and next morning rewrites his will to exclude the entire Budden family.

Theodosius Butler, alias M'Neville Walter, secretly reunites at a Minerva House boarding-school ball with Lavinia Brook Dingwall — whose MP father had placed her there to cure her of a low-born attachment — reveals his true identity, and wins her renewed promise of love.

Miss Crumpton visits M.P. Brook Dingwall to confess his daughter Lavinia has eloped with Theodosius; the furious father cuts the couple off financially and vows to abolish finishing schools, while the pair later languishes in poverty and disillusionment.

The newly-rich Tuggs family vacation at Ramsgate, where the flattering Captain and Mrs. Waters befriend them, and the romantic Cymon Tuggs develops a dangerously indiscreet attachment to the married Belinda Waters.

Cymon Tuggs, hiding behind Mrs. Waters' curtain when her husband and the Tuggs family burst in, is discovered and a violent scene erupts; the affair is hushed up only after Joseph Tuggs pays £1,500, and the narrator reveals the whole acquaintance was a deliberate swindle by Captain Waters, Belinda, and Lieutenant Slaughter.

The status-obsessed Malderton family courts the mysterious, eloquent Horatio Sparkins as a potential noble suitor for daughter Teresa, only to discover he is Samuel Smith, a lowly shop assistant at a cheap linen-draper's.

A veiled woman visits a young surgeon at night begging him to see a dying man the next morning; he arrives to find the man already dead — executed by hanging — and the woman, his mother, collapses in madness when she confesses her son was murdered by the law.

Percy Noakes organises a Thames steam excursion for London acquaintances; rival families the Tauntons and Briggses sabotage each other's social manoeuvres throughout the voyage while Hardy plays pranks and Captain Helves's attentions shift against Mrs Taunton's calculations.

The steam excursion party endures a brutal return voyage in worsening weather, with passengers struck by sea-sickness and chaos at dinner, ending with the group's social facades crumbling and the charming Captain Helves later exposed as a fraudster.

Cowardly Alexander Trott, fleeing a duel challenge from rival Horace Hunter, is mistaken by mayor Overton for the nobleman Lord Peter (expected by Miss Julia Manners for a secret elopement), and through a farcical chain of mix-ups ends up bundled into a post-chaise with Julia; they discover the error but pragmatically marry each other at Gretna Green, while Hunter has already married Emily Brown and Lord Peter dies in a steeplechase.

The Gattleton family stages a lavish private production of Othello and Masaniello, but scheming neighbor Mrs. Joseph Porter manipulates Shakespeare-obsessed Uncle Tom into heckling the performers with corrections, while costume failures, drunken extras, near-fires, and general incompetence reduce the evening to a celebrated catastrophe.
Unit contains only the chapter heading "A Passage in the Life of Mr. Watkins Tottle" with no narrative text; no plot content to extract.

Timid bachelor Watkins Tottle, urged by friend Gabriel Parsons, dines at Parsons's house to meet prospective bride Miss Lillerton; the evening goes promisingly, but Parsons's comic tale of hiding in a chimney on his own wedding night frames the chapter, and Tottle's actual wooing is deferred to the next.

Parsons bails Tottle out of a debtors' sponging-house on condition he proposes to Miss Lillerton, but Tottle's blundering courtship is exploited by Miss Lillerton to send a note to Mr. Timson—the clergyman she is secretly engaged to—leaving Tottle duped, humiliated, and implied drowned in the Regent's Canal.

Misanthropic bachelor Dumps reluctantly agrees to be godfather at nephew Kitterbell's christening, endures a chaotic omnibus ride and a festive party, gets pickpocketed of the silver mug gift, and ruins the celebration with a sardonic speech predicting the child's suffering, delighting in the ensuing hysteria.

A London drunkard (Warden) watches his wife die neglected, drives his sons away, unwittingly betrays his fugitive son William to the police while drunk in a tavern, loses his daughter, and finally drowns himself in the Thames, unrecognised and unpitied.

Mock proceedings of a fictional scientific conference present absurdly comic reports — a doctor who "cures" a perfectly healthy man by reducing him to an invalid, a swallowed door-key used to forge a burglar's copy, infinitesimal rum doses that still cause drunkenness, and ludicrous statistics on children's fairy-tale reading and London dog-meat skewers — satirising Victorian scientific and philanthropic pretension.

Mock-journalistic report concludes first Mudfog Association meeting with absurd inventions (portable railway, share-price machine, defective fire-escape) then chronicles correspondent's chaotic steamer voyage with eccentric professors to Oldcastle and the Second Meeting's farcical scientific debates on dancing bears, bears-grease, and beadle authority.

A mock learned-society meeting debates absurd inventions (a mechanical pickpocket, an automaton police force for aristocratic mischief, spectacles that blind you to nearby faults), followed by two satirical sketches equating everyday life to a pantomime and observing a celebrated "literary lion" fawned over at a fashionable supper party.

Self-styled press insider Robert Bolton holds court at a Westminster pub, dazzling regulars with a lurid tale of a baker who boiled his son alive, then the unit closes with Dickens's farewell letter passing editorship of Bentley's Miscellany to Ainsworth.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/The_Battle_of_Lif.plot: On the ancient battle-ground estate of Doctor Jeddler, Alfred Heathfield formally receives his trust fund from the lawyers Snitchey and Craggs and bids farewell to the household—including his betrothed Marion and her devoted sister Grace—before departing on a three-year medical tour abroad, while philosophical debate about whether life is serious or mere farce runs through the breakfast gathering.

Michael Warden confesses his financial ruin and romantic designs on Marion to his lawyers, then secretly meets her at night with Clemency's reluctant help; on the very evening Alfred Heathfield joyfully returns home after years abroad, Marion is discovered to have fled, leaving only a note begging forgiveness.

Six years on, Michael Warden returns and is recognised by Clemency at the Nutmeg-Grater inn; that same evening Marion reappears on her birthday to confess she voluntarily fled so that Grace could marry Alfred, and the whole family is joyfully reunited.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/The_Chimes/Chapte.plot: Elderly ticket-porter Trotty Veck, sustained by his devotion to the church Chimes, shares a meal with daughter Meg who reveals Richard's New Year's Day marriage proposal, but Alderman Cute and Mr. Filer mock and belittle the poor couple's plans with callous condescension, crushing their joy and driving Trotty into despair over whether the poor have any right to exist.

Trotty delivers Alderman Cute's letter to Sir Joseph Bowley, who hypocritically condemns Will Fern as a vagabond; Trotty then meets Will Fern and his niece Lilian on the street, warns them, shelters them in his home, and finally—driven by the haunting chimes—climbs the church tower alone and collapses in a swoon.

Trotty's ghost, guided by the spirit-child, witnesses visions of future suffering: the Bells arraign him for despair toward the poor; Will Fern delivers an impassioned indictment of class injustice at Bowley Hall while Alderman Cute smirks; Meg toils in grinding poverty as Richard degrades into drunkenness; and Lilian, fallen and broken, returns to die repentant in Meg's arms.

Trotty witnesses in his vision Meg's descent into destitution after her husband's death, nearly drowning her infant before Trotty's anguished plea saves her; he then awakens to find it was a nightmare and Meg, Richard, Will Fern, and little Lilian are joyfully celebrating the New Year and Meg's impending wedding.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/The_Cricket_on_th.plot: Critic George Alfred Williams contextualizes The Cricket on the Hearth within Dickens's Christmas Books series, ranking it second in popularity after A Christmas Carol, and argues that Dickens's genius for humanizing characters — not caricature — drives the story's emotional power.

Front-matter page listing three Chirps and illustration captions that preview Bertha's lament over her blindness, John's wordplay pun on Dot's name while holding the baby, Tilly Slowboy's presence, and the cricket's first chirp as the hearth fire blazes to life.
Unit is a title-page stub containing only the heading "THE CRICKET ON THE HEARTH" with no narrative content or character action.
Unit contains only the subtitle "A Fairy Tale of Home" — no narrative content or characters are present.

On a winter evening the kettle and cricket herald John Peerybingle's return home; a deaf old Stranger is taken in for the night; Tackleton arrives to announce his mismatched wedding, drops cynical hints about Dot's fidelity, and Dot reacts with mysterious shock when the Stranger approaches her, planting unease in John's mind even as the Cricket conjures visions of lifelong domestic bliss.

Caleb's blind daughter Bertha, raised on her father's loving lies about their poverty and Tackleton's kindness, breaks down confessing her love for Tackleton just as he announces his engagement to May; the gathering ends with John Peerybingle, led by Tackleton to a dark window, witnessing what seems to be Dot in an intimate scene with the disguised old lodger.

John Peerybingle, tormented by jealousy and guided back to mercy by the cricket's chirp and fairy visions, declares Dot innocent and offers to free her; Edward Plummer (the disguised stranger) is revealed as May Fielding's true love, Caleb confesses his lifelong deception to Bertha who forgives him with joy, Dot explains her innocent secret-keeping, and the reunited company celebrates with a wedding feast and dance while even Tackleton repents and joins them.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/The_Haunted_Man_a.plot: Redlaw, a tormented chemist haunted by grief over betrayal and loss, is confronted by a spectral double that offers to erase his painful memories; he accepts the bargain, only to learn the gift will involuntarily strip memory and its emotional bonds from every person he approaches.

Redlaw wanders through the Tetterby household and a sick student's room spreading his curse of memory-erasure, then guides a feral boy to a squalid lodging house where he watches Philip Swidger and William Swidger lose all filial feeling for dying George Swidger under his influence, before fleeing back to his chamber while Milly Swidger pounds on the door begging him to reverse the harm he has wrought.

Redlaw confronts the Phantom at dawn, learns only Milly can undo the harm of his curse, and through her intercession — reconciling the Tetterbys, aiding the fallen Longford, and hearing her testament of lost-child love — has his memory fully restored and leads the assembled Swidger clan in a Christmas feast under the motto "Lord keep my memory green."

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/The_Mystery_of_Ed.plot: John Jasper wakes in a London opium den after smoking through the night, surveys his debased surroundings with cold contempt, pays the haggard hostess, and hastens to Cloisterham Cathedral to take his place in the vesper choir.

After evensong, Mr Crisparkle checks on the ailing Jasper at the Cathedral gatehouse; Edwin Drood arrives for dinner and the two men talk intimately — Edwin complaining about his pre-arranged betrothal to Rosa Bud while Jasper confesses his crushing monotony and reveals he takes opium, all while casting a covertly hungry, watchful gaze on his nephew.

Edwin Drood visits Rosa Bud at the Nuns' House seminary in Cloisterham, and their bickering, affection-less exchange lays bare that their willed betrothal breeds mutual resignation rather than love, though a fleeting moment of honest compassion briefly disarms them both.

Edwin and Rosa walk near the Cathedral, hear the organ (Edwin thinks he detects Jack's voice), then part at the Nuns' House gate with a playful but hollow farewell, neither glimpsing a happy present or future.

Jasper visits the pompous auctioneer Sapsea, who brags of worldly knowledge and recites the absurdly self-glorifying epitaph he wrote for his dead wife; stonemason Durdles arrives to collect the monument key, and Jasper lingers over examining his keys before the evening ends in backgammon and cold beef.

Jasper stops a street boy named Deputy from pelting the drunken stonemason Durdles, walks him home through Cloisterham's churchyard while Durdles demonstrates his uncanny ability to locate entombed remains by tapping walls, then returns alone to his gatehouse where he fills a pipe with opium and stands in silence over his sleeping nephew Edwin.

Mr Crisparkle arranges to receive Neville and Helena Landless as wards placed by their bullying guardian Honeythunder; the two arrive in Cloisterham, are welcomed at a dinner that Honeythunder's overbearing harangues reduce to misery, and he is finally hustled away.

Neville confides his abusive past to Mr Crisparkle; that evening Rosa breaks down singing under Jasper's controlling gaze, and later Helena privately draws from Rosa her terrified confession of Jasper's silent, obsessive hold over her.

Neville Landless and Edwin Drood trade insults after dinner; Jasper intervenes and draws both to his rooms where wine inflames the quarrel until Neville flings his goblet at Edwin and storms out, whereupon Jasper visits Crisparkle to brand Neville as murderous and dangerous.

Mr Grewgious visits Rosa to clarify her betrothal is non-binding and review her finances, then meets Jasper outside the Cathedral where Jasper's ominous slip — "God save them" versus Grewgious's "God bless them" — hints at dark intent toward the engaged couple.

Mr Crisparkle walks with the Landless siblings, extracts Neville's secret love for Rosa Bud and his pledge to keep peace, then visits Jasper to secure Edwin Drood's agreement to make the first advance, which Drood does via letter inviting Neville to Christmas Eve dinner.

Edwin Drood visits Mr Grewgious at Staple Inn, dines with him, and receives Rosa's mother's diamond-and-ruby ring to place on Rosa's finger as a solemn seal of fidelity; alone afterward, Grewgious broods over his own long-suppressed love for Rosa's mother.

Jasper takes Durdles on a moonlit night expedition through Cloisterham's cathedral crypt and tower, deliberately plies him with drink, covertly spies on Neville Landless from the shadows with predatory intensity, and while Durdles sleeps appears to handle the crypt key — suggesting sinister premeditation.

Rosa Bud and Edwin Drood mutually and tenderly dissolve their childhood betrothal during a riverside walk, agreeing to become brother and sister instead of spouses, while John Jasper watches them unseen from under the cathedral trees.

On Christmas Eve in Cloisterham, Neville prepares a solitary walking departure, Edwin wanders the town and receives a cryptic warning from an opium woman that the name "Ned" is dangerous, Jasper hosts both at the gatehouse with an unsettlingly composed manner, and on Christmas morning Edwin is discovered missing — last seen going to the river with Neville in the storm.

Neville is hunted down and dragged back to Cloisterham under suspicion of murdering the vanished Edwin Drood; Jasper orchestrates his impeachment before Mayor Sapsea while Grewgious then shatters Jasper by revealing that Edwin and Rosa had already broken off their engagement before Edwin disappeared.

Mr Crisparkle dives into Cloisterham Weir and recovers Edwin Drood's monogrammed watch and shirt-pin; the evidence triggers Neville Landless's arrest and eventual forced expulsion from town under murder suspicion, while Jasper privately records a sworn oath to hunt down and destroy the murderer.

Mr Crisparkle confronts the bullying philanthropist Honeythunder then visits Neville's bleak London garret to offer support, calls briefly on Mr Grewgious who spots Jasper lurking and spying on the lodgings, and at midnight Neville meets his cheerful ex-naval neighbor Tartar on the staircase.

Mysterious stranger Dick Datchery arrives in Cloisterham, takes lodgings next to Jasper's gatehouse, flatters Mayor Sapsea into confirming suspicions about Edwin Drood's fate, and meets Durdles and Deputy while covertly positioning himself to investigate Jasper.

Jasper corners Rosa alone in the Nuns' House garden, confesses his mad obsessive love, and threatens to destroy Neville Landless with fabricated evidence unless she yields to him; Rosa, paralysed by terror, cannot flee and faints after he departs.
Terrified by Jasper's declaration of love and fearing his power over Neville, Rosa flees Cloisterham alone to London and takes refuge with her guardian Grewgious, who vows fierce protection.

Rosa Bud, sheltered at Mr Grewgious's lodgings, is joined by Mr Crisparkle; sailor Mr Tartar arrives and is recognised as Crisparkle's old school rescuer, then Grewgious devises a scheme to use Tartar's adjacent Staple Inn chambers as a covert rendezvous so Rosa can pass news of Jasper's threat to Helena Landless without Jasper's spies detecting the contact.
